additions.gap: Being-blamed walk-through: the pool has yatsuatari and yaomote ni tatsu but not hokosaki.

additions.kana: あたまごなしにおこる
additions.english: scold without hearing someone out
additions.why: 4 subtitle hits, drama rank #16225. The standard complaint about a parent or boss ('atamagonashi ni okoranaide yo').
additions.gap: Pushy-boss and nagging-parent walk-throughs: the pool has kaminari ga ochiru and kogoto-type entries but not atamagonashi.

selectorNotes:
I picked 263 ids, mostly by corpus count. After cuts, the list fills down to about 30 occurrences. Topics: relations 65, fortune 46, attention 40, effort 33, mood 30, talk 25, character 24. I recounted the doubtful phrase counts with my own script. Whether English has an equivalent played no part.

What I cut from the top of the counts:
- Count errors. sama ni naru (131) is almost all 〜様になる ("come to") and 王様になる, so the real idiom is close to zero. ippai yaru (100) includes 12 hits from 精一杯やる; I kept it. nayami no tane comes to 34 and toriko ni naru to 57 on recount; both still made the list.
- Literal twins: me o samasu (mostly "wake up", and the collocation list has me ga sameru), te o kiru, shiri o tataku, atama o sageru.
- English phrases translated into Japanese, whose counts are inflated by subtitles of foreign films: koi ni ochiru (247), me ni wa me o, kami nomi zo shiru. Plain alternative: suki ni naru.
- Lines from crime and medical dramas: kuchi o waru, te o yogosu, te o tsukusu, ki o shikkari motsu, nozomu tokoro da, kuchi o tsutsushimu, haji o shire, kataki o utsu, michizure ni suru, ki wa tashika, te o sashinoberu, zendai mimon, kimo ni meijiru.
- Single words. Plain alternatives for the notes: kanben shite, oteage, otagaisama, hatsumimi, zuboshi, dame moto, yatsuatari, inochibiroi, muda ashi, shiodoki, setogiwa, dotanba, shuraba, yatterarenai, oboetero.
- Literal four-character compounds: kibun tenkan, imi fumei, shinpai muyou, higai mousou, rikai funou.
- Plain literal phrases, or overlaps with the versatility list: baka iwanaide, katte ni shite (versatility has katte ni), jitsu o iu to (versatility has jitsu wa), atama o tsukau, chikara o ireru, kane ni naru, hoka o ataru, muri o iu, kokoro no junbi, me o mukeru, kao o awaseru, okure o toru, issho ni shinaide, ittai zentai.
- ome ni kakaru (128): this is the humble keigo verb for au, not an idiom.

Variants (one entry each):
- kentou mo tsukanai is the most-said form (113, against 26 for ga tsukanai and 33 for ga tsuku). souzou mo tsukanai goes in its note.
- aite ni suru also covers shinai; aite ni naru was dropped.
- tsujitsuma ga awanai, mizu no awa and saki wa nagai (over saki ga nagai) are the forms kept.
- me o hanasu covers me ga hanasenai. kokoro o ubawareru covers ubau. kari ga aru covers kashi ga aru.
- kata o tsukeru was dropped as a third "settle it" next to keri o tsukeru and kecchaku o tsukeru. me o somukeru and koke ni suru were dropped as lower-count synonyms.

Transitive/intransitive pairs with different meanings are kept as separate entries: te ni ireru / te ni hairu, kubi ni suru / kubi ni naru, ki ni kakeru / ki ni kakaru, hone ga oreru / hone o oru. A merge step may want to fold them together.

Exceptions below the cutoff, as corrections for casual talk the subtitles under-count: the brief's named examples kao ga hiroi (13), mimi ga itai (5), saba o yomu (0), saru mo ki kara ochiru (0) and isseki nichou (20), plus kuuki o yomu (13) and kiki ippatsu (22).

Two gaps follow from the counts:
- Sayings: most kotowaza count 0, so this list has very few (uwasa o sureba, saru mo ki kara ochiru, plus jigou jitoku and isseki nichou). The judgement lens should supply nana korobi ya oki, hana yori dango, nido aru koto wa sando aru, fukouchuu no saiwai and seken wa semai.
- The 20–29 band: ni no mai, fu ni ochinai, kokoro ga hiroi, nami ni noru, iyake ga sasu, me mo kurenai and the like are good idioms that only lost on count.

I picked 251 idioms through the everyday-Japan lens. By topic: relations 46, mood 38, effort 36, character 36, fortune 35, attention 31, talk 29. I scored about 680 strong candidates from 6 to 10 on how often they come up in daily talk. I kept every 8+ and filled the rest from the 7s, favouring talk, fortune and attention, which were thin. Every id was checked against candidates.tsv or this run's new-candidate list, and none is in the collocation list or the versatility list's four ki items.

Hardest calls:
(1) Lifted despite near-zero corpus counts: casual idioms the foreign-film subtitles miss, such as hatsumimi, hitokoto ooi, hito no koto ienai, hanashi o moru, kuwazu girai, oshi ni yowai, ichiyazuke, betsubara, nekojita, baka ni naranai, share ni naranai, moto o toru, nokorimono ni wa fuku ga aru, haadoru ga takai, kibun tenkan, chuuto hanpa, isshou kenmei and jibun katte. Spot-checks confirmed these count far below how often they're said; several score 0–7 (kuwazu girai, oshi ni yowai, share ni naranai, baka ni naranai, moto o toru: 0).
(2) Figurative compound words: I kept mikka bouzu, nekojita, betsubara, hatsumimi, ichiyazuke, dame moto, kuwazu girai, otagaisama, tanabota and imi fumei, because their meaning isn't the sum of their parts. I treated plain words as out (rakushou, kiraku, yabai, houkou onchi, kuro rekishi). If the merge counts all compound words as single words, those ten are the ones to drop.
(3) Dropped as too literal, close to collocations: tayori ni naru, jikkan ga waku, jitsu o iu to (jitsu wa is the everyday form), kao o awaseru, seki o hazusu and me o samasu (me ga sameru is already in the collocation list).
(4) Variants kept once: kentou mo tsukanai, tsujitsuma ga awanai, mizu no awa, okotoba ni amaete, mikake ni yoranai, aite ni suru and kubi ni naru (kubi ni suru dropped). te ni ireru / te ni hairu are both kept, since both are very common. kiri ga nai and kiri ga ii are separate idioms.
(5) Sayings: I took the ones people really say aloud. These are saru mo ki kara ochiru, isogaba maware, chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru, toudai moto kurashi, uso mo houben, ato no matsuri, fukouchuu no saiwai, nido aru koto wa sando aru, nokorimono ni wa fuku ga aru, i no naka no kawazu, hara hachibunme and yo no naka sonna ni amaku nai. Four-character phrases: ichigo ichie, ishin denshin, isseki nichou, jigou jitoku, yuujuu fudan, rinki ouhen, tantou chokunyuu, kyoumi shinshin, hanshin hangi and kiyou binbou. I left out bookish ones with high counts that mostly come from dramatic lines (jakuniku kyoushoku, zendai mimon, ichimou dajin, kimo ni meijiru).
(6) Near misses that are just as everyday as the bottom of my list: kigen o toru, kata o motsu, yori o modosu, myaku ga aru, sewa ga yakeru, shitta kotcha nai, nanisama no tsumori, ashidematoi, en o kiru, nakittsura ni hachi, sandome no shoujiki, juunin toiro, te o utsu, ii ki ni naru and kaya no soto.

Coverage lens: 265 ids, at the top of the 235-265 range because the pool has far more common idioms than slots. All ids exist (iu-made-mo-nai and 12 others come from this run's new candidates). Topic counts: mood 38, relations 40, talk 31, attention 36, character 38, effort 37, fortune 45. The list holds about 22 sayings (saru mo ki kara ochiru, nido aru koto wa sando aru, uwasa o sureba, mimi ni tako, toudai moto kurashi, hana yori dango, deru kui wa utareru, ishi no ue ni mo sannen...) and about 12 four-character phrases (jigou jitoku, isseki nichou, isshou kenmei, chuuto hanpa, ikken rakuchaku, kiki ippatsu, ishin denshin, tantou chokunyuu...). Japanese-only idioms come first: kuuki o yomu, mendou o miru, mushi no idokoro, goma/saba/neko. Calques of English idioms that are mostly heard in subtitles or songs are left out: koi ni ochiru, koi wa moumoku, toki wa kane nari, chinmoku wa kin, chi wa mizu yori mo koi.
Natural pairs kept: kubi ni naru/suru, te ni ireru/hairu, kuchi ga katai/karui, kari ga aru/kashi ga aru, kiri ga nai/ii, ki ga tsuyoi/yowai, hito ga ii/warui. Variants merged: kentou mo tsukanai (over ga tsuku/tsukanai), aite ni suru (over aite ni shinai), mizu no awa (over mizu no awa ni naru), tsujitsuma ga awanai (over au).
Hardest calls, all cut:
- High-count items left out as literal twins or overlaps: me o samasu (twin of the listed me ga sameru), ki ni kakeru (near the versatility list's ki ni suru), chikara o kasu (repeats te o kasu), atama o sageru / kao o miseru (mostly literal), jitsu o iu to (overlaps jitsu wa), iu koto o kiku / tayori ni naru / wake ga wakaranai (largely literal), katte ni shite (overlaps katte ni).
- Drama or narration lines the corpus over-counts: ki ga kuruu, sugata o kesu, inochi o kakeru, tada ja sumanai, sou wa ikanai, nanisama no tsumori, zettai zetsumei.
- Single words, cut under the single-word rule (plain alternatives): otagaisama, oteage, zuboshi, nekojita, betsubara, houkou onchi, kuwazu girai, ichiyazuke, jibun katte, hatsumimi, shuraba, dotanba. Literal compounds cut the same way: kibun tenkan, imi fumei, shinpai muyou.
- Exceptions kept: asameshi mae and mikka bouzu are two-word idioms; tanabota is short for a saying; dame moto is a fixed phrase.
- Common idioms that just missed the cut: kotoba no aya, kao ni doro o nuru / kao o tateru, te o hiku, te o tsukeru, hara o kukuru, tsuru no hitokoe, nagai me de miru, me ga mawaru, kokoro o komete, atama o hiyasu, happou bijin, rinki ouhen, junbi bantan, zen wa isoge, isogaba maware, furidashi ni modoru, ashita wa ashita no kaze ga fuku, tada yori takai mono wa nai, kurushii toki no kamidanomi, wakage no itari, muri mo nai, jikkan ga waku, kage ga usui.
boundaryNotes:
I settled the list at 260 idioms, the top of the 240–260 range, because the user asked for more. The pool easily supports that many. By topic: relations 41, fortune 40, talk 37, mood 36, attention 36, effort 36, character 34. Every id exists. 17 come from this run's new candidates and the rest from candidates.tsv. None is in the collocation list (I checked against its 208 list items) or among the versatility list's items.

HOW I BUILT IT: I kept all 218 items with 2+ votes except one, sama ni naru (see below), and added 43 items with 1 vote. I chose those 43 on how often people say them in everyday Japanese, weighted toward the topics that were thinnest (talk, character, mood).
- talk: hitokoto ooi, mi mo futa mo nai, tana ni ageru, kuchi o suppaku shite iu, guu no ne mo denai, hanashi o sorasu, men to mukatte, kotchi no serifu, aa ieba kou iu.
- character: mendoumi ga ii, akirame ga warui, yuujuu fudan, nita mono doushi, ne wa ii, oshi ni yowai, iji o haru, uri futatsu, juunin toiro, atama no kaiten ga hayai.
- mood: ki ga muku, gutto kuru, kata no chikara o nuku, mune ga ippai, yakimochi o yaku, hana ga takai, ki ga meiru, ni mo hodo ga aru, atama o hiyasu.
- attention: oku ga fukai, atama ga mawaranai, fu ni ochinai, yume ni mo omowanai, kao ni kaite aru.
- relations: ne ni motsu, okotoba ni amaete, kata o motsu, nanisama no tsumori, ashidematoi ni naru.
- fortune: naru you ni naru, moto o toru, hayai mono gachi.
- effort: yowane o haku, me ga mawaru.

Many of these count 0–20 in the subtitles: oshi ni yowai 0, hitokoto ooi 0, mi mo futa mo nai 2, moto o toru 3, mendoumi ga ii 4. They go in as corrections for casual speech, which the subtitles under-count.

The list is Japanese-first, as the user asked. Whether English has an equivalent played no part. I left out English sayings translated into Japanese, whose counts come from foreign-film subtitles: koi ni ochiru, me ni wa me o, kami nomi zo shiru, toki wa kane nari, chinmoku wa kin, chi wa mizu yori mo koi, koi wa moumoku, tonari no shibafu wa aoi. Plain alternative for koi ni ochiru: suki ni naru. Japanese idioms with no English counterpart stay in: kuuki o yomu, goma o suru, saba o yomu, neko o kaburu, mendoumi ga ii, ne ni motsu, okotoba ni amaete.

CUT FROM THE 2+ VOTE BASE: sama ni naru. I recounted it: 128 of its 131 hits are the suffix in phrases like 王様になる (become a king), so the idiom itself has about 3. On judgement it is only moderately common, so it lost its place to commoner items.

TOPIC MOVES: kuchi ga katai, kuchi ga karui, kuchi ga warui and kuchi dake go from character to talk. They are about what people say, and keeping the "kuchi" family together lets it be learned as a contrast group.

VARIANTS: one entry each.
- kentou mo tsukanai covers ga tsukanai and souzou mo tsukanai.
- aite ni suru covers aite ni shinai (aite ni naru dropped).
- kari ga aru covers kashi ga aru and kari o kaesu.
- me o hanasu covers me ga hanasenai.
- The forms kept are mizu no awa and tsujitsuma ga awanai.

Natural pairs are kept whole: kubi ni suru / naru, te ni ireru / hairu, kiri ga nai / ii, hito ga ii / warui, kuchi ga katai / karui, ki ga tsuyoi / yowai. The merge step can fold kubi ni suru / naru and te ni ireru / hairu if it wants.

SINGLE WORDS ARE OUT. Plain alternatives for the notes: nekojita, betsubara, hatsumimi, ichiyazuke, otagaisama, yatsuatari, shuraba, dotanba, zuboshi, oteage, and kuwazu girai (a borderline compound). As the selectors agreed, four exceptions in the base stay: tanabota (short for a saying), mikka bouzu, asameshi mae and dame moto.

Also cut, as literal or overlapping: katte ni shite (versatility has katte ni), jitsu o iu to (versatility has jitsu wa), atama o tsukau, kokoro no junbi, ki ni kakaru (too close to ki ni naru), chikara o kasu (repeats te o kasu), kao o miseru, baka iwanaide.

THE CAP, NOT THE POOL, LIMITS THE SIZE. About 60 more candidates are as common in everyday talk as the bottom of this list:
- relations: isshou no onegai, shitta kotcha nai, te o hiku, uma ga au, kaoiro o ukagau, atama ga agaranai, dotchi mo dotchi, te no hira o kaesu, sewa ga yakeru, myaku ga aru, takane no hana, en o kiru, nagai me de miru, honno kimochi.
- fortune: kekka oorai, jibara o kiru, urame ni deru, boketsu o horu, kami hitoe, fundari kettari, e ni kaita mochi, nakittsura ni hachi, umai hanashi, binbou kuji o hiku, aji o shimeru, furidashi ni modoru, saki o kosareru, yo no naka sonna ni amaku nai, nokorimono ni wa fuku ga aru.
- effort: te o tsukeru, hane o nobasu, te mo ashi mo denai, oyasui goyou, tsume ga amai, isogaba maware, nanigoto mo keiken, toshi ni wa katenai, hara hachibunme, keizoku wa chikara nari.
- attention: hanshin hangi, me ni ukabu, atama ga ippai, nodo made dekakatteru, sono te ni wa noranai, uwa no sora, mushi no shirase.
- mood: mushi no idokoro ga warui, kao kara hi ga deru, yake ni naru, kimari ga warui, iyake ga sasu, hoppe ga ochiru, mune ga itamu.
- character: nomikomi ga hayai, mie o haru, yuuzuu ga kikanai, kiyou binbou, kaeru no ko wa kaeru, i no naka no kawazu, sotsu ga nai.
- talk: kotoba no aya, komimi ni hasamu, hanashi no koshi o oru, ma ga motanai, jiga jisan, hara o watte hanasu.

Raising the target to about 320 would take all of them in without lowering the bar on commonness. The cut-verdict step should mark these as near misses rather than as not common enough.

entries.politeJa: いい加減にしてください
entries.use: Snapped at someone whose behaviour has gone on too long, usually as mou ii kagen ni shite!, and men often use the rough ii kagen ni shiro. It's a different thing from the adjective ii kagen na (sloppy, half-baked), as in ii kagen na hito.

example.romaji: nankai onaji koto iwaseru no? ii kagen ni shite.
example.ja: 何回同じこと言わせるの？いい加減にして。
example.english: How many times do I have to tell you? Enough already.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro ii kagen ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろいい加減にしてください。
examplePolite.english: That's quite enough now.

entries.notes: Rough: ii kagen ni shiro; short plain version: mou ii.

entries.english: no way, you've got to be kidding
entries.englishIdiom: you've got to be kidding me
entries.use: An indignant refusal or outburst at something outrageous: joudan ja nai yo! (rough male: joudan ja nee). Uso! reacts to surprising news, but joudan ja nai rejects what's being asked or done. It can also simply mean 'I'm not joking' (joudan ja nai, honki da yo); the indignant one is snapped out on its own.

example.romaji: mata zangyou? joudan ja nai yo.
example.ja: また残業？冗談じゃないよ。
example.english: Overtime again? You've got to be kidding.

examplePolite.romaji: mata zangyou desu ka? joudan ja nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: また残業ですか？冗談じゃないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Overtime again? You can't be serious.

entries.notes: Softer disbelief: joudan deshou? (you're joking, right?).

entries.use: The anger you feel inside about a person or thing. In casual speech ga drops (maji hara tatsu). Okoru is showing anger or telling someone off, and hara o tateru is the 'get angry over it' form, heard mostly in sonna koto de hara o tateru na (don't get angry over that).

example.romaji: nanka jibun ni hara tatsu.
example.ja: なんか自分に腹立つ。
example.english: I'm kind of mad at myself.

examplePolite.romaji: jibun ni hara ga tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 自分に腹が立ちました。
examplePolite.english: I was angry with myself.

entries.notes: Plain alternatives: mukatsuku, iraira suru.

entries.use: Mostly in the past (ki ga kawatta, I changed my mind) and in ki ga kawaranai uchi ni (before I change my mind). It's about plans and intentions; a changed opinion is kangae ga kawaru.

example.romaji: yappari ikanai. ki ga kawatta.
example.ja: やっぱり行かない。気が変わった。
example.english: Actually, I'm not going. I changed my mind.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ki ga kawatte, yappari ikanai koto ni shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、気が変わって、やっぱり行かないことにしました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I changed my mind and decided not to go after all.

entries.notes: ki ga kawattara oshiete = let me know if you change your mind.

entries.use: For anything eerie or unsettling, like a silent house, a stranger staring or a fixed smile. You'll mostly hear kimi warui (no ga). Kimochi warui is broader (gross, nauseating), while kimi ga warui only means eerie. Same sound as kimi ga warui 'it's your fault' (kimi = you), but the creepy one is said about a thing or person, not to someone.

example.romaji: nanka kono heya, kimi warui ne.
example.ja: なんかこの部屋、気味悪いね。
example.english: This room is kind of creepy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono heya, chotto kimi ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この部屋、ちょっと気味が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: This room is a bit creepy, isn't it?

entries.notes: Single-word alternative: bukimi (eerie).

entries.englishIdiom: get it out of one's system
entries.use: You'll hear ki ga sumu made (as much as you need), ki ga sumanai (won't rest until) and the exasperated kore de ki ga sunda? (happy now?). It's about getting an urge or grudge out, not being pleased with a result (manzoku).

example.romaji: ki ga sumu made naite ii yo.
example.ja: 気が済むまで泣いていいよ。
example.english: Cry as much as you need to.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga sumu made yatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 気が済むまでやってください。
examplePolite.english: Go ahead until you're satisfied.

entries.notes: Not sumu 'live'; plain word for satisfied: manzoku.

entries.use: A soft way to say you'd rather not, often to turn something down: chotto ki ga susumanai n da kedo. Almost always negative. Ki ga noranai is about your mood right now, while ki ga susumanai is reluctance about the thing itself.

example.romaji: ano nomikai, ki ga susumanai n da yo ne.
example.ja: あの飲み会、気が進まないんだよね。
example.english: I'm not too keen on that drinking party.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi wa chotto ki ga susumimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: その話はちょっと気が進みませんね。
examplePolite.english: I'm a little reluctant about that idea.

entries.notes: Blunter one-word alternative: iya.

entries.use: Mostly an outburst about what someone did: atama kita! or honto atama kuru. It's stronger and more sudden than hara ga tatsu. Not 'go to one's head' (getting conceited is choushi ni noru).

example.romaji: ano hito no taido, maji atama kuru.
example.ja: あの人の態度、マジ頭来る。
example.english: That person's attitude really pisses me off.

examplePolite.romaji: ano taido ni wa atama ni kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの態度には頭に来ました。
examplePolite.english: That attitude made me really angry.

entries.notes: Plain one-word alternative: mukatsuku.

entries.english: don't like, rubs you the wrong way
entries.use: Blunt dislike of a person or how they act, often vague with nanka or doumo: aitsu, nanka ki ni kuwanai. You'll also hear nani ga ki ni kuwanai n da? (what's your problem with it?). The softer form is ki ni iranai, and the plain word is kirai.

example.romaji: aitsu, nanka ki ni kuwanai na.
example.ja: あいつ、なんか気に食わないな。
example.english: Something about that guy rubs me the wrong way.

entries.notes: Softer: ki ni iranai; plain word: kirai.

entries.use: Said when pressure lifts or something feels less daunting, most often as ki ga raku ni naru: sou kiku to ki ga raku ni natta. Also for low pressure in general (hitori no hou ga ki ga raku). Kiraku (carefree) is a separate single word for a person or lifestyle.

example.romaji: sou itte kureru to ki ga raku ni naru.
example.ja: そう言ってくれると気が楽になる。
example.english: It's a relief to hear you say that.

examplePolite.romaji: sou itte itadakeru to ki ga raku ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: そう言っていただけると気が楽になります。
examplePolite.english: It puts my mind at ease to hear that.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: hotto suru (feel relieved); kiraku = carefree.

entries.english: get worked up, take it too seriously
entries.use: Mostly teasing someone who overreacts to a joke or a small thing (nani muki ni natteru no?), or owning up yourself (tsui muki ni natchatta). It isn't plain anger. It means taking something trivial too seriously.

example.romaji: sonna muki ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: そんなムキにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't get so worked up.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni muki ni naranaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなにムキにならないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no need to get so worked up.

entries.use: Said of whatever helps you forget a worry for a while: hataraiteru to ki ga magireru. Ki ga chiru is the opposite kind of distraction, an unwanted loss of focus, and ki ga hareru is when the gloom actually lifts.

example.romaji: hanashitara sukoshi ki ga magireta.
example.ja: 話したら少し気が紛れた。
example.english: Talking took my mind off it a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashitara sukoshi ki ga magiremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話したら少し気が紛れました。
examplePolite.english: Talking helped take my mind off things a little.

entries.notes: Transitive: ki o magirawasu (distract yourself on purpose).

entries.use: A sudden flash of anger that makes you act without thinking. You'll mostly hear it in the apology tsui katto natte (I just snapped). It's short-lived, unlike the lingering hara ga tatsu.

example.romaji: gomen, tsui katto natchatta.
example.ja: ごめん、ついカッとなっちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I just snapped.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tsui katto natte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ついカッとなってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I lost my temper.

entries.notes: Plain slang alternative: kireru (snap).

entries.use: Not having the mood or energy for something right now: kyou wa ki ga noranai. Ki ga susumanai is reluctance about the thing itself, and the positive ki ga noru is much rarer.

example.romaji: kyou wa nanka ki ga noranai.
example.ja: 今日はなんか気が乗らない。
example.english: I'm just not feeling it today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto ki ga noranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと気が乗らないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm just not in the mood today.

entries.notes: Also said: kinori shinai (from the noun kinori).

entries.english: it stings to hear (because it's true)
entries.use: Said ruefully, often with a wry laugh, when criticism or advice applies to you: sore wa mimi ga itai, or mimi ga itai hanashi. It can also mean a literal earache, so context decides.

example.romaji: sore iwareru to mimi ga itai na.
example.ja: それ言われると耳が痛いな。
example.english: Ouch, that hits close to home.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa mimi ga itai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは耳が痛いですね。
examplePolite.english: That one stings a bit.

entries.notes: Literal sense too: an earache.

entries.english: give me a break, spare me
entries.use: The groan when something is too much or happening again: mou kanben shite yo. Men also say kanben shite kure, or the rough kanben shiro. Kanben shite kudasai can be a real plea to be excused.

example.romaji: sono hanashi, mou kanben shite.
example.ja: その話、もう勘弁して。
example.english: Spare me that story already.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi wa mou kanben shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その話はもう勘弁してください。
examplePolite.english: Please, let's not go over that again.

entries.notes: Male casual: kanben shite kure; rough: kanben shiro.

entries.use: The sharp flash of irritation at a remark or tone, mostly in the past: ima no, chotto kachin to kita. It's milder than atama ni kuru, and it's set off by words rather than events.

example.romaji: ima no iikata, chotto kachin to kita.
example.ja: 今の言い方、ちょっとカチンときた。
example.english: The way you just said that kind of got to me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano iikata ni wa chotto kachin to kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの言い方にはちょっとカチンときました。
examplePolite.english: The way he put it rubbed me up the wrong way.

entries.english: dread it, not look forward to it
entries.use: What you say before a task or conversation you're dreading: ashita no mensetsu, ki ga omoi naa. It's the opposite of ki ga raku. Ki ga meiru is general gloom, not dread of something ahead.

example.romaji: ashita no kaigi, ki ga omoi naa.
example.ja: 明日の会議、気が重いなあ。
example.english: I'm dreading tomorrow's meeting.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no kaigi, chotto ki ga omoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の会議、ちょっと気が重いですね。
examplePolite.english: I'm not looking forward to tomorrow's meeting.

entries.notes: Single-word alternative: yuuutsu (gloomy, dreading it).

entries.kana: あたまがまっしろになる
entries.politeJa: 頭が真っ白になります
entries.use: How people describe freezing up from nerves or shock in an exam, speech or interview, nearly always in the past: kinchou shite atama ga masshiro ni natta. You'll also hear atama no naka ga masshiro.

example.romaji: kinchou shite atama masshiro ni natta.
example.ja: 緊張して頭真っ白になった。
example.english: I got so nervous my mind went blank.

examplePolite.romaji: kinchou shite atama ga masshiro ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 緊張して頭が真っ白になりました。
examplePolite.english: I was so nervous my mind went blank.

entries.english: your feelings show on your face
entries.literal: it comes out on the face
entries.use: Feelings leaking onto your face in spite of you. It's used about yourself (sugu kao ni deru taipu) and to tease others (kao ni deteru yo). Kao ni kaite aru is the stronger 'it's written all over your face'.

example.romaji: watashi, sugu kao ni deru n da yo ne.
example.ja: 私、すぐ顔に出るんだよね。
example.english: My face always gives me away.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, sugu kao ni deru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私、すぐ顔に出るんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Everything I feel shows on my face.

entries.notes: Keep it hidden: kao ni dasanai. Of drink: sugu kao ni deru (go red).

entries.english: gave me a scare, too nerve-racking
entries.englishIdiom: nearly give someone a heart attack
entries.use: A joking complaint after a scare, or about a nail-biting game or film: bikkuri shita, shinzou ni warui yo. It isn't a statement about health here.

example.romaji: kyuu ni dete konaide yo, shinzou ni warui.
example.ja: 急に出てこないでよ、心臓に悪い。
example.english: Don't jump out like that, you nearly gave me a heart attack.

examplePolite.romaji: mou, shinzou ni warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もう、心臓に悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Goodness, you nearly gave me a heart attack.

entries.literal: the load comes off the shoulders
entries.use: Said after handing over or finishing a duty you carried for a long time, nearly always in the past: yatto kata no ni ga orita. It's a bigger, longer-felt relief than ki ga raku ni naru.

example.romaji: hikitsugi mo owatte, yatto kata no ni ga orita.
example.ja: 引き継ぎも終わって、やっと肩の荷が下りた。
example.english: The handover's done, so that's finally a weight off my shoulders.

examplePolite.romaji: purojekuto ga owatte, kata no ni ga orimashita.
examplePolite.ja: プロジェクトが終わって、肩の荷が下りました。
examplePolite.english: With the project finished, it's a weight off my shoulders.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: hotto suru (feel relieved).

entries.use: Said when doing something feels like imposing or taking too much: zenbu ogotte morau no wa ki ga hikeru. Ki ga susumanai is plain reluctance, while ki ga hikeru is reluctance out of guilt or modesty.

example.romaji: zenbu ogotte morau no wa ki ga hikeru yo.
example.ja: 全部おごってもらうのは気が引けるよ。
example.english: I'd feel bad letting you pay for everything.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu gochisou ni naru no wa ki ga hikemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 全部ごちそうになるのは気が引けます。
examplePolite.english: I'd feel bad letting you treat me to all of it.

entries.notes: Plain alternatives: moushiwakenai, warui (I feel bad).

entries.ja: 穴があったら入りたい
entries.kana: あながあったらはいりたい
entries.politeJa: 穴があったら入りたいです
entries.english: so embarrassed I want to disappear
entries.literal: if there were a hole, I'd want to get in it
entries.englishIdiom: I wish the ground would swallow me up
entries.use: The stock reaction after embarrassing yourself, often half-joking: hazukashikute ana ga attara hairitai. It's a fixed form and only used for your own feelings.

example.romaji: hazukashikute, ana ga attara hairitai.
example.ja: 恥ずかしくて、穴があったら入りたい。
example.english: I'm so embarrassed I want to crawl into a hole.

examplePolite.romaji: hazukashikute, ana ga attara hairitai kimochi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 恥ずかしくて、穴があったら入りたい気持ちです。
examplePolite.english: I'm so embarrassed I could just disappear.

entries.notes: Partner phrase: kao kara hi ga deru (face burning with shame).

entries.use: Almost always the comfort line ki o otosanaide (don't let it get you down), or sonna ni ki o otosu na. To describe yourself feeling down, people say ochikomu instead.

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o otosanaide yo.
example.ja: そんなに気を落とさないでよ。
example.english: Don't let it get you down so much.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki o otosanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気を落とさないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't be too discouraged.

entries.notes: Plain word for being down: ochikomu.

entries.use: Mostly heard as ki ga muitara (whenever you feel like it), the no-pressure invitation, and as ki ga mukanai (don't feel like it). Also ki ga muita toki ni (when the mood takes me).

example.romaji: ki ga muitara asobi ni kite ne.
example.ja: 気が向いたら遊びに来てね。
example.english: Come over whenever you feel like it.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga muitara, itsu demo asobi ni kite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 気が向いたら、いつでも遊びに来てくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Drop by any time you feel like it.

entries.english: be moved, it really gets you
entries.use: A reaction to a moving scene, song, line or gesture, mostly in the past: ano serifu, gutto kita. It's also used for being charmed by someone: sono shigusa, gutto kuru. Pin to kuru is the same pattern, but it means something clicked in your understanding, not your feelings.

example.romaji: saigo no shiin, gutto kita.
example.ja: 最後のシーン、グッときた。
example.english: The last scene really got me.

examplePolite.romaji: saigo no supiichi, gutto kimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 最後のスピーチ、グッときましたね。
examplePolite.english: That last speech was really moving.

entries.notes: Plain word: kandou suru (be moved).

entries.literal: take the strength out of the shoulders
entries.use: Advice to someone nervous or trying too hard, mostly as kata no chikara nuite: it doesn't have to be perfect. Kata no chikara ga nuketeru also praises a relaxed, natural manner. The same words are the literal 'relax your shoulders' at a massage or in yoga.

example.romaji: kanpeki ni yaranakute ii n da kara, motto kata no chikara nuitara?
example.ja: 完璧にやらなくていいんだから、もっと肩の力抜いたら？
example.english: You don't have to be perfect, so why not stop trying so hard?

examplePolite.romaji: hajimete na n desu kara, kata no chikara o nuite daijoubu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 初めてなんですから、肩の力を抜いて大丈夫ですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's your first time, so there's no need to try so hard.

entries.notes: Opposite: kata ni chikara ga hairu (tense up); plain word: rirakkusu suru.

entries.use: Said at graduations, farewells, reunions and big thank-yous, usually when you're too moved to get the words out: mune ga ippai de nanimo ienai. Mune ga ippai de taberarenai is being too emotional to eat, and onaka ga ippai is a full stomach.

example.romaji: nanka mune ga ippai de, umaku kotoba ni dekinai.
example.ja: なんか胸がいっぱいで、うまく言葉にできない。
example.english: I'm so overwhelmed I can't find the words.

examplePolite.romaji: minasan no kotoba de mune ga ippai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 皆さんの言葉で胸がいっぱいです。
examplePolite.english: Your kind words fill my heart.

entries.literal: grill rice cakes (yaku is also the word for being jealous)
entries.use: Jealousy over someone's affection or attention, whether a partner, a child about a new sibling or a friend, with yakimochi yaiteru no? as the classic tease. Shitto suru is the heavier plain word, and urayamashii is envy of what someone has.

example.romaji: moshikashite, yakimochi yaiteru no?
example.ja: もしかして、やきもち焼いてるの？
example.english: Wait, are you jealous?

examplePolite.romaji: kare, sugu yakimochi o yaku n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼、すぐやきもちを焼くんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He gets jealous so easily.

entries.notes: Single words: yakimochi (jealousy), shitto; envious: urayamashii.

entries.use: Pride in a child, friend or team member whose success reflects on you: watashi mo hana ga takai yo. It can also literally mean a prominent nose. Don't mix it up with tengu ni naru (get conceited).

example.romaji: yuushou shita nante, watashi mo hana ga takai yo.
example.ja: 優勝したなんて、私も鼻が高いよ。
example.english: You won? I'm so proud of you.

examplePolite.romaji: buka ga homerarete, watashi mo hana ga takai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部下が褒められて、私も鼻が高いです。
examplePolite.english: My team member got praised, and I'm proud too.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: jiman (something to be proud of).

entries.use: Grumbling about grey days, bad news or a draining situation, usually naming the cause: ame bakkari de ki ga meiru. Ki ga omoi is dread of something ahead, and ochikomu is feeling down after a setback.

example.romaji: ame bakkari de ki ga meiru ne.
example.ja: 雨ばっかりで気が滅入るね。
example.english: All this rain really gets you down.

examplePolite.romaji: ame bakari de ki ga meirimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 雨ばかりで気が滅入りますね。
examplePolite.english: All this rain is so depressing.

entries.notes: Plain alternatives: ochikomu, yuuutsu.

entries.use: Attaches to a noun or adjective as an exasperated rebuke: baka ni mo hodo ga aru, shitsurei ni mo hodo ga aru, usually ending in yo or daro. It's also used playfully for praise: kawaii ni mo hodo ga aru (way too cute).

example.romaji: joudan ni mo hodo ga aru yo.
example.ja: 冗談にも程があるよ。
example.english: A joke's a joke, but that's too far.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan ni mo hodo ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談にも程がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: That's taking the joke much too far.

entries.notes: The frame varies: joudan, gaman, shitsurei, baka ni mo hodo ga aru.

entries.use: Said after an argument, either as an order (atama hiyashite koi, go cool your head) or about yourself (chotto atama hiyashite kuru). It can also literally mean cooling a feverish head.

example.romaji: chotto soto de atama hiyashite kuru.
example.ja: ちょっと外で頭冷やしてくる。
example.english: I'm going outside to cool off.

examplePolite.romaji: sukoshi atama o hiyashite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 少し頭を冷やしてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll go cool off for a bit.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: ochitsuku (calm down).

entries.literal: the mind looks about to go haywire
entries.use: Exaggerated frustration at noise, heat, waiting or a person: kono oto, ki ga kuruisou. Ki ga kurutta no? (have you lost your mind?) is the other form you'll hear. It's strong and TV tends to avoid it, so atama ga okashiku narisou is the softer everyday swap.

example.romaji: tonari no kouji, urusakute ki ga kuruisou.
example.ja: 隣の工事、うるさくて気が狂いそう。
example.english: The construction next door is so loud it's driving me crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: kou atsui to ki ga kuruisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: こう暑いと気が狂いそうですね。
examplePolite.english: This heat is enough to drive you mad.

entries.notes: Softer: atama ga okashiku narisou; ki ga kurutta no? = have you lost your mind?

entries.use: Ends an argument when you give up on persuading someone: mou ii, katte ni shite. The rough male katte ni shiro is the form films use most, and katte ni sureba (go ahead, then) is colder. Suki ni shite is the friendly 'do as you like'.

example.romaji: mou ii, katte ni shite.
example.ja: もういい、勝手にして。
example.english: Forget it. Do whatever you want.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. jaa, katte ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。じゃあ、勝手にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Fine. Suit yourself, then.

entries.notes: Rough: katte ni shiro; colder: katte ni sureba.

entries.kana: こころのじゅんびができる
entries.use: Mostly negative, when news or a big moment comes too fast: mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai. Kokoro no junbi wa ii? asks if someone is ready to hear something. Plain junbi ga dekiru is being ready in practical terms.

example.romaji: chotto matte, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、まだ心の準備ができてない。
example.english: Wait, I'm not ready for this yet.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni iwarete mo, kokoro no junbi ga dekite imasen.
examplePolite.ja: 急に言われても、心の準備ができていません。
examplePolite.english: You can't spring that on me. I'm not ready.

entries.notes: Also: kokoro no junbi o suru (brace yourself).

entries.use: The stock gloat at someone getting their comeuppance, often said jokingly among friends or muttered at a rival; zamaa! on its own is common too. Ii kimi is the quieter 'serves them right', said about someone rather than at them.

example.romaji: warikonda kuruma, tsukamatteru. zamaa miro.
example.ja: 割り込んだ車、捕まってる。ざまあみろ。
example.english: The car that cut in got pulled over. Serves him right.

entries.notes: Also: zamaa!, zama miro.

entries.use: Quiet satisfaction when someone who had it coming slips up, usually ii kimi da: said about someone more than to them, unlike zamaa miro. The kimi here is 'feeling' (as in kimi ga warui), not kimi 'you'.

example.romaji: itsumo ibatteta kara, ii kimi da yo.
example.ja: いつも威張ってたから、いい気味だよ。
example.english: He was always so full of himself, so serves him right.

entries.use: Doing something rash after a breakup, a failure or bad news because nothing seems to matter, mostly as the warning yake ni naranaide (don't do anything stupid). Tohou ni kureru is being stuck and helpless; yake ni naru is lashing out.

example.romaji: ikkai shippai shita kurai de, yake ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: 一回失敗したくらいで、ヤケにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't go off the rails just because you failed once.

examplePolite.romaji: yake ni naranaide, mou ichido kangaete mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ヤケにならないで、もう一度考えてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Don't do anything rash. Let's think it over again.

entries.notes: yakekuso (desperate, all-or-nothing); yakezake (drinking to drown it).

entries.literal: the mind clears up (like the sky)
entries.use: Said after venting, a good cry or a change of scene, usually in the past: hanashitara ki ga hareta. Ki ga magireru only takes your mind off a worry for a while; ki ga hareru means it actually lifts.

example.romaji: omoikkiri naitara, chotto ki ga hareta.
example.ja: 思いっきり泣いたら、ちょっと気が晴れた。
example.english: I had a good cry and feel a bit better.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi o kiite moratte, sukoshi ki ga haremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話を聞いてもらって、少し気が晴れました。
examplePolite.english: Having you listen made me feel a little better.

entries.notes: Single word for a pick-me-up: kibarashi.

entries.use: A complaint about a tense or controlling home, office or relationship: ano ie, iki ga tsumaru, often as iki ga tsumarisou. It can also be literal, not being able to breathe.

example.romaji: jikka ni zutto iru to, iki ga tsumaru.
example.ja: 実家にずっといると、息が詰まる。
example.english: Being at my parents' the whole time is suffocating.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kaigi, iki ga tsumarisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの会議、息が詰まりそうでした。
examplePolite.english: That meeting was suffocating.

entries.notes: Single word: ikigurushii (stifling).

entries.literal: night falls on the way ahead
entries.use: Being stranded with no idea what to do next, mostly in the past: saifu nakushite tohou ni kureta. It's helpless rather than upset; yake ni naru is lashing out in despair.

example.romaji: shuuden nogashite, tohou ni kureta.
example.ja: 終電逃して、途方に暮れた。
example.english: I missed the last train and had no idea what to do.

examplePolite.romaji: saifu o nakushite, tohou ni kurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 財布をなくして、途方に暮れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'd lost my wallet and was completely at a loss.

entries.notes: Not kureru 'give'; casual alternative: dou shiyou.

entries.english: get fed up, be sick of it
entries.literal: a feeling of dislike creeps in
entries.englishIdiom: be sick and tired of it
entries.use: Said about a job, a place, a routine or yourself, often as iyake ga sashite kita (I'm getting sick of it): shigoto ni iyake ga sasu. Akiru is being bored of something; iyake ga sasu is real dislike.

example.romaji: mainichi onaji koto no kurikaeshi de, iyake ga sashite kita.
example.ja: 毎日同じことの繰り返しで、嫌気がさしてきた。
example.english: Same thing every day. I'm getting sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, ima no shigoto ni iyake ga sashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、今の仕事に嫌気がさしています。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm fed up with my job.

entries.notes: Plain word: unzari suru (be fed up).

entries.english: beat yourself up over it, brood
entries.literal: fall ill in the mind over it
entries.use: Almost always the comfort line ki ni yamanaide (don't let it eat at you), to someone blaming themselves. Ki ni suru is everyday minding; ki ni yamu is brooding until it hurts.

example.romaji: anata no sei ja nai n da kara, ki ni yamanaide.
example.ja: あなたのせいじゃないんだから、気に病まないで。
example.english: It's not your fault, so don't beat yourself up over it.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki ni yamanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気に病まないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't let it weigh on you too much.

entries.notes: Everyday version: ki ni shinaide.

entries.use: The awkward feeling of being caught out or having to face someone after a slip, often in the past: uso ga barete kimari ga warukatta. Batsu ga warui means the same and is just as common; hazukashii is plain embarrassment.

example.romaji: uso ga barete, sugoku kimari ga warukatta.
example.ja: 嘘がバレて、すごくきまりが悪かった。
example.english: My lie got found out and I felt so sheepish.

examplePolite.romaji: onaji hito ni nido mo ayamaru no wa, kimari ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 同じ人に二度も謝るのは、きまりが悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: Apologising to the same person twice is a bit awkward.

entries.notes: Same meaning: batsu ga warui.

entries.english: it pains me, it breaks my heart
entries.use: Said about sad news, someone's hardship, or guilt at hurting someone: aa iu nyuusu o miru to mune ga itamu. Kokoro ga itamu means the same and is heard as often. Mune ga itai can also be literal chest pain.

example.romaji: aa iu nyuusu o miru to, mune ga itamu yo ne.
example.ja: ああいうニュースを見ると、胸が痛むよね。
example.english: News like that really breaks your heart.

examplePolite.romaji: hisaichi no eizou o miru to, mune ga itamimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 被災地の映像を見ると、胸が痛みます。
examplePolite.english: Seeing footage of the disaster area pains me.

entries.notes: Same meaning: kokoro ga itamu.

entries.literal: strike out at all eight sides
entries.use: Venting your bad mood on someone who had nothing to do with it, mostly in the complaint yatsuatari shinaide yo or the apology gomen, yatsuatari shita. The noun works alone too: sore, tada no yatsuatari ja n.

example.romaji: kocchi ni yatsuatari shinaide yo.
example.ja: こっちに八つ当たりしないでよ。
example.english: Don't take it out on me.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki wa yatsuatari shite, sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: さっきは八つ当たりして、すみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry for taking it out on you earlier.

entries.politeJa: 気持ちを切り替えます
entries.use: Said after a loss, a mistake or a bad day to move on to the next thing, often as kimochi kirikaete ikou. Shinki itten is a whole fresh start; kimochi o kirikaeru is a quick reset.

example.romaji: maketa no wa shouganai. kimochi kirikaete tsugi ikou.
example.ja: 負けたのはしょうがない。気持ち切り替えて次行こう。
example.english: Losing can't be helped. Shake it off and on to the next one.

examplePolite.romaji: kimochi o kirikaete, mata ganbarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 気持ちを切り替えて、また頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll put it behind me and keep at it.

entries.notes: Noun: kirikae (kirikae ga hayai = bounces back fast).

entries.polite: ki ga ki ja nai desu
entries.use: Anxious waiting, when you can't settle until you hear news, often in the past: kekka ga deru made ki ga ki ja nakatta. Munasawagi ga suru is a hunch something's wrong; ki ga ki ja nai is fretting over something you already know about.

example.romaji: kekka ga deru made, ki ga ki ja nakatta.
example.ja: 結果が出るまで、気が気じゃなかった。
example.english: I was a nervous wreck until the results came out.

examplePolite.romaji: renraku ga kuru made, ki ga ki ja nakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 連絡が来るまで、気が気じゃなかったです。
examplePolite.english: I was on pins and needles until I heard from you.

entries.notes: Slightly formal: ki ga ki de nai; plain word: shinpai.

entries.use: A rough reaction to a nasty story, an unfair ending or a bully: munakuso warui hanashi da na. The disgust is moral, not physical; kimochi warui is the physical 'gross'.

example.romaji: ano nyuusu, hontou ni munakuso warui.
example.ja: あのニュース、本当に胸くそ悪い。
example.english: That news is genuinely sickening.

entries.notes: Slang short form: munakuso.

entries.englishIdiom: have a bad feeling about this
entries.use: A sense that something is wrong before you know it, built like ki ga suru: nanka munasawagi ga suru. Often when someone can't be reached or something feels off.

example.romaji: nanka iya na munasawagi ga suru.
example.ja: なんか嫌な胸騒ぎがする。
example.english: I've got a bad feeling about this.

examplePolite.romaji: renraku ga tsukanakute, munasawagi ga shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 連絡がつかなくて、胸騒ぎがします。
examplePolite.english: I can't reach them, and I have a bad feeling.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: iya na yokan ga suru.

entries.literal: the heart's workings turn over once
entries.use: Said at a new job, a move, a new school year or New Year, usually leading the sentence: shinki itten, ganbarimasu. Kimochi o kirikaeru is a quick reset after a setback; shinki itten is a whole fresh start.

example.romaji: shinki itten, atarashii heya de ganbaru.
example.ja: 心機一転、新しい部屋で頑張る。
example.english: Fresh start: new place, new effort.

examplePolite.romaji: shinki itten, ganbarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 心機一転、頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'm making a fresh start.

entries.use: A comic reaction to something absurd or unexpected, almost always in the past: sono kotae ni me ga ten ni natta. It comes from manga, where shocked eyes shrink to dots. Atama ga masshiro ni naru is freezing up; me ga ten is staring in disbelief.

example.romaji: kare no kotae ni, me ga ten ni natta.
example.ja: 彼の答えに、目が点になった。
example.english: His answer left me speechless.

examplePolite.romaji: nedan o kiite, me ga ten ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 値段を聞いて、目が点になりました。
examplePolite.english: When I heard the price, I was dumbfounded.

entries.use: A blunt jab at someone acting crazy: atama okashii n ja nai? (ga is often dropped in speech), or about a third person, ano hito atama okashii yo. About yourself, atama okashiku narisou (I'm going to lose my mind) is a safe everyday complaint. Harsher than dou ka shiteru (you're not yourself).

example.romaji: atama okashii n ja nai?
example.ja: 頭おかしいんじゃない？
example.english: Are you out of your mind?

entries.notes: About yourself: atama okashiku narisou (I'm going to lose my mind); for just 'weird', hen.

entries.use: The standard complaint about someone who does what suits them and ignores everyone else: jibun katte da yo, jibun katte na hito. When apologising for your own request, people drop jibun: katte na onegai desu ga... Not the same as katte ni (without asking).

example.romaji: ano hito, honto jibun katte da yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと自分勝手だよね。
example.english: He's so selfish, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni jibun katte desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に自分勝手ですよね。
examplePolite.english: He really is selfish, isn't he?

entries.notes: Single words: wagamama (selfish, spoilt), jikochuu (self-centred, slang).

entries.use: Praise for a professional's skill, such as a doctor, cook, hairdresser or mechanic: ano isha, ude ii yo, or before a noun ude no ii shokunin. For everyday 'good at', jouzu is the plain word; ude ga ii judges someone's work as a pro.

example.romaji: ano biyoushi-san, ude ii yo.
example.ja: あの美容師さん、腕いいよ。
example.english: That hairdresser's really good.

examplePolite.romaji: ano biyoushi-san wa ude ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの美容師さんは腕がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That hairdresser is very skilled.

entries.notes: Ude ga agaru = get better at it; plain single word: jouzu (good at).

entries.english: thoughtful, attentive; (of a remark or gift) clever, apt
entries.use: Praise for someone who does what's needed before being asked, like refilling drinks: ki ga kiku ne! (kiku here means 'work well', not 'listen'). Before a noun it often describes words or gifts: ki no kiita koto ga ienai (I can't think of anything clever to say). To a boss, skip the praise and just say thank you.

example.romaji: ki ga kiku ne, arigatou!
example.ja: 気が利くね、ありがとう！
example.english: That's so thoughtful, thanks!

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga kikimasu ne, arigatou gozaimasu!
examplePolite.ja: 気が利きますね、ありがとうございます！
examplePolite.english: How thoughtful of you, thank you!

entries.notes: Opposite: ki ga kikanai (thoughtless).

entries.english: good-natured and trusting (often too much so)
entries.englishIdiom: too nice for one's own good
entries.use: Said with fondness and worry about someone who trusts everyone or can't refuse, often as hito ga yosugiru (way too nice). Not the same as ii hito (a nice person): the idiom hints at naive; hito ga warui is not its opposite but means sly.

example.romaji: mata hikiuketa no? hito ga yosugiru yo.
example.ja: また引き受けたの？人が良すぎるよ。
example.english: You said yes again? You're too nice.

examplePolite.romaji: mata hikiuketa n desu ka? hito ga yosugimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: また引き受けたんですか？人が良すぎますよ。
examplePolite.english: You took that on again? You're too kind for your own good.

entries.notes: Single word: ohitoyoshi (a soft touch, too trusting).

entries.use: Said when someone pays for everyone, tips big or hands out treats: kimae ii ne! or, as an adverb, kimae yoku ogotte kureta (treated us generously). It's about money and gifts (a kind person is yasashii), and politely it's said about a third party, not to a senior who is treating you.

example.romaji: kyou wa ogori? kimae ii ne!
example.ja: 今日はおごり？気前いいね！
example.english: Your treat today? That's generous!

examplePolite.romaji: buchou tte, kimae ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長って、気前がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is really generous, isn't he?

entries.notes: Opposite single word: kechi (stingy); casual: futoppara (open-handed).

entries.english: nasty, vicious, hard to deal with
entries.use: For something nasty or hard to deal with: a cruel prank, a scam, a cold that won't go away, or a person who hurts others on purpose (tachi warui yo, tachi no warui joudan); a mean drunk is nomu to tachi ga warui. Much stronger than hito ga warui, which is only playful slyness.

example.romaji: sono joudan, tachi warui yo.
example.ja: その冗談、たち悪いよ。
example.english: That joke's just nasty.

examplePolite.romaji: sono joudan wa tachi ga warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: その冗談はたちが悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's a rather nasty joke.

entries.notes: Also written タチが悪い or 質が悪い; tachi alone is someone's nature (sou iu tachi = that's how I am).

entries.use: A mild, often fond complaint when someone teased you, kept a secret or let you worry for nothing: mou, hito ga warui naa. Not the opposite of hito ga ii, and far lighter than tachi ga warui or seikaku ga warui (nasty).

example.romaji: nan da, shitteta no? hito ga warui naa.
example.ja: なんだ、知ってたの？人が悪いなあ。
example.english: You knew all along? That's sneaky.

examplePolite.romaji: shitteta n desu ka? hito ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 知ってたんですか？人が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: You knew? That's a bit sneaky of you.

entries.english: suit one's nature, be one's thing
entries.use: About jobs, lifestyles and ways of doing things, mostly in the negative: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai. It's for activities; food that suits you is kuchi ni au, and clicking with a person is ki ga au.

example.romaji: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai n da.
example.ja: 事務仕事は性に合わないんだ。
example.english: Office work just isn't me.

examplePolite.romaji: jimu shigoto wa shou ni awanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 事務仕事は性に合わないんです。
examplePolite.english: Office work doesn't really suit me.

entries.notes: Plainer: watashi ni wa muitenai (not suited to me), or nigate.

entries.english: be a poor judge (of people or things)
entries.use: Mostly about picking the wrong partner or hiring the wrong person (otoko o miru me ga nai), and as praise, miru me aru ne (you've got a good eye). Not me ga nai, which means you can't resist something.

example.romaji: watashi tte, otoko o miru me nai naa.
example.ja: 私って、男を見る目ないなあ。
example.english: I'm such a bad judge of men.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, otoko o miru me ga nai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私、男を見る目がないんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just a poor judge of men.

entries.notes: Praise form: miru me ga aru (have a good eye).

entries.use: About someone who speaks their mind and won't back down, often said of a woman or a child: kanojo, ki ga tsuyoi kara. Praise or complaint depending on tone; the opposite is ki ga yowai (timid).

example.romaji: uchi no imouto, ki ga tsuyoi n da yo.
example.ja: うちの妹、気が強いんだよ。
example.english: My little sister's pretty feisty.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no imouto wa ki ga tsuyoi n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの妹は気が強いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My younger sister is quite strong-willed.

entries.notes: Before a noun: ki no tsuyoi hito.

entries.use: About someone who smiles sweetly but is calculating underneath, often half-joking, about a coworker, a celebrity or a friend's new partner. It is fused from hara ga kuroi, which people hardly ever say in full. Neko o kaburu is only the sweet act, without the scheming.

example.romaji: ano ko, jitsu wa haraguroi yo.
example.ja: あの子、実は腹黒いよ。
example.english: She's actually a schemer.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, jitsu wa haraguroi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、実は腹黒いですよ。
examplePolite.english: She's actually quite calculating.

entries.notes: Noun: haraguro (a schemer).

entries.use: About someone who loses patience or temper fast, such as a parent, a boss or yourself. Not ki ga hayai, which means jumping the gun.

example.romaji: kare, chotto ki ga mijikai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ちょっと気が短いんだよね。
example.english: He's a bit short-tempered.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa chotto ki ga mijikai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はちょっと気が短いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: He can be a little short-tempered.

entries.notes: Single word people say more: tanki (short-tempered); plainest: sugu okoru (gets angry fast).

entries.use: The usual complaint about bosses, parents or teachers who won't accept new ideas: atama katai na, with ga dropped. It means closed-minded, not stupid (that's atama ga warui); it also teases someone stuck on a riddle or a new way of doing things: atama katai naa.

example.romaji: uchi no oya, atama katai n da yo.
example.ja: うちの親、頭固いんだよ。
example.english: My parents are so set in their ways.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no oya wa atama ga katai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの親は頭が固いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My parents are rather old-fashioned in their thinking.

entries.notes: Opposite: atama ga yawarakai (flexible); single word: ganko (stubborn).

entries.english: at your age (you should know better)
entries.use: A jab at a grown-up acting childish or silly: ii toshi shite nani yatteru no? Also said about yourself with embarrassment (ii toshi shite naichatta, I cried, at my age); the o of ii toshi o shite is usually dropped.

example.romaji: ii toshi shite, nani yatteru no?
example.ja: いい年して、何やってるの？
example.english: What are you doing, at your age?

entries.notes: Also written いい歳して; rougher: ii toshi koite.

entries.use: The modern catch-all for a condescending tone, from a boss, a know-it-all friend or a customer: nani sono ue kara mesen? Used as a noun (ue kara mesen da) or with de (ue kara mesen de iwanaide).

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo ue kara mesen da yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、いつも上から目線だよね。
example.english: He always talks down to people.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa itsumo ue kara mesen desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はいつも上から目線ですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's always rather condescending, isn't he?

entries.notes: Single word: erasou (bossy, full of yourself).

entries.politeJa: 見かけによらないです
entries.english: not what you'd guess from looks
entries.englishIdiom: you can't judge a book by its cover
entries.use: Said when someone turns out different from how they look, like a gentle-looking guy who boxes: hito wa mikake ni yoranai ne. Always negative; as an adverb, mikake ni yorazu (despite looks): mikake ni yorazu yoku taberu.

example.romaji: ano hito ga? mikake ni yoranai ne.
example.ja: あの人が？見かけによらないね。
example.english: Him? You'd never guess from looking.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito ga desu ka? hito wa mikake ni yoranai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人がですか？人は見かけによらないですね。
examplePolite.english: Him? You really can't judge people by their looks.

entries.notes: Full saying: hito wa mikake ni yoranai; plain word: igai (unexpected).

entries.english: savvy, gets things done the smart way
entries.use: About someone who gets results with little effort or knows how to stay on the boss's good side, said with admiration or a little envy. The opposite youryou ga warui (clumsy, inefficient) is often said about yourself; not the same as atama ga ii (smart).

example.romaji: kare, honto youryou ii yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ほんと要領いいよね。
example.english: He really knows how to work things.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa hontou ni youryou ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は本当に要領がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's really good at getting things done efficiently.

entries.notes: Opposite: youryou ga warui (inefficient, clumsy at it).

entries.use: About someone shy and timid who can't refuse or speak up, very often yourself: ki ga yowakute kotowarenai. The opposite of ki ga tsuyoi; oshi ni yowai is narrower (caves when pushed).

example.romaji: watashi, ki ga yowai kara kotowarenai n da.
example.ja: 私、気が弱いから断れないんだ。
example.english: I'm too timid to say no.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, ki ga yowai node kotowarenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私、気が弱いので断れないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm too timid to turn people down.

entries.notes: Close: ki ga chiisai (faint-hearted); single word: okubyou (cowardly).

entries.english: game for anything, fun to be around
entries.use: About a friend or coworker who joins in jokes, karaoke and last-minute plans: nori ii ne! The opposite nori ga warui (no fun, a wet blanket) is just as common; nori is the mood and rhythm of a group, written ノリ.

example.romaji: suzuki-san tte, nori ii yo ne.
example.ja: 鈴木さんって、ノリいいよね。
example.english: Suzuki's always up for anything.

examplePolite.romaji: suzuki-san tte, nori ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 鈴木さんって、ノリがいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Suzuki's always a good sport, isn't she?

entries.notes: Opposite: nori ga warui (no fun); nori de = on a whim.

entries.english: someone who gives up after a few days
entries.use: Self-mockery about diets, diaries, the gym and New Year resolutions that didn't last: mata mikka bouzu da. Mostly about yourself; mikka bouzu de owaru = it didn't stick.

example.romaji: daietto, mata mikka bouzu datta.
example.ja: ダイエット、また三日坊主だった。
example.english: My diet lasted three days again.

examplePolite.romaji: daietto wa mata mikka bouzu deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ダイエットはまた三日坊主でした。
examplePolite.english: My diet only lasted a few days again.

entries.notes: Plain way: sugu yamechau (I always quit right away).

entries.use: Praise for someone important who still treats everyone modestly and politely: shachou na noni koshi ga hikui. The opposite attitude is erasou or ue kara mesen; not koshi ga itai (my back hurts).

example.romaji: ano hito, shachou na noni koshi hikui yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、社長なのに腰低いよね。
example.english: He's the boss, yet he's so humble.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa shachou na noni koshi ga hikui desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は社長なのに腰が低いですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's the company president, yet so modest.

entries.notes: Single word: kenkyo (modest).

entries.english: put on a sweet, innocent act
entries.use: About someone acting sweet, shy or well-behaved to hide their real self, in front of a boss, a date or the in-laws; usually neko kabutteru with o dropped. Close to haraguroi, but this is only the act, not scheming.

example.romaji: ano ko, kachou no mae da to neko kabutteru yo.
example.ja: あの子、課長の前だと猫かぶってるよ。
example.english: She acts all sweet in front of the boss.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko, kachou no mae da to neko kabuttemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの子、課長の前だと猫かぶってますよ。
examplePolite.english: She puts on an innocent act in front of the manager.

entries.notes: Noun: nekokaburi (someone putting on an act).

entries.english: caring, good at looking after people
entries.use: Top praise for a senpai, boss, older sibling or teacher who takes care of juniors and newcomers: senpai, mendoumi ii yo ne. It names the trait; looking after someone in the moment is mendou o miru.

example.romaji: tanaka-senpai, honto mendoumi ii yo ne.
example.ja: 田中先輩、ほんと面倒見いいよね。
example.english: Tanaka's such a caring senpai.

examplePolite.romaji: tanaka-senpai wa hontou ni mendoumi ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 田中先輩は本当に面倒見がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka really looks after us, doesn't she?

entries.notes: The act itself: mendou o miru (look after someone).

entries.english: won't give up, can't let go
entries.use: About someone who keeps trying or can't move on, like an ex who keeps texting or a rival who won't concede; also about yourself, half proud: akirame ga warui kara. Less often the opposite, akirame ga ii / hayai (lets go easily). Oujougiwa ga warui is narrower: refusing to admit you've lost.

example.romaji: watashi, akirame ga warui kara ne.
example.ja: 私、諦めが悪いからね。
example.english: I don't give up that easily.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, akirame ga warui n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私、諦めが悪いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not one to give up easily.

entries.notes: Verb: akirameru (give up).

entries.english: indecisive, can't make up one's mind
entries.use: About someone who takes forever to choose, at a menu, between two partners or at work, very often yourself: yuujuu fudan de kimerarenai. One of the four-character phrases people really say aloud.

example.romaji: watashi, yuujuu fudan da kara kimerarenai.
example.ja: 私、優柔不断だから決められない。
example.english: I'm so indecisive, I can't choose.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, yuujuu fudan na node kimerarenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私、優柔不断なので決められないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm indecisive, so I can't make up my mind.

entries.notes: Plain way: nakanaka kimerarenai (I just can't decide).

entries.use: Teasing two friends or a couple who share the same quirks or faults: futari tte nita mono doushi da yo ne. About character and habits, not looks; looking alike is uri futatsu or sokkuri.

example.romaji: futari tte, nita mono doushi da yo ne.
example.ja: 二人って、似た者同士だよね。
example.english: You two are two of a kind.

examplePolite.romaji: ofutari wa nita mono doushi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お二人は似た者同士ですね。
examplePolite.english: You two are very much alike.

entries.notes: Related saying, said aloud too: rui wa tomo o yobu (birds of a feather), for a group drawn together; clipped to ruitomo.

entries.englishIdiom: one's heart is in the right place
entries.use: Defending someone who seems rude, scary or lazy, nearly always as ne wa ii yatsu or ne wa ii hito. Ne (root) is someone's true nature: ne wa majime (serious at heart), ne wa yasashii (kind at heart).

example.romaji: kuchi warui kedo, ne wa ii yatsu da yo.
example.ja: 口悪いけど、根はいいやつだよ。
example.english: He's mouthy, but he's a good guy at heart.

examplePolite.romaji: kuchi wa warui desu kedo, ne wa ii hito desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 口は悪いですけど、根はいい人ですよ。
examplePolite.english: He can be blunt, but he's a good person at heart.

entries.notes: Same pattern: ne wa majime, ne wa yasashii.

entries.use: About someone who gives in when asked insistently, by a salesperson, a persistent admirer or a friend begging a favour; constant in dating talk (kanojo, oshi ni yowai kara). Narrower than ki ga yowai (timid in general).

example.romaji: watashi, oshi ni yowai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 私、押しに弱いんだよね。
example.english: I always cave if someone pushes.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi, oshi ni yowai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私、押しに弱いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I tend to give in when people push.

entries.notes: Opposite: oshi ga tsuyoi (pushy).

entries.use: Said to someone refusing help or refusing to apologise out of pride (iji haranaide yo), or about yourself after a fight: tsui iji hatchatta. Atama ga katai is about rigid ideas; this is about pride. Not mie o haru (show off).

example.romaji: tsui iji hatchatta.
example.ja: つい意地張っちゃった。
example.english: I let my pride get in the way.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui iji o hatte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい意地を張ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ended up being stubborn about it.

entries.notes: Noun: ijippari (a stubborn person).

entries.use: Said about a child and parent, siblings or a celebrity lookalike: okaasan to uri futatsu da ne. Only about looks; the everyday single word sokkuri is said more often, and nita mono doushi is about personality.

example.romaji: okaasan to uri futatsu da ne!
example.ja: お母さんと瓜二つだね！
example.english: You're the spitting image of your mum!

examplePolite.romaji: okaasan to uri futatsu desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: お母さんと瓜二つですね！
examplePolite.english: You look exactly like your mother!

entries.notes: Single word: sokkuri (just like), far more common in speech.

entries.use: Ends a debate about taste, opinions or how to do something: konomi wa juunin toiro da kara ne. It sounds a little proverbial; hito sorezore is the plain everyday way.

example.romaji: konomi wa juunin toiro da kara ne.
example.ja: 好みは十人十色だからね。
example.english: Everyone's got their own taste.

examplePolite.romaji: konomi wa juunin toiro desu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: 好みは十人十色ですからね。
examplePolite.english: Tastes differ from person to person.

entries.notes: Plain everyday way: hito sorezore (it depends on the person).

entries.polite: atama no kaiten ga hayai desu
entries.kana: あたまのかいてんがはやい
entries.use: Praise for someone who thinks and answers fast, like a sharp debater or a friend with quick comebacks: atama no kaiten hayai ne. Different from atama ga ii (smart, does well at school); the opposite is atama no kaiten ga osoi.

example.romaji: kare, atama no kaiten hayai yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、頭の回転速いよね。
example.english: He's a really quick thinker.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa atama no kaiten ga hayai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は頭の回転が速いですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's very quick-witted, isn't he?

entries.notes: Close: atama ga kireru (sharp, brilliant) and nomikomi ga hayai (a quick learner).

entries.use: About someone who promises or boasts and never follows through, like a friend who always says he'll quit smoking: aitsu, kuchi dake da kara. Kuchi bakkari means the same, and kuchi dake ja nai (it's not just talk) defends someone.

example.romaji: aitsu, kuchi dake da kara.
example.ja: あいつ、口だけだから。
example.english: He's all talk.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, kuchi dake desu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、口だけですからね。
examplePolite.english: He's all talk, you know.

entries.notes: Also kuchi bakkari, kuchisaki dake.

entries.use: Reassurance when a secret is shared: kare wa kuchi ga katai kara daijoubu, or about yourself, watashi, kuchi katai kara. The pair to kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

example.romaji: daijoubu, watashi, kuchi katai kara.
example.ja: 大丈夫、私、口堅いから。
example.english: Don't worry, I can keep a secret.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, watashi, kuchi wa katai desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、私、口は堅いですから。
examplePolite.english: Don't worry, I won't tell anyone.

entries.notes: Opposite: kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

entries.use: A warning not to tell someone something, or a jab after a secret got out: ano ko, kuchi karui kara. The pair to kuchi ga katai; not kuchi ga warui (sharp-tongued).

example.romaji: ano ko, kuchi karui kara iwanai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: あの子、口軽いから言わない方がいいよ。
example.english: Better not tell her, she can't keep a secret.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa kuchi ga karui node, iwanai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は口が軽いので、言わない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: She can't keep a secret, so better not tell her.

entries.notes: Opposite: kuchi ga katai (can keep a secret).

entries.english: sharp-tongued, blunt to the point of rude
entries.use: About how someone talks, not who they are, often defended in the same breath: kuchi wa warui kedo ne wa ii. Also an apology for your own bluntness: kuchi ga warukute gomen. Not kuchi ga karui (can't keep a secret).

example.romaji: gomen, kuchi ga warukute.
example.ja: ごめん、口が悪くて。
example.english: Sorry, I've got a sharp tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kuchi ga warukute.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、口が悪くて。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I can be blunt.

entries.english: a smooth talker, good at flattery
entries.use: A warning about a salesperson or charmer who talks people round (kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete), or a laughing reply to a compliment: mata, kuchi ga umai n da kara. Not umai alone (tasty, good at).

example.romaji: kare, kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete.
example.ja: 彼、口がうまいから気をつけて。
example.english: He's a smooth talker, so watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kuchi ga umai node, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は口がうまいので、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: He's a smooth talker, so do be careful.

entries.notes: Also kuchi ga jouzu; written 口が上手い too.

entries.use: The host's line when serving food, politely with o: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen kedo; and the guest's soft way to decline: chotto kuchi ni awanakute. Shou ni au is for activities, not food.

example.romaji: kore, kuchi ni au ka wakannai kedo, tabete mite.
example.ja: これ、口に合うかわかんないけど、食べてみて。
example.english: Not sure you'll like it, but give it a try.

examplePolite.romaji: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen ga, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お口に合うかわかりませんが、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not sure it'll be to your taste, but please have some.

entries.notes: Polite with o: okuchi ni au; plain way: suki ka wakannai (not sure you'll like it).

entries.english: a loner who goes their own way
entries.use: About a coworker or classmate who works alone and keeps out of groups, said neutrally or with a little admiration: kare wa ippiki ookami da kara. Often softened with tte kanji (kind of a lone wolf).

example.romaji: kare tte, ippiki ookami tte kanji da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼って、一匹狼って感じだよね。
example.english: He's kind of a lone wolf, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa ippiki ookami tte kanji desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は一匹狼って感じですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's a bit of a lone wolf, isn't he?

entries.notes: Plain way: hitori de iru no ga suki (likes being on their own).

entries.use: A complaint about a parent, partner or boss who won't hear any advice or objection, usually with o dropped: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai. Always negative; it's refusing to listen, not being unable to hear (kikoenai).

example.romaji: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai n da yo.
example.ja: 何言っても聞く耳持たないんだよ。
example.english: Whatever I say, he just won't listen.

examplePolite.romaji: nani o itte mo kiku mimi o motanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 何を言っても聞く耳を持たないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: No matter what I say, he won't listen.

entries.notes: Plain way: zenzen kiite kurenai (just won't listen to me).

entries.use: Grudging admiration for someone who covers every angle or grabs every advantage, like a coworker who has already booked the good meeting room: nukeme nai na, with ga dropped. Sharper than youryou ga ii, and it can hint at calculating.

example.romaji: ano hito, honto nukeme nai yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと抜け目ないよね。
example.english: She never misses a trick.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni nukeme ga nai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に抜け目がないですよね。
examplePolite.english: She really never misses a chance, does she?

entries.notes: Adverb: nukeme naku (shrewdly, without missing a thing).

entries.use: Praise, often grudging, for a sharp strategist, lawyer, boss or rival; before a noun, atama no kireru hito. Not kireru alone, which means snap or lose it (ano hito sugu kireru).

example.romaji: ano bengoshi, atama kireru yo.
example.ja: あの弁護士、頭切れるよ。
example.english: That lawyer's really sharp.

examplePolite.romaji: ano bengoshi-san wa atama ga kiremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの弁護士さんは頭が切れますよ。
examplePolite.english: That lawyer is very sharp.

entries.notes: Plain: atama ga ii (smart); kireru alone = snap, lose your temper.

entries.use: Praise for someone who forgives mistakes or lets things go, like a partner who laughs off a forgotten anniversary: kokoro hiroi ne. The opposite kokoro ga semai (petty) is a common jab.

example.romaji: sore de yurushita no? kokoro hiroi ne.
example.ja: それで許したの？心広いね。
example.english: You forgave him for that? You're so big-hearted.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de yurushita n desu ka? kokoro ga hiroi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それで許したんですか？心が広いですね。
examplePolite.english: You forgave him for that? That's big of you.

entries.notes: Opposite: kokoro ga semai (petty, narrow-minded).

entries.use: About someone who changes completely when drunk, angry or behind the wheel (nomu to hito ga kawaru), or someone who has changed for good or bad: hito ga kawatta mitai. Mostly with -to or in the past.

example.romaji: kare, osake nomu to hito ga kawaru n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お酒飲むと人が変わるんだよ。
example.english: He turns into a different person when he drinks.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa osake o nomu to hito ga kawaru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお酒を飲むと人が変わるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He becomes a different person when he drinks.

entries.notes: Like a different person: hito ga kawatta you ni / mitai ni.

entries.use: The staple complaint about a boss, clerk or system that won't make an exception: yuuzuu kikanai na. Mostly negative; yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible) is praise. Atama ga katai is about ideas; this is about rules and requests.

example.romaji: uchi no buchou, honto yuuzuu kikanai n da yo.
example.ja: うちの部長、ほんと融通利かないんだよ。
example.english: My boss just won't bend the rules.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no buchou wa hontou ni yuuzuu ga kikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの部長は本当に融通が利かないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Our manager really won't make any exceptions.

entries.notes: Opposite: yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible, accommodating).

entries.english: jumping the gun, getting ahead of oneself
entries.use: A light tease for someone planning or celebrating too early, like booking the honeymoon before the proposal: mada ki ga hayai yo. Not ki ga mijikai (short-tempered).

example.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi? ki ga hayai ne.
example.ja: もうクリスマスの準備？気が早いね。
example.english: Getting ready for Christmas already? Bit early, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi desu ka? ki ga hayai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もうクリスマスの準備ですか？気が早いですね。
examplePolite.english: Preparing for Christmas already? You're getting ahead of yourself.

entries.notes: Also about yourself: chotto ki ga hayai kedo (it's early, but...).

entries.kana: おうじょうぎわがわるい
entries.literal: the moment of dying is bad
entries.use: A tease for someone who keeps arguing a lost point, won't pay up on a bet or makes excuses when caught: mou, oujougiwa warui na. Narrower than akirame ga warui, which can be praise.

example.romaji: mou maketan da kara, oujougiwa warui yo.
example.ja: もう負けたんだから、往生際悪いよ。
example.english: You've already lost, just accept it.

examplePolite.romaji: mou maketan desu kara, oujougiwa ga warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もう負けたんですから、往生際が悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: You've already lost, so stop fighting it.

entries.notes: Oujou = passing away; people hear oujougiwa as one word.

entries.use: About spending or pretending beyond your means to look good, like a pricey date or a brand bag on credit: mie hatte takai mise ni shichatta, with o dropped. Iji o haru is pride that won't back down, not showing off.

example.romaji: mie hatte takai mise yoyaku shichatta.
example.ja: 見栄張って高い店予約しちゃった。
example.english: I showed off and booked a pricey place.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui mie o hatte, takai mise o yoyaku shichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい見栄を張って、高い店を予約しちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I wanted to look good, so I booked a pricey restaurant.

entries.notes: Noun: mieppari (a show-off, someone vain).

entries.use: Praise for a new hire, student or kid who picks up a task fast: nomikomi hayai ne! The opposite nomikomi ga osoi (slow to pick things up) is often said of yourself. It's about learning; atama no kaiten ga hayai is about thinking on your feet.

example.romaji: nomikomi hayai ne! mou oboeta no?
example.ja: 飲み込み早いね！もう覚えたの？
example.english: You're a quick learner! You've got it already?

examplePolite.romaji: nomikomi ga hayai desu ne! mou oboeta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 飲み込みが早いですね！もう覚えたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You pick things up fast! You've learned it already?

entries.notes: Opposite: nomikomi ga osoi (slow to pick things up).

entries.use: A jab at someone, often a man, who sulks or gets angry over something trivial, like splitting a bill to the yen: utsuwa chiisai naa. The opposite utsuwa ga ookii praises a big-hearted leader; kokoro ga semai is close.

example.romaji: sonna koto de okoru nante, utsuwa chiisai naa.
example.ja: そんなことで怒るなんて、器小さいなあ。
example.english: Getting angry over that? How petty.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto de okoru nante, utsuwa ga chiisai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことで怒るなんて、器が小さいですね。
examplePolite.english: Getting angry over something like that is rather petty.

entries.notes: Opposite: utsuwa ga ookii (big-hearted, a natural leader).

entries.english: help out, give someone a hand
entries.use: The everyday ask or offer for a quick bit of hands-on help, usually chotto te kashite (give me a hand). chikara o kasu is backing for something bigger, and chikara ni naru is any support ('anything I can do'). Also an accomplice's help: hanzai ni te o kasu (help with a crime).

example.romaji: kore omoi kara, chotto te kashite.
example.ja: これ重いから、ちょっと手貸して。
example.english: This is heavy, give me a hand.

examplePolite.romaji: kore omoi node, chotto te o kashite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ重いので、ちょっと手を貸してもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: This is heavy, could you give me a hand?
