examplePolite.english: Please don't criticise my cooking.

entries.polite: ne mo ha mo nai desu
entries.use: Almost always before uwasa (rumour): ne mo ha mo nai uwasa (a groundless rumour). It's the fixed way to deny gossip about yourself or someone else; makka na uso is a flat lie, this is talk with nothing behind it.

example.romaji: sonna no, ne mo ha mo nai uwasa da yo.
example.ja: そんなの、根も葉もない噂だよ。
example.english: That's a totally groundless rumour.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ne mo ha mo nai uwasa desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは根も葉もない噂ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That rumour has no basis at all.

entries.ja: 口が裂けても言えない
entries.kana: くちがさけてもいえない
entries.politeJa: 口が裂けても言えません
entries.english: would never say it, not in a million years
entries.literal: can't say it even if my mouth tears open
entries.use: An emphatic refusal to say something, either a secret or something too embarrassing or proud to admit: kare ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo ienai (I could never tell him). Also kuchi ga sakete mo iwanai (I'll never tell).

example.romaji: honnin ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo ienai yo.
example.ja: 本人には口が裂けても言えないよ。
example.english: I'd never tell her that, not in a million years.

examplePolite.romaji: honnin ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo iemasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 本人には口が裂けても言えませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I could never say that to her, not ever.

entries.use: A slightly more formal kuchi ni dasu, used for words and names: sono namae, nido to kuchi ni suru na (never mention that name again). It also means eating or drinking: kyou wa mada nani mo kuchi ni shite nai (I haven't had a thing today). It's the mouth twin of mimi ni suru.

example.romaji: sore, ano hito no mae de kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: それ、あの人の前で口にしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Better not mention that in front of him.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ano kata no mae de kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それはあの方の前で口にしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to mention that in front of her.

entries.use: Shock at news or at something someone said, almost always in the past: kiita toki, mimi o utagatta yo (when I heard, I couldn't believe my ears). Also jibun no mimi o utagau.

example.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, mimi o utagatta yo.
example.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、耳を疑ったよ。
example.english: When I heard he was getting married, I couldn't believe my ears.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, mimi o utagaimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、耳を疑いましたよ。
examplePolite.english: When I heard he was getting married, I couldn't believe my ears.

entries.english: as hard as one can, with all one's might
entries.literal: a whole life, staking one's life
entries.use: The everyday way to say someone tried their hardest, mostly as an adverb before a verb: isshou kenmei ganbatta, isshou kenmei hataraite iru. It also works before nouns (isshou kenmei na hito) and describes the manner of effort, where ganbaru is the effort itself.

example.romaji: isshou kenmei ganbatta n da kedo na
example.ja: 一生懸命頑張ったんだけどな
example.english: I really did try my hardest, though.

examplePolite.romaji: isshou kenmei ganbatta n desu kedo ne
examplePolite.ja: 一生懸命頑張ったんですけどね
examplePolite.english: I really did try my hardest, though.

entries.notes: Older spelling 一所懸命 (issho kenmei, literally staking one's life on one plot of land) means the same.

entries.use: Everyday exaggeration for a huge amount, most often of work or things to do: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru. Yama hodo also goes before other verbs (yama hodo katta, iitai koto ga yama hodo aru).

example.romaji: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru n da yo
example.ja: やることが山ほどあるんだよ
example.english: I've got tons to do.

examplePolite.romaji: yaru koto ga yama hodo aru n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: やることが山ほどあるんですよ
examplePolite.english: I've got tons to do.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: takusan aru, ippai aru.

entries.english: in no time, over in a flash
entries.literal: the time it takes to say 'ah'
entries.englishIdiom: in the blink of an eye
entries.use: Said all the time about time flying (atto iu ma datta ne) and about things happening fast (atto iu ma ni owatta). Takes ni before a verb and da / datta at the end; iu is pronounced yuu.

example.romaji: ichinen tte atto iu ma da ne
example.ja: 一年ってあっという間だね
example.english: A year goes by in no time, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinen tte atto iu ma desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 一年ってあっという間ですね
examplePolite.english: A year goes by in no time, doesn't it.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: sugu (right away).

entries.use: Criticises half-finished work or half-hearted commitment (chuuto hanpa ni yaru nara yamero, chuuto hanpa na kimochi), and describes anything stuck awkwardly in between (chuuto hanpa na jikan, an awkward time). Na before nouns, ni before verbs.

example.romaji: nanka chuuto hanpa ni owatchatta
example.ja: なんか中途半端に終わっちゃった
example.english: It kind of ended up half-finished.

examplePolite.romaji: nandaka chuuto hanpa ni owatte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: なんだか中途半端に終わってしまいました
examplePolite.english: It kind of ended up half-finished.

entries.notes: Slang hanpa nai (from hanpa ja nai) means insane, incredible.

entries.english: pick up (a skill or habit); wear
entries.use: How people talk about gaining skills, knowledge and habits through practice: eigo o mi ni tsuketai, shuukan o mi ni tsukeru; the intransitive mi ni tsuku (it sticks) is just as common. With clothes and accessories it means wear or carry on you, a more formal ring than kiru.

example.romaji: shigoto shinagara mi ni tsuketa n da
example.ja: 仕事しながら身につけたんだ
example.english: I picked it up on the job.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto shinagara mi ni tsuketa n desu
examplePolite.ja: 仕事しながら身につけたんです
examplePolite.english: I picked it up on the job.

entries.notes: Intransitive: renshuu shinai to mi ni tsukanai (it won't stick without practice).

entries.use: Mostly in the negative about work you haven't started, as X ni te o tsukeru: mada zenzen te o tsukete nai, doko kara te o tsukereba ii ka wakaranai (don't know where to start). It also means leaving food or money untouched (chokin ni wa te o tsukenai); in speech the o often drops.

example.romaji: repooto, mada zenzen te tsuketenai
example.ja: レポート、まだ全然手つけてない
example.english: I haven't even started on the report.

examplePolite.romaji: repooto ni wa mada zenzen te o tsukete inai n desu
examplePolite.ja: レポートにはまだ全然手をつけていないんです
examplePolite.english: I haven't even started on the report.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: hajimeru (start).

entries.use: Said when a problem has beaten you and there's nothing more you can do, usually as mou oteage (da): a broken computer, homework, a stubborn person, a hopeless situation. It is giving up on solving something, not quitting a task.

example.romaji: kore wa mou oteage da yo
example.ja: これはもうお手上げだよ
example.english: I give up on this one.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa mou oteage desu
examplePolite.ja: これはもうお手上げです
examplePolite.english: I give up on this one.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: mou muri.

entries.english: more than one can handle, out of control
entries.literal: can't bear it in one's hands
entries.use: Said of a kid, pet, person or problem beyond your control or skill: ano ko wa te ni oenai, watashi no te ni wa oenai. Only ever said in the negative (te ni ou is not used); not ha ga tatanai, which is being outmatched by a strong opponent or a hard problem.

example.romaji: uchi no inu, mou te ni oenai yo
example.ja: うちの犬、もう手に負えないよ
example.english: Our dog is out of control now.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no inu, mou te ni oenai n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: うちの犬、もう手に負えないんですよ
examplePolite.english: Our dog is out of control now.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: muri (mou muri).

entries.english: warm to the idea; get carried away, take it seriously
entries.literal: come into that frame of mind
entries.use: Most heard as sono ki ni nareba dekiru (you can if you put your mind to it), sono ki ni natte kita (I'm warming to it) and sono ki ni saseru (talk someone into it, or lead someone on). It is also taking praise or a joke at face value: homeraretara sugu sono ki ni naru (gets carried away as soon as he's praised), sono ki ni naru na yo (don't take it seriously). Not ki ni naru, which is being curious or bothered.

example.romaji: nanka sono ki ni natte kita
example.ja: なんかその気になってきた
example.english: I'm kind of warming to the idea.

examplePolite.romaji: nandaka sono ki ni natte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: なんだかその気になってきました
examplePolite.english: I'm kind of warming to the idea.

entries.notes: No intention at all: sono ki wa nai.

entries.english: be tied up, can't step away now
entries.use: The stock excuse when someone calls or asks for help mid-task: ima te ga hanasenai kara ato de ne. It is about this moment only; for being swamped in general say te ippai, and once you're free again, te ga aku.

example.romaji: gomen, ima te ga hanasenai
example.ja: ごめん、今手が離せない
example.english: Sorry, I'm tied up right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima chotto te ga hanasenakute
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今ちょっと手が離せなくて
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm a bit tied up right now.

entries.notes: In speech the ga often drops: ima te hanasenai.

entries.english: have your hands full, at full capacity
entries.use: Turning down more work or responsibility, usually as X de te ippai: jibun no shigoto de te ippai. Unlike te ga hanasenai (busy this minute), it means your plate is full in general.

example.romaji: gomen, ima jibun no shigoto de te ippai nan da
example.ja: ごめん、今自分の仕事で手一杯なんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got my hands full with my own work right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima jibun no shigoto de te ippai nan desu
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今自分の仕事で手一杯なんです
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got my hands full with my own work right now.

entries.notes: Slangier: ippai ippai (at my absolute limit).

entries.english: take a breather, have a short break
entries.use: Pausing after a stretch of work or a rush (chotto hitoiki tsukou), or feeling the pressure lift (yatto hitoiki tsuketa, I can finally breathe). Not yasumi o toru, which is taking days off.

example.romaji: chotto hitoiki tsukou ka
example.ja: ちょっと一息つこうか
example.english: Shall we take a breather?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto hitoiki tsukimashou ka
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと一息つきましょうか
examplePolite.english: Shall we take a breather?

entries.notes: Also hitoiki ireru (take a short break); hotto hitoiki = a sigh of relief.

entries.use: Doing a task with less effort than it deserves, about chores, cooking, work or a game: kyou wa ryouri te o nuichatta, te o nuku na. Not ki o nuku, which is losing focus rather than deliberately doing less.

example.romaji: kyou wa bangohan te nuichatta
example.ja: 今日は晩ご飯手抜いちゃった
example.english: I cut corners on dinner tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no bangohan wa chotto te o nuichaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 今日の晩ご飯はちょっと手を抜いちゃいました
examplePolite.english: I cut corners on dinner tonight.

entries.notes: Noun: tenuki (tenuki ryouri = a lazy meal).

entries.use: Said when something could go on forever, so you have to stop somewhere, usually after a -tara clause: ittara kiri ga nai (I could go on and on), ki ni shitara kiri ga nai. Not kiri ga ii, which is a good place to stop.

example.romaji: ki ni shidashitara kiri ga nai yo
example.ja: 気にしだしたらキリがないよ
example.english: Once you start worrying, there's no end to it.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ni shidashitara kiri ga nai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 気にしだしたらキリがないですよ
examplePolite.english: Once you start worrying, there's no end to it.

entries.notes: Casually kiri nai; kiri ga arimasen is the formal, written-sounding version.

entries.english: at a good stopping point; a nice round number
entries.use: At work or study, a natural place to stop: kiri no ii tokoro de yasumou. Also a round number (kiri ga ii kara sen'en de ii yo); not kiri ga nai, which is endless.

example.romaji: kiri ga ii kara, kyou wa koko made ni shiyou
example.ja: キリがいいから、今日はここまでにしよう
example.english: Good place to stop, let's call it a day.

examplePolite.romaji: kiri ga ii node, kyou wa koko made ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: キリがいいので、今日はここまでにしましょう
examplePolite.english: This is a good place to stop, let's call it a day.

entries.notes: Also kugiri ga ii, same meaning.

entries.english: no matter what, at all costs
entries.use: Shows firm resolve to get something done, usually before a deadline or goal: nani ga nandemo maniawaseru, nani ga nandemo katsu. Stronger than zettai, and always about someone's will.

example.romaji: nani ga nandemo kyoujuu ni owaraseru
example.ja: 何が何でも今日中に終わらせる
example.english: I'm finishing it today, no matter what.

examplePolite.romaji: nani ga nandemo kyoujuu ni owarasemasu
examplePolite.ja: 何が何でも今日中に終わらせます
examplePolite.english: I'll finish it today, no matter what.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: zettai (definitely).

entries.politeJa: それどころじゃありません
entries.english: no time for that; far from it
entries.literal: it's not that place (not the point for that)
entries.use: The brush-off when you're swamped or something more urgent is going on: ima sore dokoro ja nai! It also corrects someone, 'far from it' (tanoshikatta? sore dokoro ja nai yo, saiaku datta).

example.romaji: gomen, ima sore dokoro ja nai n da
example.ja: ごめん、今それどころじゃないんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got no time for that right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima sore dokoro ja nai n desu
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今それどころじゃないんです
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got no time for that right now.

entries.notes: Formal: sore dokoro de wa nai.

entries.english: can't keep this up, it'll wear me out
entries.use: The standard complaint about overtime, late nights, drinking or training you can't sustain, often after konna ... ja or a -tara clause: konna peesu ja karada ga motanai. The ga often drops, and mi ga motanai means the same.

example.romaji: konna ni zangyou tsuzuitara karada motanai yo
example.ja: こんなに残業続いたら体もたないよ
example.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

examplePolite.romaji: konna ni zangyou ga tsuzuitara karada ga motanai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: こんなに残業が続いたら体がもたないですよ
examplePolite.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: mou genkai (I'm at my limit).

entries.english: get the knack, work out how to do it
entries.use: Said whenever a skill, sport, game or job starts to click: yatto kotsu tsukanda! The o usually drops; kotsu ga wakaru means much the same, and kotsu alone is the trick to something (kotsu o oshiete, tell me the trick).

example.romaji: yatto kotsu tsukanda kamo
example.ja: やっとコツつかんだかも
example.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto kotsu o tsukanda ki ga shimasu
examplePolite.ja: やっとコツをつかんだ気がします
examplePolite.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: nareru (get used to it).

entries.english: lose the will to keep going
entries.use: A modern casual staple for giving up after setbacks or strain, mostly as kokoro oreta (that broke me) or kokoro oresou (about to give up), often without ga. Stronger than ki o otosu (be disappointed), and not romantic heartbreak, which is shitsuren.

example.romaji: are de kanzen ni kokoro oreta
example.ja: あれで完全に心折れた
example.english: That completely broke me.

examplePolite.romaji: are de kanzen ni kokoro ga oremashita
examplePolite.ja: あれで完全に心が折れました
examplePolite.english: That completely broke me.

entries.notes: Transitive: kokoro o oru (crush someone's spirit).

entries.english: all-out, as if your life depended on it
entries.englishIdiom: like your life depends on it
entries.use: Pep-talk exaggeration before a verb of effort: shinu ki de ganbaru, shinu ki de benkyou shiro. Sounds intense, so friends often use it half-jokingly about exams and deadlines.

example.romaji: kondo no shiken, shinu ki de ganbaru
example.ja: 今度の試験、死ぬ気で頑張る
example.english: I'm going all-out for the next exam.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo no shiken, shinu ki de ganbarimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今度の試験、死ぬ気で頑張ります
examplePolite.english: I'm going all-out for the next exam.

entries.notes: Softer: isshou kenmei.

entries.english: you can do it if you try
entries.literal: if you do it, you can
entries.use: Encouragement (yareba dekiru yo) and praise after a success, often a little teasing: yareba dekiru jan (see, you CAN do it). The bookish source naseba naru is rarely said.

example.romaji: hora, yareba dekiru jan
example.ja: ほら、やればできるじゃん
example.english: See, you can do it when you try!

examplePolite.romaji: hora, yareba dekiru ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: ほら、やればできるじゃないですか
examplePolite.english: See, you can do it when you try!

entries.notes: Stock praise: yareba dekiru ko (a kid who can do it when they try).

entries.english: daunting, too much to take on
entries.use: Very common modern way to say something feels too daunting to try, socially or in skill: hitori de yakiniku wa haadoru ga takai. Usually about yourself and often softened with chotto; the ga often drops.

example.romaji: hitori yakiniku wa chotto haadoru takai na
example.ja: 一人焼肉はちょっとハードル高いな
example.english: Yakiniku on my own? That's a bit daunting.

examplePolite.romaji: hitori yakiniku wa chotto haadoru ga takai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 一人焼肉はちょっとハードルが高いですね
examplePolite.english: Yakiniku on my own? That's a bit daunting.

entries.notes: Expectations: haadoru o ageru (raise the bar) / sageru (lower it).

entries.english: get fired up; put real effort into
entries.use: Rallying yourself or a team before a game, exam or big day: yoshi, kiai irete ikou! Also kiai irete + verb for doing something with real effort (kiai irete tsukutta), and aimed at someone else it can mean shaking them into shape (kiai o irete yaru).

example.romaji: yoshi, kiai irete ikou
example.ja: よし、気合入れていこう
example.english: Right, let's get fired up and go!

examplePolite.romaji: yoshi, kiai o irete ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: よし、気合を入れていきましょう
examplePolite.english: Right, let's get fired up and go!

entries.notes: Not trying hard enough: kiai ga tarinai.

entries.use: Delaying on purpose so you or someone else can get ready or act, at work, in a game or in a crisis: chotto jikan kasegou. Not jikan o tsubusu, which is filling spare time.

example.romaji: mada junbi dekitenai kara, chotto jikan kasegou
example.ja: まだ準備できてないから、ちょっと時間稼ごう
example.english: We're not ready yet, so let's stall a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: mada junbi ga dekite inai node, sukoshi jikan o kasegimashou
examplePolite.ja: まだ準備ができていないので、少し時間を稼ぎましょう
examplePolite.english: We're not ready yet, so let's stall for a little while.

entries.notes: Noun: jikan kasegi (a stalling tactic).

entries.use: The cheerful yes when someone asks you a favour, said by the helper about the favour: oyasui goyou da yo. Not asameshi mae, which is boasting that a task is easy for you.

example.romaji: oyasui goyou da yo, makasete
example.ja: お安い御用だよ、任せて
example.english: No problem, leave it to me.

examplePolite.romaji: oyasui goyou desu yo, makasete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: お安い御用ですよ、任せてください
examplePolite.english: No problem, leave it to me.

entries.notes: Plainer: ii yo, makasete (sure, leave it to me).

entries.english: be hard work, take a lot of effort
entries.use: Said of a job or task that takes real effort and patience, physical or not: kare o settoku suru no wa hone ga oreru, hone no oreru shigoto. The same words literally mean a bone broke, so context decides; casual talk often just says taihen.

example.romaji: kore zenbu katazukeru no, hone ga oreru na
example.ja: これ全部片付けるの、骨が折れるな
example.english: Tidying all this up is going to be hard work.

examplePolite.romaji: kore zenbu katazukeru no wa hone ga oremasu ne
examplePolite.ja: これ全部片付けるのは骨が折れますね
examplePolite.english: Tidying all this up is going to be hard work.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: taihen.

entries.english: let your guard down, ease off
entries.use: Mostly a warning to stay sharp until it's over (ki o nuku na, ki o nukanaide), or about a slip: chotto ki o nuita suki ni (the moment I let my guard down). It can also be easing off on purpose (tama ni wa ki o nuku no mo daiji). Not te o nuku, which is deliberately doing less.

example.romaji: saigo made ki o nuku na yo
example.ja: 最後まで気を抜くなよ
example.english: Don't let up till the very end.

examplePolite.romaji: saigo made ki o nukanaide kudasai ne
examplePolite.ja: 最後まで気を抜かないでくださいね
examplePolite.english: Please don't let up until the very end.

entries.notes: Intransitive ki ga nukeru: feel deflated; (drinks) go flat.

entries.english: need a lot of looking after
entries.use: Mostly about kids, pets or people who need constant looking after, often as te no kakaru ko (a handful of a kid). For a fiddly task people usually say tema ga kakaru instead; jikan ga kakaru is just taking time.

example.romaji: uchi no ko, honto te ga kakaru n da yo
example.ja: うちの子、ほんと手がかかるんだよ
example.english: My kid is such a handful.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ko, hontou ni te ga kakaru n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: うちの子、本当に手がかかるんですよ
examplePolite.english: My kid is such a handful.

entries.notes: Opposite: te ga kakaranai (low-maintenance).

entries.english: be elaborate, made with real care
entries.use: Praise for cooking, gifts, crafts or plans that clearly took a lot of work, and also for elaborate pranks or scams. You hear te no konda before nouns and te ga konderu at the end, almost never the dictionary form te ga komu.

example.romaji: kore, sugoi te ga konderu ne
example.ja: これ、すごい手が込んでるね
example.english: Wow, a lot of work went into this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, sugoku te ga konde imasu ne
examplePolite.ja: これ、すごく手が込んでいますね
examplePolite.english: Wow, a lot of work went into this.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: kotteru (kotta ryouri, elaborate cooking).

entries.english: be no match for, can't crack it
entries.use: Said when an opponent or problem is too strong or too hard for you, usually with zenzen and in the past: ani ni wa zenzen ha ga tatanai, shiken, ha ga tatanakatta. Not te ni oenai, which is something out of your control.

example.romaji: shiken, zenzen ha ga tatanakatta
example.ja: 試験、全然歯が立たなかった
example.english: The exam was way beyond me.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken, zenzen ha ga tachimasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 試験、全然歯が立ちませんでした
examplePolite.english: The exam was way beyond me.

entries.notes: Close: X ni wa kanawanai (can't beat X).

entries.english: be no match for, can't compete
entries.use: Said of a pro, a rival or a big competitor you can't hope to match, usually as X ni wa tachiuchi dekinai: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai, ookii mise no nedan ni wa tachiuchi dekinai. Close to ha ga tatanai, which leans more to a fight or a problem you can't crack.

example.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai yo
example.ja: プロには太刀打ちできないよ
example.english: There's no competing with a pro.

examplePolite.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: プロには太刀打ちできませんよ
examplePolite.english: There's no competing with a pro.

entries.use: A modest way to say a role or job is too much for you, often when turning down a position like leader or speaker: watashi ni wa ni ga omoi. Not ki ga omoi, which is dreading something.

example.romaji: riidaa nante, ore ni wa ni ga omoi yo
example.ja: リーダーなんて、俺には荷が重いよ
example.english: Me, team leader? That's too much for me.

examplePolite.romaji: riidaa nante, watashi ni wa ni ga omoi desu
examplePolite.ja: リーダーなんて、私には荷が重いです
examplePolite.english: Me, team leader? That's too much for me.

entries.notes: Relief when it's lifted: kata no ni ga oriru.

entries.use: Said when you're too stretched to deal with one more part of your duties, usually as X made te ga mawaranai: isogashikute souji made te ga mawaranai. Not te ga hanasenai (tied up this minute).

example.romaji: isogashikute souji made te ga mawaranai
example.ja: 忙しくて掃除まで手が回らない
example.english: I'm too busy to get around to cleaning.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashikute souji made te ga mawarimasen
examplePolite.ja: 忙しくて掃除まで手が回りません
examplePolite.english: I'm too busy to get around to cleaning.

entries.notes: The positive te ga mawaru is rare in talk; in dramas keisatsu no te ga mawaru means the police are closing in.

entries.use: Asking or saying whether someone is free to help right now: te aiteru? (got a sec?), te ga aitara onegai (when you're free). The opposite of te ga hanasenai; it is a free moment at work or home, not a free day.

example.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte
example.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝って
example.english: When you've got a free moment, give me a hand.

examplePolite.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka
examplePolite.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝ってもらえますか
examplePolite.english: When you've got a free moment, could you give me a hand?

entries.notes: Plain alternative: hima (hima? = are you free?).

entries.english: hit a wall, stop making progress
entries.use: How learners, athletes and workers describe a plateau or obstacle, usually as -teru (stuck now) or -ta: ima chotto kabe ni butsukatteru. The same words describe literally walking into a wall.

example.romaji: nihongo, ima kabe ni butsukatteru n da
example.ja: 日本語、今壁にぶつかってるんだ
example.english: I've hit a wall with my Japanese right now.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo, ima kabe ni butsukatte iru n desu
examplePolite.ja: 日本語、今壁にぶつかっているんです
examplePolite.english: I've hit a wall with my Japanese right now.

entries.notes: Getting past it: kabe o koeru / norikoeru.

entries.english: finally feel the pressure of a deadline
entries.use: Describes finally getting going because a deadline or exam is close, about yourself or a procrastinator: shiri ni hi ga tsuite yatto yaridashita. In speech ketsu ni hi ga tsuku (rough) is most common; oshiri ni hi ga tsuku is the softer, polite-friendly version.

example.romaji: shiri ni hi ga tsuite, yatto yaridashita
example.ja: 尻に火がついて、やっとやり出した
example.english: Once the pressure was on, I finally got going.

examplePolite.romaji: oshiri ni hi ga tsuite, yatto yaridashimashita
examplePolite.ja: お尻に火がついて、やっとやり出しました
examplePolite.english: Once the pressure was on, I finally got going.

entries.notes: Causing it: shiri o tataku (push someone to get moving).

entries.use: A playful boast that something is easy for you, mostly about your own ability: sonna no asameshi mae da. It sounds a little old-fashioned and jokey (younger speakers more often say yoyuu or rakushou); not oyasui goyou, which is the cheerful yes to a favour.

example.romaji: sonna no asameshi mae da yo
example.ja: そんなの朝飯前だよ
example.english: That's a piece of cake.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna no asameshi mae desu yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなの朝飯前ですよ
examplePolite.english: That's a piece of cake.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: kantan.

entries.english: say you can't take it, talk of giving up
entries.use: Admitting out loud that you're struggling or want to quit, often in the negative (yowane o haku na, no whining) or as a self-aware confession. Not monku o iu, which is complaining about others or things.

example.romaji: yowane hakitakunai kedo, mou genkai
example.ja: 弱音吐きたくないけど、もう限界
example.english: I don't want to whine, but I'm at my limit.

examplePolite.romaji: yowane wa hakitakunai n desu kedo, mou genkai desu
examplePolite.ja: 弱音は吐きたくないんですけど、もう限界です
examplePolite.english: I don't want to whine, but I'm at my limit.

entries.use: Literally feeling dizzy (me ga mawatta), and figuratively in the set exaggeration me ga mawaru hodo isogashii for a hectic day. The busy sense almost always comes with isogashii.

example.romaji: kyou, me ga mawaru hodo isogashikatta
example.ja: 今日、目が回るほど忙しかった
example.english: Today was so busy my head was spinning.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa me ga mawaru hodo isogashikatta desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は目が回るほど忙しかったです
examplePolite.english: Today was so busy my head was spinning.

entries.notes: Plain word for dizzy: memai (memai ga suru).

entries.polite: neko no te mo karitai kurai desu
entries.politeJa: 猫の手も借りたいくらいです
entries.literal: I'd borrow even a cat's paws
entries.use: A half-joking way to say a workplace or season is frantic, usually followed by kurai or hodo isogashii: nenmatsu wa neko no te mo karitai kurai. Said at work and at home, not only in writing.

example.romaji: ima, neko no te mo karitai kurai da yo
example.ja: 今、猫の手も借りたいくらいだよ
example.english: We're so busy we'd take any help.

examplePolite.romaji: ima, neko no te mo karitai kurai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今、猫の手も借りたいくらいですよ
examplePolite.english: We're so busy we'd take any help.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: sugoku isogashii.

entries.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru
entries.ja: 塵も積もれば山となる
entries.kana: ちりもつもればやまとなる
entries.literal: even dust, piled up, becomes a mountain
entries.use: Said about saving small change, daily study or small habits that build up, and about small costs that add up. Often only the first half is said (chiri mo tsumoreba...).

example.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru tte ne
example.ja: 塵も積もれば山となるってね
example.english: Little things add up, as they say.

examplePolite.romaji: chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: 塵も積もれば山となるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: Little things add up, as they say.

entries.notes: Slang short form: chiritsumo.

entries.english: have an idea who, why or where
entries.literal: a match in the mind exists
entries.use: Asked when something is lost, missing or odd and you want leads. You'll mostly hear it as a question, kokoroatari wa? or nanka kokoroatari aru?, and the answer is often zenzen nai. It means you know a possible cause from your own experience, while kentou ga tsuku is making a rough guess.

example.romaji: doko de nakushita ka, kokoroatari aru?
example.ja: どこでなくしたか、心当たりある？
example.english: Any idea where you lost it?

examplePolite.romaji: doko de nakushita ka, kokoroatari wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どこでなくしたか、心当たりはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any idea where you lost it?

entries.notes: Negative: kokoroatari ga nai (no idea at all). Related: omoi ataru fushi ga aru (something comes to mind that might explain it).

entries.use: Said about kids, pets, bags or a suspect. It's mostly a warning (me o hanasu na, me o hanasanaide: don't let them out of your sight) or appears in chotto me o hanashita suki ni (the moment I looked away). Hanasu here is 離す (let go), not 話す (talk), and me o sorasu means looking away to avoid someone's eyes.

example.romaji: chotto me o hanashita suki ni inaku natta.
example.ja: ちょっと目を離した隙にいなくなった。
example.english: I looked away for a second and they were gone.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto me o hanashita suki ni inaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと目を離した隙にいなくなりました。
examplePolite.english: I looked away for a second and they were gone.

entries.notes: Can't-look-away form: me ga hanasenai (gripping, or needs constant watching).

entries.english: be out of one's mind, not be oneself
entries.use: Said to someone acting crazy (anta dou ka shiteru yo: you've lost it), or about yourself in the past as an apology: gomen, dou ka shiteta (sorry, I wasn't myself). Also about a situation: kono atsusa, dou ka shiteru (this heat is crazy). Don't confuse it with the question dou ka shita? (is something wrong?). Atama ga okashii is the harsher 'you're crazy'.

example.romaji: gomen, sakki wa dou ka shiteta.
example.ja: ごめん、さっきはどうかしてた。
example.english: Sorry, I wasn't myself earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sakki wa dou ka shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、さっきはどうかしていました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I wasn't myself earlier.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: okashii yo (you're acting weird).

entries.use: The standard answer when you can't even guess who, where or how much: zenzen kentou mo tsukanai, or casually kentou tsukanai. The positive kentou ga tsuku means 'I can roughly guess'. Don't confuse it with kentou suru (look into, consider).

example.romaji: doko ni aru ka kentou mo tsukanai.
example.ja: どこにあるか見当もつかない。
example.english: I have no idea where it could be.

examplePolite.romaji: doko ni aru ka kentou mo tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: どこにあるか見当もつきません。
examplePolite.english: I have no idea where it could be.

entries.notes: Positive: kentou ga tsuku (have a rough idea).

entries.use: Used for documents, emails and menus, and means going through it once, not studying it. You'll mostly hear it in requests like me o tooshite oite (have a look over this) and in ichiou me o tooshita (I've had a look). At work: ome o tooshite itadakemasu ka (could you look this over?).

example.romaji: kore, ato de me o tooshitoite.
example.ja: これ、あとで目を通しといて。
example.english: Have a look over this later.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, ato de me o tooshite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これ、あとで目を通しておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please have a look over this later.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: zatto miru (have a quick look).

entries.english: makes no sense at all, baffling
entries.use: Your reaction when a situation, a rule or someone's behaviour is baffling or absurd; casually wake wakannai. In quick reactions it swaps freely with imi wakannai, but only wake works before a noun: wake no wakannai koto iwanaide (don't talk nonsense). Aimed at what the listener just said, it's blunt even in polite form.

example.romaji: kono ruuru, chotto wake wakannai yo ne.
example.ja: このルール、ちょっとわけわかんないよね。
example.english: This rule doesn't make any sense, does it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono ruuru, chotto wake ga wakarimasen yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: このルール、ちょっと訳が分かりませんよね。
examplePolite.english: This rule doesn't make any sense, does it?

entries.notes: Before a noun: wake no wakaranai hito (a weirdo); slangy one word: imifu (makes no sense).

entries.use: Said by someone in charge who lets a small fault slide: konkai dake me o tsuburu (I'll overlook it this once). It also means accepting a downside you can live with: tashou no ketten ni wa me o tsuburu. The same words literally mean close your eyes, so context decides; mite minu furi is the disapproving version, ignoring something that's wrong.

example.romaji: konkai dake wa me o tsuburu yo.
example.ja: 今回だけは目をつぶるよ。
example.english: I'll overlook it just this once.

examplePolite.romaji: konkai dake wa me o tsuburimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今回だけは目をつぶりましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'll overlook it just this once.

entries.notes: Also said me o tsumuru.

entries.kana: あたまからはなれない
entries.englishIdiom: can't get it out of my head
entries.use: For a song, a worry, a scene or a person that keeps coming back, with the thing as the subject: ano kotoba ga atama kara hanarenai. It's almost always negative. Atama ni ukabu is a thought popping up once.

example.romaji: ano kyoku ga atama kara hanarenai.
example.ja: あの曲が頭から離れない。
example.english: I can't get that song out of my head.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kyoku ga atama kara hanaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの曲が頭から離れません。
examplePolite.english: I can't get that song out of my head.

entries.english: have your eye on; single someone out
entries.use: Used for something or someone you want, like a bag, a house or a promising newcomer: zutto me o tsuketeta. The passive me o tsukerareta means you got on someone's bad side, and ii tokoro ni me o tsuketa ne praises someone for spotting the right point or angle. It's different from me ni tsuku, where the thing itself catches your eye.

example.romaji: zutto kono baggu ni me o tsuketeta n da.
example.ja: ずっとこのバッグに目をつけてたんだ。
example.english: I've had my eye on this bag for ages.

examplePolite.romaji: zutto kono baggu ni me o tsukete ita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ずっとこのバッグに目をつけていたんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had my eye on this bag for ages.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: nerau (go after, aim for).

entries.use: Said about an opponent, a task, a cold or the weather that turns out tougher than you thought: amaku miteta (I underestimated it). It's also a warning: amaku miru na, amaku minai hou ga ii. Don't confuse it with amai (soft on someone) or oome ni miru (let it slide); kangae ga amai judges a whole plan as naive.

example.romaji: shiken, chotto amaku miteta.
example.ja: 試験、ちょっと甘く見てた。
example.english: I kind of underestimated the exam.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken o chotto amaku mite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 試験をちょっと甘く見ていました。
examplePolite.english: I kind of underestimated the exam.

entries.notes: Slangy one word: nameru (namen na yo = don't underestimate me).

entries.use: The everyday complaint when noise, a phone or someone talking breaks your focus: urusakute ki ga chiru, ki ga chiru kara yamete. It's the annoying kind of distraction; ki o torareru names the one thing that pulled you away. Ki ga magireru is the welcome kind that takes your mind off worries.

example.romaji: mawari ga urusakute ki ga chiru.
example.ja: 周りがうるさくて気が散る。
example.english: It's so noisy around here I can't focus.

examplePolite.romaji: mawari ga urusakute ki ga chirimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 周りがうるさくて気が散ります。
examplePolite.english: It's so noisy around here I can't focus.

entries.notes: Opposite: shuuchuu suru (focus).

entries.english: make sense, be fair and logical
entries.use: Often negative, about a demand, an excuse or a way of doing things that isn't logical or fair: sore wa suji ga tooranai (that's not right). The positive is suji ga tootteru or suji no tootta hanashi (a reasonable argument). Tsujitsuma ga awanai is different: a story that contradicts itself.

example.romaji: sore ja suji ga tooranai yo.
example.ja: それじゃ筋が通らないよ。
example.english: That doesn't make sense, and it isn't fair.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de wa suji ga toorimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: それでは筋が通りませんよ。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't make sense, and it isn't fair.

entries.notes: Related: suji o toosu (do it properly, through the right channels).

entries.english: be attentive; look out for others
entries.use: Said with approval of someone who notices what everyone needs (mawari ni ki o kubaru), or about keeping an eye on details or your health. The noun kikubari is just as common: kikubari ga dekiru hito. It's close to ki o tsukau (go out of your way for someone) and ki ga kiku (be thoughtful); ki o mawasu is thinking ahead too much.

example.romaji: kanojo, itsumo mawari ni ki o kubatteru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼女、いつも周りに気を配ってるよね。
example.english: She's always looking out for everyone, isn't she.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa itsumo mawari ni ki o kubatte imasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女はいつも周りに気を配っていますよね。
examplePolite.english: She's always looking out for everyone, isn't she.

entries.notes: Noun form: kikubari (kikubari ga dekiru = attentive).

entries.use: The stock reply when someone thinks they heard or saw something: ki no sei da yo (you're imagining it). About your own hunch it's ki no sei kana (maybe it's just me), often paired with ki ga suru.

example.romaji: ki no sei da yo. nanimo kikoenai.
example.ja: 気のせいだよ。何も聞こえない。
example.english: It's just your imagination. I can't hear anything.

examplePolite.romaji: ki no sei desu yo. nanimo kikoemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 気のせいですよ。何も聞こえません。
examplePolite.english: It's just your imagination. I can't hear anything.

entries.notes: Hedge form: ki no sei kana (maybe it's just me).

entries.use: Said in sympathy once you hear why someone is tired, upset or angry, usually as X no mo muri (wa) nai: okoru no mo muri nai (no wonder she's angry). Don't confuse it with muri on its own (impossible, too much) or muri shinaide (don't overdo it).

example.romaji: tetsuya? nemui no mo muri nai ne.
example.ja: 徹夜？眠いのも無理ないね。
example.english: An all-nighter? No wonder you're sleepy.

examplePolite.romaji: tetsuya desu ka? nemui no mo muri wa arimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 徹夜ですか？眠いのも無理はありませんね。
examplePolite.english: An all-nighter? No wonder you're sleepy.

entries.notes: Also muri wa nai. Close: douri de (no wonder: douri de nemui wake da).

entries.use: The thing is the subject: a sign, a stain, a typo, someone's flaws. It often sounds slightly negative (warui toko bakari me ni tsuku). Hitome ni tsuku means being seen by other people. Me o tsukeru is different: you set your eyes on something you want.

example.romaji: kare no warui toko bakkari me ni tsuku.
example.ja: 彼の悪いとこばっかり目につく。
example.english: All I notice are his bad points.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no warui tokoro bakari me ni tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の悪いところばかり目につきます。
examplePolite.english: All I notice are his bad points.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: medatsu (stand out).

entries.english: be glued to (a screen, a sight)
entries.use: Said when your eyes or attention are stuck on something: a match on TV, a stunning view, someone gorgeous. It's usually said without naru, as X ni kugizuke (da/datta), and me ga kugizuke means your eyes were fixed on it. It also means stuck in place: ichinichijuu desuku ni kugizuke datta (chained to my desk all day).

example.romaji: minna terebi ni kugizuke datta yo.
example.ja: みんなテレビに釘付けだったよ。
example.english: Everyone was glued to the TV.

examplePolite.romaji: minna terebi ni kugizuke deshita yo.
examplePolite.ja: みんなテレビに釘付けでしたよ。
examplePolite.english: Everyone was glued to the TV.

entries.use: For ideas, faces or words that pop into your head: ii aidea ga ukanda. It's very often negative, nanimo ukabanai (nothing comes to mind), and atama ni is often dropped. It differs from omoidasu (remember on purpose), and me ni ukabu is picturing a scene.

example.romaji: ii namae ga zenzen atama ni ukabanai.
example.ja: いい名前が全然頭に浮かばない。
example.english: I can't think of a good name at all.

examplePolite.romaji: ii namae ga zenzen atama ni ukabimasen.
examplePolite.ja: いい名前が全然頭に浮かびません。
examplePolite.english: I can't think of a good name at all.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: omoitsuku (think of, hit on).

entries.english: it clicks, it rings a bell
entries.use: Said when something clicks, like a hunch, a name or the right answer: pin to kita (it clicked). The negative pin to konai is just as common, for a name that doesn't ring a bell or an idea or design that doesn't grab you (imaichi pin to konai).

example.romaji: sono namae, imaichi pin to konai.
example.ja: その名前、いまいちピンとこない。
example.english: That name doesn't really click for me.

examplePolite.romaji: sono namae wa, imaichi pin to kimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: その名前は、いまいちピンときませんね。
examplePolite.english: That name doesn't really click for me.

entries.english: there's a catch, a hidden motive
entries.use: Said with suspicion about an offer that seems too good or kindness that's out of character: nanka ura ga aru n ja nai? It's also said of a person with a hidden side (ura ga aru hito). Oku ga fukai is the admiring 'there's more to it'.

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, zettai ura ga aru yo.
example.ja: そんなうまい話、絶対裏があるよ。
example.english: A deal that good definitely has a catch.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa, zettai ura ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話は、絶対裏がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: A deal that good definitely has a catch.

entries.notes: Set phrase: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru.

entries.literal: the seams and hems don't meet
entries.use: Said when a story, an alibi or an excuse contradicts itself: hanashi no tsujitsuma ga awanai. It's mostly negative, and tsujitsuma o awaseru means patching a story so it fits. Fu ni ochinai is about your own feeling of not being convinced.

example.romaji: sore, sakki no hanashi to tsujitsuma awanai jan.
example.ja: それ、さっきの話とつじつま合わないじゃん。
example.english: That doesn't match what you said earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, sakki no ohanashi to tsujitsuma ga aimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、さっきのお話とつじつまが合いませんね。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't match what you said earlier.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: mujun shiteru (it's contradictory).

entries.english: take it at face value, take it seriously
entries.use: It's mostly negative and said after a joke or a flattering line: joudan da yo, ma ni ukenaide (I'm kidding, don't take it seriously). People also say it with regret: ma ni uketa watashi ga baka datta. It's about believing words that weren't meant literally; unomi ni suru is swallowing information or rumours whole.

example.romaji: joudan da yo, ma ni ukenaide.
example.ja: 冗談だよ、真に受けないで。
example.english: I'm kidding, don't take it seriously.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan desu yo, ma ni ukenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談ですよ、真に受けないでください。
examplePolite.english: I'm only joking, please don't take it seriously.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: honki ni suru (take seriously).

entries.literal: there is a grain of reason
entries.use: Used to concede part of someone's argument without fully agreeing: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri aru ne. It's said of the opinion, not the person: kimi no iken ni mo ichiri aru.

example.romaji: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri aru ne.
example.ja: 確かに、それも一理あるね。
example.english: True, you've got a point there.

examplePolite.romaji: tashika ni, sore mo ichiri arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 確かに、それも一理ありますね。
examplePolite.english: True, you've got a point there.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: tashika ni (fair enough).

entries.use: Always used with ni, usually about yourself, to confess a weakness for a food or hobby: amai mono ni me ga nai (I can't resist sweets). Don't confuse it with miru me ga nai (bad judgement of people) or me ga warui (poor eyesight).

example.romaji: amai mono ni wa me ga nai n da.
example.ja: 甘いものには目がないんだ。
example.english: I can't resist sweets.

examplePolite.romaji: amai mono ni wa me ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 甘いものには目がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't resist sweets.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: daisuki (love it).

entries.politeJa: 見て見ぬふりをします
entries.english: pretend not to see, look the other way
entries.literal: seeing, yet putting on not seeing
entries.use: Disapproving: ignoring bullying, cheating or someone in trouble because getting involved is a hassle. Mite minu furi wa dekinai means I can't just look the other way, and o is often dropped. Me o tsuburu is the forgiving version, letting a small fault go on purpose.

example.romaji: sonna no, mite minu furi dekinai yo.
example.ja: そんなの、見て見ぬふりできないよ。
example.english: I can't just look the other way.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa mite minu furi dekimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは見て見ぬふりできませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I can't just look the other way.

entries.notes: Casual alternative: shiranpuri suru (act like you don't know).

entries.use: Used to predict a bad outcome you can already see coming: okorareru no wa me ni mieteru (it's obvious we'll get told off). It's always about a future result and always in the -teru form. Don't confuse it with me ni miete (visibly: me ni miete yaseta = noticeably thinner) or plain me ni mieru (literally visible).

example.romaji: sonna koto shitara okorareru no me ni mieteru yo.
example.ja: そんなことしたら怒られるの目に見えてるよ。
example.english: Do that and you'll obviously get told off.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto o shitara, okorareru no wa me ni miete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことをしたら、怒られるのは目に見えていますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you do that, you'll obviously get told off.

entries.notes: Short form: kekka wa mieteru (we know how it ends).

entries.use: Said about a guess that's nearly right (ii sen itteru kedo, chigau) or an attempt that's pretty good but not quite there, and sometimes about a person who's a decent prospect. It's light and a little playful, and you'll hear it in the -teru form.

example.romaji: oshii! ii sen itteru kedo, chigau.
example.ja: 惜しい！いい線いってるけど、違う。
example.english: So close! You're on the right track, but no.

examplePolite.romaji: oshii desu ne! ii sen itte imasu kedo, chigaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 惜しいですね！いい線いっていますけど、違います。
examplePolite.english: So close! You're on the right track, but no.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: oshii (so close).

entries.english: a revelation that changes your view
entries.use: Said after a tip, a fact or a trick that changes how you see something: kore wa me kara uroko datta (that was a real eye-opener). It's casual and a TV favourite. The full saying, me kara uroko ga ochiru, is rarer in talk.

example.romaji: kono urawaza, maji de me kara uroko datta.
example.ja: この裏技、マジで目からウロコだった。
example.english: This trick was a real eye-opener.

examplePolite.romaji: kono urawaza, hontou ni me kara uroko deshita.
examplePolite.ja: この裏技、本当に目からウロコでした。
examplePolite.english: This trick was a real eye-opener.

entries.notes: Full form: me kara uroko ga ochiru.

entries.use: Said about food, music, a game or a feeling you can't get enough of. It's variety TV's favourite food verdict (kuse ni naru aji). It also warns that something will turn into a bad habit: amayakasu to kuse ni naru yo. Kuse on its own just means a habit or a quirk.

example.romaji: kono karasa, kuse ni naru ne.
example.ja: この辛さ、クセになるね。
example.english: This spiciness is addictive.

examplePolite.romaji: kono karasa, kuse ni narimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この辛さ、クセになりますね。
examplePolite.english: This spiciness is addictive.

entries.notes: Close: hamaru (get hooked on).

entries.english: you overlook what's right next to you
entries.literal: below the lamp stand is dark
entries.use: Said when a lost thing turns up somewhere obvious (keys in your pocket, glasses on your head), or when the answer was close by all along. Toudai here is an old oil-lamp stand, not a lighthouse, though many people picture a lighthouse.

example.romaji: megane, atama no ue ni atta. toudai moto kurashi da.
example.ja: メガネ、頭の上にあった。灯台下暗しだ。
example.english: My glasses were on my head. Right under my nose!

examplePolite.romaji: megane, atama no ue ni arimashita. toudai moto kurashi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: メガネ、頭の上にありました。灯台下暗しですね。
examplePolite.english: My glasses were on my head. Right under my nose!

entries.use: Describes someone, often a crowd or kids, who's intensely curious and leaning in about gossip, a new gadget or someone's love life: minna kyoumi shinshin datta. It works like a na-adjective, with da, na or de.

example.romaji: minna, atarashii buchou ni kyoumi shinshin da yo.
example.ja: みんな、新しい部長に興味津々だよ。
example.english: Everyone's dying to know about the new manager.

examplePolite.romaji: minna, atarashii buchou ni kyoumi shinshin desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: みんな、新しい部長に興味津々ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Everyone's dying to know about the new manager.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: sugoku kyoumi ga aru.

entries.english: has real depth, more to learn
entries.use: Said with admiration about a hobby, craft, language or field that keeps getting deeper the more you learn: nihongo tte oku ga fukai ne. It's said about things, not people. Ura ga aru is the suspicious 'there's more to it'.

example.romaji: koohii tte, oku ga fukai ne.
example.ja: コーヒーって、奥が深いね。
example.english: There's more to coffee than you'd think.

examplePolite.romaji: koohii wa oku ga fukai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: コーヒーは奥が深いですね。
examplePolite.english: There's more to coffee than you'd think.

entries.notes: Adjective form: okubukai (deep, profound).

entries.use: The everyday excuse when you're tired, hungry or hungover: nebusoku de atama mawannai. Casual speech squashes it to mawannai. Atama ga masshiro ni naru is different: your mind goes blank in a panic.

example.romaji: nebusoku de atama mawannai.
example.ja: 寝不足で頭回んない。
example.english: I'm too short on sleep to think straight.

examplePolite.romaji: nebusoku de atama ga mawarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 寝不足で頭が回りません。
examplePolite.english: I'm too short on sleep to think straight.

entries.notes: Positive: atama ga yoku mawaru (quick-witted). Don't confuse with kuchi ga mawaranai (can't get the words out).

entries.english: can't quite accept it, doesn't sit right
entries.use: Said when an explanation or a result leaves you unconvinced, even if you can't say why: nanka fu ni ochinai. It's almost always negative and about your own feeling, unlike tsujitsuma ga awanai, where the story itself contradicts.

example.romaji: setsumei wa kiita kedo, nanka fu ni ochinai.
example.ja: 説明は聞いたけど、なんか腑に落ちない。
example.english: I heard the explanation, but something doesn't sit right.

examplePolite.romaji: setsumei wa kikimashita kedo, dou mo fu ni ochinai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 説明は聞きましたけど、どうも腑に落ちないんです。
examplePolite.english: I heard the explanation, but something just doesn't sit right.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: nattoku dekinai (I'm not convinced).

entries.kana: ゆめにもおもわなかった
entries.politeJa: 夢にも思いませんでした
entries.literal: didn't think it even in a dream
entries.use: Said in the past, as ... nante yume ni mo omowanakatta (I never dreamed ...). It's for a big surprise, good or bad: running into a star, a friend getting married, a betrayal. Don't confuse it with yume o miru (have a dream while asleep).

example.romaji: konna tokoro de au nante yume ni mo omowanakatta.
example.ja: こんなところで会うなんて夢にも思わなかった。
example.english: I never dreamed I'd run into you here.

examplePolite.romaji: konna tokoro de au nante yume ni mo omoimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: こんなところで会うなんて夢にも思いませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never dreamed I'd run into you here.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: masaka (no way); casual: omoi mo shinakatta.

entries.english: it's written all over your face
entries.use: Teasing someone whose thoughts are obvious, like boredom, a lie or a crush: kao ni kaite aru yo. It's usually said to the person, about what they think or want. Kao ni deru is broader: any feeling showing on someone's face (sugu kao ni deru = can't hide feelings); kao ni kaite aru reads a specific thought as if it were spelled out.

example.romaji: tsumannai tte kao ni kaite aru yo.
example.ja: つまんないって顔に書いてあるよ。
example.english: 'I'm bored' is written all over your face.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumaranai tte kao ni kaite arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: つまらないって顔に書いてありますよ。
examplePolite.english: 'I'm bored' is written all over your face.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: miemie (so obvious).

entries.english: be distracted by, too caught up in
entries.use: Explaining a slip: you were caught up in one thing (X ni ki o torarete) and missed or forgot something else, as in sumaho ni ki o torarete norisugoshita. Ki ga chiru is losing focus to noise or interruptions; ki o torareru names the one thing that took your attention.

example.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshichatta.
example.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしちゃった。
example.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

entries.english: can think of nothing else, preoccupied
entries.use: Said as X no koto de atama ga ippai: an exam, a crush, money or a sick parent fills your head and leaves no room for anything else. Shika atama ni nai is the teasing version about someone else.

example.romaji: ima wa shiken no koto de atama ga ippai.
example.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱい。
example.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa shiken no koto de atama ga ippai na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱいなんです。
examplePolite.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.

entries.notes: Overwhelmed: atama ga ippai ippai (can't take any more in).

entries.romaji: nani ga nan da ka wakaranai
entries.polite: nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen
entries.ja: 何が何だか分からない
entries.kana: なにがなんだかわからない
entries.politeJa: 何が何だか分かりません
entries.english: have no idea what's going on
entries.use: Said when too much happens at once or something comes out of nowhere and you're lost. It's often cut short to nani ga nan da ka. Wake ga wakaranai judges something as absurd; this one is just being lost.

example.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakannai yo.
example.ja: 急にそんなこと言われても、何が何だか分かんないよ。
example.english: You spring that on me and I've no idea what's going on.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto o iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急にそんなことを言われても、何が何だか分かりませんよ。
examplePolite.english: You spring that on me and I've no idea what's going on.

entries.notes: Casual: nani ga nan da ka wakannai, or just nani ga nan da ka.

entries.use: For a scene or reaction you can already see in your mind, usually someone's face: okaasan no okoru kao ga me ni ukabu. Atama ni ukabu is an idea or word popping up; me ni ukabu is a picture.

example.romaji: kanojo no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabu yo.
example.ja: 彼女の喜ぶ顔が目に浮かぶよ。
example.english: I can just picture how happy she'll be.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女の喜ぶ顔が目に浮かびますね。
examplePolite.english: I can just picture how happy she'll be.

entries.use: Said of someone who nods along but isn't listening, often because they're in love or worried: sakki kara uwa no sora da yo. It works like a na-adjective: uwa no sora de kiku (half listen).

example.romaji: nee, kiiteru? sakki kara uwa no sora da yo.
example.ja: ねえ、聞いてる？さっきから上の空だよ。
example.english: Hey, are you listening? You've been miles away.

examplePolite.romaji: anou, kiite imasu ka? sakki kara uwa no sora desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの、聞いていますか？さっきから上の空ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Um, are you listening? You've been miles away.

entries.use: A slightly wry, old-style way to say someone's mind is elsewhere, usually from love or worry, said as a block with da or tte kanji. Arazu is old Japanese for nai. Uwa no sora is the everyday version.

example.romaji: kyou no kare, kokoro koko ni arazu tte kanji.
example.ja: 今日の彼、心ここにあらずって感じ。
example.english: He's totally somewhere else today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no kare wa kokoro koko ni arazu tte kanji desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の彼は心ここにあらずって感じですね。
examplePolite.english: He's totally somewhere else today.

entries.use: Said when worry or excitement leaves you unable to get anything done, with the task as the subject: shinpai de shigoto ga te ni tsukanai. It's almost always negative. Ki ga chiru is distraction from outside; this one comes from inside.

example.romaji: shinpai de, shigoto ga zenzen te ni tsukanai.
example.ja: 心配で、仕事が全然手につかない。
example.english: I'm too worried to get any work done.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai de, shigoto ga zenzen te ni tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 心配で、仕事が全然手につきません。
examplePolite.english: I'm too worried to get any work done.

entries.notes: Close: mi ga hairanai (can't put your heart into it).

entries.use: About information: rumours, something online, what an expert or a salesperson says. It's mostly advice in the negative: unomi ni shinai hou ga ii. Ma ni ukeru is believing a joke or a line that wasn't meant seriously.

example.romaji: netto no uwasa, unomi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: ネットの噂、鵜呑みにしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

examplePolite.romaji: netto no uwasa wa unomi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ネットの噂は鵜呑みにしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

entries.kana: はなしはんぶんにきく
entries.english: only half believe what you hear
entries.englishIdiom: take it with a pinch of salt
entries.use: Advice about someone who exaggerates, or about boasts, gossip and sales talk; you'll mostly hear it as hanashi hanbun ni kiite oku. Unomi ni suru is the opposite: swallowing it all.

example.romaji: kare no hanashi, hanashi hanbun ni kiitoita hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 彼の話、話半分に聞いといたほうがいいよ。
example.english: Take what he says with a pinch of salt.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no hanashi wa, hanashi hanbun ni kiite oita hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の話は、話半分に聞いておいたほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Take what he says with a pinch of salt.

entries.use: Said about how you felt at first about news, a rumour or a too-good offer, usually in the past: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta. It works like a na-adjective: hanshin hangi de kiku.

example.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta kedo, hontou datta.
example.ja: 最初は半信半疑だったけど、本当だった。
example.english: I only half believed it at first, but it was true.

examplePolite.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi deshita kedo, hontou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 最初は半信半疑でしたけど、本当でした。
examplePolite.english: I only half believed it at first, but it was true.

entries.use: Said defensively when someone warns you about a risk or downside you've already weighed, often followed by but: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi da kedo...

example.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi da yo. demo yaru.
example.ja: 危ないのは百も承知だよ。でもやる。
example.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

examplePolite.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi desu. demo yarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 危ないのは百も承知です。でもやります。
examplePolite.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: wakatteru tte (I know, I know).

entries.politeJa: 身に覚えがありません
entries.english: never did it, know nothing about it
entries.literal: no memory of it in oneself
entries.use: The standard denial when you're blamed or billed for something you didn't do: zenzen mi ni oboe ga nai. You'll also hear it about unknown charges, mi ni oboe no nai seikyuu. Kokoroatari ga nai is having no idea about a cause; this one denies your own part.

example.romaji: e, watashi ga? zenzen mi ni oboe nai n da kedo.
example.ja: え、私が？全然身に覚えないんだけど。
example.english: Me? I never did anything like that.

examplePolite.romaji: e, watashi ga desu ka? zenzen mi ni oboe ga nai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: え、私がですか？全然身に覚えがないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Me? I never did anything like that.

entries.literal: nothing but X is in the head
entries.use: A complaint or tease about someone obsessed: X no koto shika atama ni nai (all he thinks about is X). Without shika, atama ni nakatta means it never crossed your mind: sonna koto zenzen atama ni nakatta.

example.romaji: kare, sakkaa no koto shika atama ni nai n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、サッカーのことしか頭にないんだよ。
example.english: Football's all he ever thinks about.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa sakkaa no koto shika atama ni nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はサッカーのことしか頭にないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Football's all he ever thinks about.

entries.notes: Also zenzen atama ni nakatta (it never crossed my mind).

entries.use: Said as X wa ni no tsugi, usually criticising someone's priorities: looks, money, studying or family pushed to second place.

example.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n da yo.
example.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんだよ。
example.english: With him, his family always comes second.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: With him, his family always comes second.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: atomawashi (put off till later).

entries.politeJa: その手には乗りません
entries.use: A playful or wary comeback when someone tries a trick, flattery or bait you've seen before. Te here means a trick or move, as in a game.

example.romaji: mata sore? sono te ni wa noranai yo.
example.ja: またそれ？その手には乗らないよ。
example.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

examplePolite.romaji: mata sore desu ka? sono te ni wa norimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: またそれですか？その手には乗りませんよ。
examplePolite.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

entries.notes: Also sono te ga atta! (oh, that's an option!).

entries.use: Said mostly in the past about someone who did something wrong for money or a prize: okane ni me ga kuranda. It also literally means dazzled by light, or dizzy.

example.romaji: kare, okane ni me ga kuranda n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お金に目がくらんだんだよ。
example.english: He was blinded by the money.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa okane ni me ga kuranda n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお金に目がくらんだんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He was blinded by the money.

entries.ja: どういう風の吹き回し
entries.kana: どういうかぜのふきまわし
entries.literal: what kind of turn of the wind
entries.use: A teasing question when someone does something nice or out of character, like cooking, paying or cleaning, said with a smile.

example.romaji: ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi?
example.ja: おごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回し？
example.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

examplePolite.romaji: ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: おごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回しですか？
examplePolite.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

entries.use: A hunch that turned out right, usually about bad news or someone close, often named afterwards: mushi no shirase ka na. The mushi is the old idea of a bug inside you that senses things. Ki no sei is the opposite: a feeling that turns out to be nothing.

example.romaji: mushi no shirase ka na. kyuu ni denwa shitaku natta n da.
example.ja: 虫の知らせかな。急に電話したくなったんだ。
example.english: Call it a premonition. I suddenly felt like calling.

examplePolite.romaji: mushi no shirase deshou ka. kyuu ni denwa shitaku natta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 虫の知らせでしょうか。急に電話したくなったんです。
examplePolite.english: Call it a premonition. I suddenly felt like calling.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: iya na yokan (a bad feeling).

entries.kana: のどまででかかってる
entries.politeJa: 喉まで出かかっています
entries.english: on the tip of my tongue
entries.literal: it's come out as far as the throat
entries.englishIdiom: on the tip of my tongue
entries.use: Said while you're straining to remember a name or word, usually after are, nan datta kke... It's about yourself, in the -teru form.

example.romaji: are, nan datta kke... nodo made dekakatteru n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、何だったっけ…喉まで出かかってるんだけど。
example.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: are, nan deshita kke... nodo made dekakatte iru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、何でしたっけ…喉まで出かかっているんですけど。
examplePolite.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

entries.notes: Also koko made dekakatteru (with a hand at the throat).

entries.use: Said while studying, reading or listening when you're tired or distracted and nothing stays, with the material as the subject. Atama ga mawaranai is not being able to think at all; atama ni ireru is the other side, making yourself take it in.

example.romaji: nemukute, zenzen atama ni hairanai.
example.ja: 眠くて、全然頭に入らない。
example.english: I'm so sleepy nothing's going in.

examplePolite.romaji: nemukute, zenzen atama ni hairimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 眠くて、全然頭に入りません。
examplePolite.english: I'm so sleepy nothing's going in.

entries.english: keep in mind, take it in
entries.use: Mostly a request before something important: kore dake wa atama ni irete oite (just keep this in mind). It also means memorising facts or a route: chizu o atama ni ireru.

example.romaji: kore dake wa atama ni iretoite.
example.ja: これだけは頭に入れといて。
example.english: Just keep this one thing in mind.

examplePolite.romaji: kore dake wa atama ni irete oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これだけは頭に入れておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please just keep this one thing in mind.

entries.english: come to your senses, wake up to reality
entries.use: Said to someone fooled by a partner, a scam or their own wishful thinking: ii kagen me o samashite! About yourself it's me ga sameta (I've come to my senses). The same words literally mean wake up from sleep, which the collocation list covers as me ga sameru.

example.romaji: ii kagen me o samashite! damasareteru yo.
example.ja: いい加減目を覚まして！騙されてるよ。
example.english: Wake up! You're being played.

examplePolite.romaji: ii kagen me o samashite kudasai. damasarete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いい加減目を覚ましてください。騙されていますよ。
examplePolite.english: Please wake up. You're being played.

entries.notes: Rough command: me o samase!

entries.use: Two senses: something too gripping to stop watching (a close match, a drama's final episode), or someone who needs constant watching (a toddler, a reckless friend). Me o hanasu na is the warning not to look away.

example.romaji: kono shiai, saigo made me ga hanasenai ne.
example.ja: この試合、最後まで目が離せないね。
example.english: You can't take your eyes off this match.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shiai wa saigo made me ga hanasemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: この試合は最後まで目が離せませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can't take your eyes off this match.

entries.use: Said of someone watching for trouble or rule-breaking: parents, teachers, a strict boss, the police. You'll hear it in the -teru form. Me ga hanasenai is needing to watch; me o hikaraseru is standing guard.

example.romaji: buchou ga me o hikaraseteru kara, sumaho tsukaenai.
example.ja: 部長が目を光らせてるから、スマホ使えない。
example.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou ga me o hikarasete iru node, sumaho wa tsukaemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長が目を光らせているので、スマホは使えませんね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

entries.use: The thing is the subject and it draws attention by standing out: a sign, an outfit, a bright colour. Hitome o hiku is drawing other people's looks. Me ni tsuku is just noticing, often something you'd rather not.

example.romaji: ano kanban, sugoku me o hiku ne.
example.ja: あの看板、すごく目を引くね。
example.english: That sign really grabs your attention.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kanban wa sugoku me o hikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの看板はすごく目を引きますね。
examplePolite.english: That sign really grabs your attention.

entries.use: Said when your eyes keep drifting to something, often with tsui and -chau: tsui X ni me ga itchau. The negative me ga ikanakatta means you didn't notice it at all.

example.romaji: tsui hito no kutsu ni me ga itchau.
example.ja: つい人の靴に目が行っちゃう。
example.english: I always end up looking at people's shoes.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui hito no kutsu ni me ga itte shimaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: つい人の靴に目が行ってしまいます。
examplePolite.english: I always end up looking at people's shoes.

entries.english: look away from, refuse to face
entries.use: Said about avoiding an unpleasant truth: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide. It's also literal, turning your eyes from something painful to see. Mite minu furi is ignoring someone else's trouble; me o somukeru is avoiding facing it yourself.

example.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide.
example.ja: 現実から目を背けないで。
example.english: Stop running away from reality.

examplePolite.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 現実から目を背けないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't run away from reality.

entries.romaji: mune ni te o atete kangaeru
entries.polite: mune ni te o atete kangaemasu
entries.ja: 胸に手を当てて考える
entries.kana: むねにてをあててかんがえる
entries.politeJa: 胸に手を当てて考えます
entries.english: think honestly about what you did
entries.literal: think with a hand on your chest
entries.use: A scolding line to someone who claims not to know why you're upset. It's almost always a request in the -te mite form: jibun no mune ni te o atete kangaete mite.

example.romaji: jibun no mune ni te o atete kangaete mite.
example.ja: 自分の胸に手を当てて考えてみて。
example.english: Put your hand on your heart and think about it.

examplePolite.romaji: jibun no mune ni te o atete kangaete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 自分の胸に手を当てて考えてみてください。
examplePolite.english: Put your hand on your heart and think about it.

entries.use: Said when a comparison, a chart or a before-and-after makes the answer instantly clear, often after mireba (if you look). It's used with da or desu.

example.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen da yo.
example.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然だよ。
example.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

examplePolite.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: mireba wakaru (you'll see if you look).

entries.english: a temptation you'd better not see
entries.use: A joking line about something tempting you can't or shouldn't have: cake while dieting, a gadget you can't afford. It's said with da: kore wa me no doku da.

example.romaji: daietto chuu ni kore wa me no doku da yo.
example.ja: ダイエット中にこれは目の毒だよ。
example.english: That's torture to look at when I'm on a diet.

examplePolite.romaji: daietto chuu ni kore wa me no doku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ダイエット中にこれは目の毒ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's torture to look at when I'm on a diet.

entries.englishIdiom: in one ear and out the other
entries.use: Said about words that go straight through someone: a lecture, advice, a long speech. It's also said of money that comes in and goes straight out (kyuuryou ga migi kara hidari).

example.romaji: kouchou no hanashi, zenbu migi kara hidari datta.
example.ja: 校長の話、全部右から左だった。
example.english: The principal's speech went in one ear and out the other.

examplePolite.romaji: kouchou no hanashi wa, zenbu migi kara hidari deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 校長の話は、全部右から左でした。
examplePolite.english: The principal's speech went in one ear and out the other.

entries.use: Said with disapproval about someone whose choices baffle you: X suru hito no ki ga shirenai (I don't get people who X). It's about a person or a type of person; dou ka shiteru says they've lost it.

example.romaji: konna samui no ni oyogu hito no ki ga shirenai.
example.ja: こんな寒いのに泳ぐ人の気が知れない。
example.english: I don't get people who swim when it's this cold.

examplePolite.romaji: konna ni samui no ni oyogu hito no ki ga shiremasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: こんなに寒いのに泳ぐ人の気が知れませんね。
examplePolite.english: I don't get people who swim when it's this cold.

entries.english: think ahead too much, read into things
entries.use: Said when someone anticipates needs or reads too much into things, kindly or needlessly: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii yo. Ki o kubaru is plain attentiveness, always a compliment.

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii yo.
example.ja: そんなに気を回さなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't need to think that far ahead for me.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなに気を回さなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to think that far ahead for me.

entries.notes: Overdoing it: ki o mawashisugi.

entries.use: Mostly in the past, omoi mo yoranakatta (I never imagined), or before a noun, omoi mo yoranai tenkai (a turn nobody saw coming). It's a touch more neutral than yume ni mo omowanakatta and works in work talk too.

example.romaji: konna koto ni naru nante, omoi mo yoranakatta.
example.ja: こんなことになるなんて、思いもよらなかった。
example.english: I never imagined it would come to this.

examplePolite.romaji: konna koto ni naru to wa, omoi mo yorimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: こんなことになるとは、思いもよりませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never imagined it would come to this.

entries.notes: Casual: omoi mo shinakatta (never even thought of it).

entries.english: weigh on your mind, nag at you
entries.use: For a worry or a small detail that keeps nagging: chotto ki ni kakaru koto ga aru (something's bothering me). It's heavier and lasts longer than ki ni naru.

example.romaji: kanojo no sakki no kotoba ga ki ni kakaru n da.
example.ja: 彼女のさっきの言葉が気にかかるんだ。
example.english: What she said earlier is weighing on my mind.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo no sakki no kotoba ga ki ni kakaru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女のさっきの言葉が気にかかるんです。
examplePolite.english: What she said earlier is weighing on my mind.

entries.notes: Close: ki ni naru (be curious about, bother you).

entries.english: be naive, not think it through
entries.use: A blunt judgement on a plan that ignores how hard things are, usually from someone more experienced: sonna no kangae ga amai yo. Amaku miru is underestimating one task or opponent.

example.romaji: ichinichi de owaru? sore wa kangae ga amai yo.
example.ja: 一日で終わる？それは考えが甘いよ。
example.english: Done in a day? That's naive.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichi de owaru n desu ka? sore wa kangae ga amai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一日で終わるんですか？それは考えが甘いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Done in a day? That's naive.

entries.notes: Past misjudgement: yomi ga amakatta (I misread it).

entries.english: it depends how you look at it
entries.literal: things are as you think them
entries.use: Said to cheer someone up by finding a better angle on a setback, then giving that angle. It's a stock phrase, always with da or desu.

example.romaji: mono wa kangaeyou da yo. ii keiken ni natta jan.
example.ja: ものは考えようだよ。いい経験になったじゃん。
example.english: It's how you look at it. It was good experience.

examplePolite.romaji: mono wa kangaeyou desu yo. ii keiken ni natta ja nai desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: ものは考えようですよ。いい経験になったじゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: It's how you look at it. It was good experience.

entries.romaji: nen ni wa nen o ireru
entries.polite: nen ni wa nen o iremasu
entries.kana: ねんにはねんをいれる
entries.literal: put care on top of care
entries.use: Said when you check again or take an extra precaution though it's probably fine. You'll mostly hear the -te form, nen ni wa nen o irete, or just nen ni wa nen o.

example.romaji: nen ni wa nen o irete, mou ikkai kakunin shiyou.
example.ja: 念には念を入れて、もう一回確認しよう。
example.english: Just to be extra safe, let's check once more.

examplePolite.romaji: nen ni wa nen o irete, mou ichido kakunin shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 念には念を入れて、もう一度確認しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Just to be extra safe, let's check once more.

entries.notes: Short version: nen no tame (just in case).

entries.romaji: nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii
entries.polite: nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii desu
entries.ja: 喉から手が出るほど欲しい
entries.kana: のどからてがでるほどほしい
entries.politeJa: 喉から手が出るほど欲しいです
entries.literal: want it so much a hand comes out of the throat
entries.use: Said about something you want badly but can't easily get: a rare item, a ticket, a job, a player a team needs. It's always with hodo hoshii, and people often stop at nodo kara te ga deru hodo.

example.romaji: ano chiketto, nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii.
example.ja: あのチケット、喉から手が出るほど欲しい。
example.english: I'd give anything for that ticket.

examplePolite.romaji: ano chiketto, nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii desu.
examplePolite.ja: あのチケット、喉から手が出るほど欲しいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd give anything for that ticket.

entries.use: Said when you finally get something hard to come by, like tickets, a rare item or information. You mostly hear the past, te ni ireta. You are the one doing the getting; with te ni hairu, the thing itself is the subject.

example.romaji: yatto chiketto te ni ireta yo
example.ja: やっとチケット手に入れたよ
example.english: I finally got my hands on tickets.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto chiketto o te ni iremashita
examplePolite.ja: やっとチケットを手に入れました
examplePolite.english: I finally got hold of the tickets.

entries.notes: Everyday alternatives: getto suru (casual); toreta (managed to get, for tickets and seats).

entries.english: be obtainable, come into one's hands
entries.use: The partner of te ni ireru, with the thing as the subject. You hear it most in the negative, nakanaka te ni hairanai (hard to get hold of), in questions like doko de te ni hairu no? (where can you get it?), and in the cheer yatto te ni haitta! (got it at last!).

example.romaji: kore, nakanaka te ni hairanai n da yo
example.ja: これ、なかなか手に入らないんだよ
example.english: This is really hard to get hold of.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, nakanaka te ni hairanai n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: これ、なかなか手に入らないんですよ
examplePolite.english: This is really hard to get hold of.

entries.notes: Formal word: nyuushu (obtaining), as in nyuushu konnan (hard to get).

entries.literal: meet a terrible eye (me = an experience)
entries.use: How people tell any bad-experience story, from a ruined trip to being cheated. It is almost always in the past: hidoi me ni atta. Here me means 'experience', not 'eye'.

example.romaji: kinou hidoi me ni atta yo
example.ja: 昨日ひどい目に遭ったよ
example.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou hidoi me ni aimashita yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日ひどい目に遭いましたよ
examplePolite.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

entries.notes: Stronger variant: sanzan na me ni atta; making someone suffer is hidoi me ni awaseru.
