entries.use: The boss's side of firing. You hear it as a threat (kubi ni suru zo) or in the passive from the person who lost the job (kubi ni sareta). Use kubi ni naru for a plain 'got fired' that doesn't say who did it.

example.romaji: tenchou ni kubi ni sareta
example.ja: 店長にクビにされた
example.english: The manager fired me.

examplePolite.romaji: tenchou ni kubi ni saremashita
examplePolite.ja: 店長にクビにされました
examplePolite.english: The manager let me go.

entries.notes: Formal equivalent: kaiko suru (dismiss).

entries.use: The everyday way to say you or someone else lost a job. It is nearly always in the past (kubi ni natta), or just kubi da. It is not for quitting by choice, which is yameru.

example.romaji: kare, kaisha kubi ni natta rashii yo
example.ja: 彼、会社クビになったらしいよ
example.english: Apparently he got fired.

examplePolite.romaji: kare, kaisha o kubi ni natta rashii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 彼、会社をクビになったらしいですよ
examplePolite.english: I hear he was let go from his company.

entries.notes: A bare kubi! means 'You're fired!'; the formal word is kaiko sareru.

entries.use: Said when something is bound to happen sooner or later, most often being found out, caught or a collapse: bareru no wa jikan no mondai da, mou jikan no mondai da.

example.romaji: bareru no wa jikan no mondai da yo
example.ja: バレるのは時間の問題だよ
example.english: It's only a matter of time before they find out.

examplePolite.romaji: bareru no wa jikan no mondai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: バレるのは時間の問題ですよ
examplePolite.english: It's only a matter of time before they find out.

entries.english: take action; settle for (a price or compromise)
entries.literal: strike a hand (a move in go; a clap that seals a deal)
entries.use: It has two uses: dealing with a problem (nanka te o utanai to, we have to do something), and agreeing on terms while haggling (kono hen de te o utou, let's call it a deal). Don't confuse it with te o dasu (hit, meddle).

example.romaji: hayaku nanka te o utanai to
example.ja: 早くなんか手を打たないと
example.english: We need to do something about it, fast.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku nanika te o utanai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: 早く何か手を打たないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: We need to take some action soon.

entries.notes: Literal twin: te o utsu = clap one's hands (everyday clapping is te o tataku). Related: utsu te ga nai (nothing more can be done); formal: taisaku o toru.

entries.english: end up having to do something unpleasant
entries.literal: come to a hame (a tight spot)
entries.use: The everyday grumble about getting stuck with a chore or a bad outcome: after a plain verb (zangyou suru hame ni natta) or konna (konna hame ni naru nante). Mostly past, or as a warning (... suru hame ni naru yo). Only for results you didn't want.

example.romaji: kekkyoku hitori de katazukeru hame ni natta
example.ja: 結局一人で片付ける羽目になった
example.english: I ended up stuck cleaning up alone.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkyoku hitori de katazukeru hame ni narimashita
examplePolite.ja: 結局一人で片付ける羽目になりました
examplePolite.english: I ended up having to clean up by myself.

entries.notes: Neutral alternative: ... koto ni natta (it turned out that ...).

entries.literal: one's own deeds, one's own receiving (of their result)
entries.use: Said, often bluntly, when someone's trouble is their own fault, like a hangover or a failed test after no studying: jigou jitoku da yo. It can sound cold, so use it with friends or about other people, not to a superior's face.

example.romaji: are wa jigou jitoku da yo
example.ja: あれは自業自得だよ
example.english: He brought that on himself.

examplePolite.romaji: are wa jigou jitoku desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あれは自業自得ですよ
examplePolite.english: He really brought that on himself.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: jibun no sei (your own fault).

entries.english: get hurt; get burned (pay for a mistake)
entries.literal: meet a painful eye (me = an experience)
entries.use: Three uses: a threat of harm (itai me ni aitakunakattara damatte ro, if you don't want to get hurt, shut up), a warning about consequences (amaku miteru to itai me ni au yo) and a look back (mukashi itai me ni atta). hidoi me is about having a bad time; itai me is about getting hurt or paying for a mistake.

example.romaji: amaku miteru to itai me ni au yo
example.ja: 甘く見てると痛い目に遭うよ
example.english: Take it lightly and you'll get burned.

examplePolite.romaji: amaku miteru to itai me ni aimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 甘く見てると痛い目に遭いますよ
examplePolite.english: If you underestimate it, you'll get burned.

entries.notes: Same meaning: itai me o miru; the threat 'you'll pay for this' is itai me ni awaseru zo.

entries.english: settle it, put an end to it
entries.literal: attach a keri (the classical verb ending that closed poems and tales)
entries.use: Said when you decide to end something for good: a feud or rivalry (aitsu to keri o tsukeru), or a relationship or job that has dragged on. It has a showdown flavour, so in everyday talk it is often half-joking. The intransitive keri ga tsuku (it got settled) exists but is much rarer.

example.romaji: sorosoro keri o tsukenai to
example.ja: そろそろケリをつけないと
example.english: Time I settled this once and for all.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro keri o tsukenai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: そろそろケリをつけないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: We need to settle this soon.

entries.notes: Near-synonym: kecchaku o tsukeru (settle a contest).

entries.englishIdiom: let it go to one's head
entries.use: Usually a tease or a scolding (choushi ni noranaide yo, choushi notteru), or an apology (choushi ni notchatta). There is a rarer positive sense, 'get on a roll'. Don't confuse it with choushi ga warui (feel off).

example.romaji: gomen, choushi ni notchatta
example.ja: ごめん、調子に乗っちゃった
example.english: Sorry, I got carried away.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, choushi ni notte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: すみません、調子に乗ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I got carried away.

entries.notes: Casual: choushi notteru (ni dropped); a person who does this is an ochoushimono.

entries.use: Said when you're out of options and have to go with the one that's left: hoka ni te wa nai, kore shika te ga nai. The same te (move, option) appears in utsu te ga nai (nothing more can be done). It sounds a little dramatic; in casual talk people more often say kore shika nai.

example.romaji: shouganai yo, hoka ni te ga nai n da kara
example.ja: しょうがないよ、他に手がないんだから
example.english: Can't be helped, there's no other way.

examplePolite.romaji: shouganai desu yo, hoka ni te ga nai n desu kara
examplePolite.ja: しょうがないですよ、他に手がないんですから
examplePolite.english: It can't be helped; there's no other option.

entries.notes: Variants: kore shika te ga nai (this is the only way); utsu te ga nai (nothing more to try).

entries.use: Said when effort, time or savings are wiped out in one go, usually as zenbu mizu no awa da or mizu no awa ni natta. People say it about their own wasted work far more often than about anyone else's.

example.romaji: kore de zenbu mizu no awa da yo
example.ja: これで全部水の泡だよ
example.english: Now it's all gone down the drain.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de zenbu mizu no awa desu yo
examplePolite.ja: これで全部水の泡ですよ
examplePolite.english: Now it's all been for nothing.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: muda ni natta (went to waste).

entries.literal: the (dice) cup one has in mind
entries.use: Almost always X no omou tsubo da: if you react, you're doing just what the other side wants. People use it to talk someone out of taking the bait, as in sore ja aite no omou tsubo da yo.

example.romaji: okottara aitsu no omou tsubo da yo
example.ja: 怒ったらあいつの思うつぼだよ
example.english: Get angry and you play right into his hands.

examplePolite.romaji: okottara aite no omou tsubo desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 怒ったら相手の思うつぼですよ
examplePolite.english: If you get angry, that's exactly what they want.

entries.notes: Usually with aite (the other side): aite no omou tsubo.

entries.english: go straight, quit a shady life
entries.use: Said about leaving crime, gambling or a dubious job for good, and jokingly about any bad habit: X kara ashi o arau. It does not mean 'wash one's hands of', which is te o hiku.

example.romaji: pachinko kara wa mou ashi o aratta yo
example.ja: パチンコからはもう足を洗ったよ
example.english: I've quit pachinko for good.

examplePolite.romaji: pachinko kara wa mou ashi o araimashita
examplePolite.ja: パチンコからはもう足を洗いました
examplePolite.english: I've given up pachinko for good.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: yameru (quit).

entries.english: falsely accuse, pin it on someone
entries.use: Mostly heard from the person who was wrongly blamed: nureginu o kiserareta (I was falsely accused), or just nureginu da! (I didn't do it!). It works for small blame at school or work, not only for crimes.

example.romaji: nureginu o kiserareta n da yo
example.ja: 濡れ衣を着せられたんだよ
example.english: I got blamed for something I didn't do.

examplePolite.romaji: nureginu o kiserareta n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 濡れ衣を着せられたんですよ
examplePolite.english: I was blamed for something I didn't do.

entries.notes: The bare noun is common: nureginu da! (that's a false accusation!).

entries.kana: とりかえしがつかない
entries.politeJa: 取り返しがつきません
entries.use: A warning before damage that can't be fixed (torikaeshi no tsukanai koto ni naru) or regret afterwards (torikaeshi no tsukanai koto o shita). It mostly appears in the no form before koto.

example.romaji: torikaeshi no tsukanai koto shichatta
example.ja: 取り返しのつかないことしちゃった
example.english: I've done something I can't undo.

examplePolite.romaji: torikaeshi no tsukanai koto o shite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 取り返しのつかないことをしてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I've done something that can't be undone.

entries.notes: Before a noun it's torikaeshi no tsukanai; torikaesu alone means get back, win back.

entries.english: take the gamble, all or nothing
entries.use: Said before a risky, all-out attempt, nearly always as ichi ka bachi ka yatte miru (I'll just risk it). It works like an adverb and goes before the verb.

example.romaji: ichi ka bachi ka yatte miyou
example.ja: 一か八かやってみよう
example.english: Let's just risk it and go for it.

examplePolite.romaji: ichi ka bachi ka yatte mimashou
examplePolite.ja: 一か八かやってみましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's take the gamble and try.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: kake (a gamble), as in kake da ne.

entries.english: past neglect or excess catches up with you
entries.use: Said when skipped study, lost sleep, overspending or cut corners catch up with you, usually in the past: tsuke ga mawatte kita. tsuke is a bar tab, and tsuke o harau (pay the price) uses the same picture.

example.romaji: nebusoku no tsuke ga mawatte kita
example.ja: 寝不足のツケが回ってきた
example.english: The lack of sleep is catching up with me.

examplePolite.romaji: nebusoku no tsuke ga mawatte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 寝不足のツケが回ってきました
examplePolite.english: The lack of sleep is catching up with me.

entries.notes: Same image: tsuke o harau (pay the price for it).

entries.use: Said about parties, trips and celebrations, usually as a caution: hame o hazushisuginaide ne (don't go too wild). It's fine for a well-earned blowout and negative only when it goes too far.

example.romaji: hame hazushisuginai you ni ne
example.ja: 羽目外しすぎないようにね
example.english: Don't go too wild, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: hame o hazushisuginai you ni shite kudasai ne
examplePolite.ja: 羽目を外しすぎないようにしてくださいね
examplePolite.english: Please don't go too overboard.

entries.notes: Unrelated to hame ni naru (end up stuck doing) despite the shared word hame.

entries.use: Said, often half-jokingly, the moment a problem or squabble gets sorted: kore de ikken rakuchaku. It echoes the magistrate's closing line in old samurai dramas but is used for small everyday fixes.

example.romaji: yoshi, kore de ikken rakuchaku da ne
example.ja: よし、これで一件落着だね
example.english: Right, that's that sorted.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de ikken rakuchaku desu ne
examplePolite.ja: これで一件落着ですね
examplePolite.english: That settles it, then.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: kaiketsu (solved).

entries.use: Said about an illness, a crunch period or a crisis once the hardest part is behind you, usually in the past: yama o koeta, yama wa koeta (the worst is over). The crunch point itself is the yama (koko ga yama da).

example.romaji: shigoto, yatto yama koeta yo
example.ja: 仕事、やっと山越えたよ
example.english: Work's finally over the hump.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto mo yatto yama o koemashita
examplePolite.ja: 仕事もやっと山を越えました
examplePolite.english: Work is finally past the worst.

entries.notes: Literal twin: crossing a real mountain. For an illness people also say touge o koeta (past the crisis).

entries.use: Said when something happens at just the wrong moment, like walking in on an argument: ma ga warui naa. It also describes someone with a knack for bad timing. Before a noun it's ma no warui, and ma no warui koto ni means 'as (bad) luck would have it'. It isn't un ga warui, which means bad luck in general.

example.romaji: ma no warui koto ni, choudo kachou ga kita n da yo
example.ja: 間の悪いことに、ちょうど課長が来たんだよ
example.english: As luck would have it, the boss showed up right then.

examplePolite.romaji: ma no warui koto ni, choudo kachou ga kita n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 間の悪いことに、ちょうど課長が来たんですよ
examplePolite.english: As luck would have it, the boss showed up just then.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: taimingu ga warui.

entries.englishIdiom: kill two birds with one stone
entries.use: Said casually about any double win, for example walking to work saves money and gets you exercise: isseki nichou jan. It comes up more lightly and more often than the English, usually as a cheerful aside.

example.romaji: sore isseki nichou jan
example.ja: それ一石二鳥じゃん
example.english: That's two birds with one stone!

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa isseki nichou desu ne
examplePolite.ja: それは一石二鳥ですね
examplePolite.english: That kills two birds with one stone.

entries.notes: Formal near-synonym: ikkyo ryoutoku.

entries.use: Said kindly or teasingly when someone skilled slips up. It calls the person a monkey, so never say it to or about a superior (koubou ni mo fude no ayamari is the respectful version). Said about yourself, it's a joke that casts you as the expert. For ordinary mistakes say dare ni demo aru (it happens to everyone).

example.romaji: saru mo ki kara ochiru tte yatsu da ne
example.ja: 猿も木から落ちるってやつだね
example.english: Even the pros slip up, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: puro demo misu suru n desu ne. saru mo ki kara ochiru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: プロでもミスするんですね。猿も木から落ちるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: So even pros make mistakes. Even monkeys fall from trees, as they say.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: dare ni demo machigai wa aru (anyone can make a mistake).

entries.use: Said right after a narrow escape from real danger, like nearly being hit by a car or a bike: kiki ippatsu datta. It sounds a bit dramatic; abunakatta (that was close) is the everyday version. For just making it in time, say girigiri or kan ippatsu de maniatta: kan ippatsu means 'by a hair', kiki ippatsu 'a moment of danger'.

example.romaji: ima no, kiki ippatsu datta ne
example.ja: 今の、危機一髪だったね
example.english: That was a close shave.

examplePolite.romaji: ima no wa kiki ippatsu deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 今のは危機一髪でしたね
examplePolite.english: That was a really close call.

entries.notes: Everyday alternative: abunakatta! (that was close). Near-twin: kan ippatsu (by a hair).

entries.literal: if it fails, back to where you started
entries.use: Said before trying a long shot: damemoto de kiite miru (I'll ask anyway, nothing to lose). It is also a common softener before a cheeky request (damemoto na n da kedo ...), even at work.

example.romaji: damemoto de kiite miru yo
example.ja: ダメ元で聞いてみるよ
example.english: I'll ask anyway, nothing to lose.

examplePolite.romaji: damemoto de kiite mimasu
examplePolite.ja: ダメ元で聞いてみます
examplePolite.english: I'll ask anyway; it's worth a shot.

entries.notes: Short for dame de motomoto.

entries.english: it's no joke, it's seriously bad
entries.use: A reaction to something that is past being funny, like dangerous heat, a huge bill or a prank gone wrong: kore wa share ni naranai. Casual speech shortens it to share ni nannai.

example.romaji: kono atsusa, share ni nannai yo
example.ja: この暑さ、シャレになんないよ
example.english: This heat is no joke.

examplePolite.romaji: kono atsusa wa share ni narimasen ne
examplePolite.ja: この暑さはシャレになりませんね
examplePolite.english: This heat is seriously no joke.

entries.notes: Casual: share ni nannai; plain alternative: yabai.

entries.polite: sono toki wa sono toki desu
entries.english: we'll deal with it if it happens
entries.englishIdiom: cross that bridge when we come to it
entries.use: The everyday shrug at a what-if worry: dame dattara sono toki wa sono toki (if it fails, we'll deal with it then). You say it to calm yourself or someone else, often with maa in front.

example.romaji: maa, sono toki wa sono toki da yo
example.ja: まあ、その時はその時だよ
example.english: Eh, we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, sono toki wa sono toki desu yo
examplePolite.ja: まあ、その時はその時ですよ
examplePolite.english: Well, we'll deal with it if it happens.

entries.notes: Rougher casual form: son toki wa son toki.

entries.literal: doesn't become foolish (= can't be laughed off as trivial)
entries.use: Said mostly about money that seems small but adds up, like train fares, coffee or phone bills: koutsuuhi mo baka ni naranai. Don't confuse it with baka ni suru (make fun of) or baka o miru (end up the loser).

example.romaji: koutsuuhi mo baka ni naranai yo
example.ja: 交通費もバカにならないよ
example.english: Train fares really add up too.

examplePolite.romaji: koutsuuhi mo baka ni narimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: 交通費もバカになりませんよ
examplePolite.english: Travel costs really add up as well.

entries.notes: Variant: baka ni dekinai; plain alternative: kekkou kakaru (costs quite a bit).

entries.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru
entries.ja: 二度あることは三度ある
entries.kana: にどあることはさんどある
entries.english: if it happened twice, it'll happen again
entries.literal: what happens twice happens three times
entries.use: Quoted after a second mishap, like losing an umbrella again or a second breakdown, as a half-joking warning that a third one is coming. The comeback is sandome no shoujiki (third time lucky).

example.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru tte iu shi, ki o tsukete ne
example.ja: 二度あることは三度あるって言うし、気をつけてね
example.english: They say what happens twice happens again, so be careful.

examplePolite.romaji: nido aru koto wa sando aru tte iimasu kara ne
examplePolite.ja: 二度あることは三度あるって言いますからね
examplePolite.english: They do say what happens twice happens again.

entries.notes: Comeback: sandome no shoujiki (third time's the charm).

entries.english: be punished by heaven, get bad karma
entries.use: A half-joking warning to someone who wastes food, is ungrateful or disrespects something sacred: bachi ga ataru yo. People also say it about themselves when life feels too good, as in konna ni shiawase de bachi ga ataranai kana.

example.romaji: gohan nokoshitara bachi ga ataru yo
example.ja: ご飯残したらバチが当たるよ
example.english: Leave food and heaven will punish you.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o nokoshitara bachi ga atarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を残したらバチが当たりますよ
examplePolite.english: Leaving food will bring bad karma.

entries.notes: Written 罰 but read bachi here; an ungrateful person is a bachiatari.

entries.use: A grumble when the reward doesn't cover the effort or risk, like low pay for a hard job: kono kyuuryou ja wari ni awanai. It's nearly always negative; the positive wari ni au (it pays) is rare.

example.romaji: kono jikyuu ja wari ni awanai yo
example.ja: この時給じゃ割に合わないよ
example.english: It's not worth it for this hourly pay.

examplePolite.romaji: kono jikyuu ja wari ni aimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: この時給じゃ割に合いませんよ
examplePolite.english: It doesn't pay at this hourly rate.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: son (a loss), as in son da yo.

entries.literal: shelf rice-cake (a rice cake falling off the shelf)
entries.use: Said when something good lands in your lap without effort, like a ticket from someone's cancellation or a rival dropping out: tanabota da! It's the clipped, everyday form of the saying tana kara botamochi.

example.romaji: tanabota datta ne
example.ja: 棚ぼただったね
example.english: That just fell into your lap, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: tanabota deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 棚ぼたでしたね
examplePolite.english: That was a lucky windfall.

entries.notes: Full saying: tana kara botamochi.

entries.use: Said when regret or a fix comes too late, usually about a missed chance, often your own: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri da (no use saying it now).

example.romaji: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri da yo
example.ja: 今さら言っても後の祭りだよ
example.english: No use saying that now, it's too late.

examplePolite.romaji: imasara itte mo ato no matsuri desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今さら言っても後の祭りですよ
examplePolite.english: It's too late to say that now.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: mou osoi (it's too late).

entries.kana: ふこうちゅうのさいわい
entries.english: the one lucky part of a bad situation
entries.literal: good fortune in the middle of misfortune
entries.use: Said after an accident or setback about the one thing that went right, such as nobody getting hurt or the data being backed up: kega ga nakatta no wa fukouchuu no saiwai datta. Heard often from sympathetic listeners.

example.romaji: kega nakute fukouchuu no saiwai datta ne
example.ja: 怪我なくて不幸中の幸いだったね
example.english: At least nobody got hurt.

examplePolite.romaji: kega ga nakute fukouchuu no saiwai deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 怪我がなくて不幸中の幸いでしたね
examplePolite.english: It's lucky nobody was hurt, at least.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: ... dake de yokatta (lucky it was only ...).

entries.literal: it becomes the way it becomes
entries.use: A relaxed shrug about something out of your hands, usually maa, naru you ni naru sa. It sounds comforting rather than defeated; naru you ni shika naranai (it'll go how it goes) is more resigned.

example.romaji: maa, naru you ni naru tte
example.ja: まあ、なるようになるって
example.english: Eh, it'll work out somehow.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, naru you ni narimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: まあ、なるようになりますよ
examplePolite.english: Well, things will work out somehow.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: nantoka naru (it'll work out).

entries.use: Said about buffets, gym memberships, passes and pricey gadgets: tabehoudai de moto o toru (eat enough to make the buffet worth it). The negative moto ga torenai (it won't pay for itself) is just as common.

example.romaji: tabehoudai da kara moto toranakya
example.ja: 食べ放題だから元取らなきゃ
example.english: It's all-you-can-eat, gotta get our money's worth.

examplePolite.romaji: tabehoudai desu kara, moto o toranai to ikemasen ne
examplePolite.ja: 食べ放題ですから、元を取らないといけませんね
examplePolite.english: It's all-you-can-eat, so we should get our money's worth.

entries.notes: Intransitive: moto ga toreru (it pays for itself).

entries.use: Said about the last snack, good seats, sale items or a free spot: hayai mono gachi da yo! It's often a playful call to grab something before others do.

example.romaji: nokori wa hayai mono gachi da yo
example.ja: 残りは早い者勝ちだよ
example.english: The rest is first come, first served.

examplePolite.romaji: nokori wa hayai mono gachi desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 残りは早い者勝ちですよ
examplePolite.english: The rest is first come, first served.

entries.notes: Casual: hayai mon gachi.

entries.use: Said right after a near miss, from a car that nearly hit you to a scolding you just avoided: inochibiroi shita. Almost always past, and used half-jokingly for small escapes too.

example.romaji: abunakatta, inochibiroi shita yo
example.ja: 危なかった、命拾いしたよ
example.english: That was close. I got lucky there.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni inochibiroi shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 本当に命拾いしました
examplePolite.english: I really had a lucky escape.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: tasukatta (that saved me).

entries.use: The groan when someone else gets there first: the last item, a seat, a confession, a promotion, a rival company's launch. Mostly past and often without o: saki kosareta! For getting in first on purpose, say sente o utsu.

example.romaji: aa, saki kosareta!
example.ja: あー、先越された！
example.english: Argh, someone beat me to it!

examplePolite.romaji: tasha ni saki o kosarete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 他社に先を越されてしまいました
examplePolite.english: Another company beat us to it.

entries.notes: Rarer active form: saki o kosu (get there ahead of someone).

entries.english: act first, get in before the other side
entries.literal: play the first move (in shogi or go)
entries.use: Said about heading off a problem or a rival before they move, like complaints, a competitor or a parent's objection. Mostly advice (sente o utte okou) or past (sente o utareta, they got in first). It shares te (a move) with te o utsu.

example.romaji: monku iwareru mae ni sente utte okou
example.ja: 文句言われる前に先手打っておこう
example.english: Let's get in first, before they complain.

examplePolite.romaji: kujou ga kuru mae ni, sente o utte okimashou
examplePolite.ja: 苦情が来る前に、先手を打っておきましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's act before any complaints come in.

entries.notes: Opposite feeling: saki o kosareru (someone beat you to it).

entries.english: throw away (a chance, a career, years)
entries.use: Said about wasting something big through one bad choice: jinsei o bou ni furu (throw your life away), chansu o bou ni furu. Often a warning: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo. For effort that simply comes to nothing, say mizu no awa.

example.romaji: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo
example.ja: そんなことで人生棒に振るなよ
example.english: Don't throw your life away over that.

examplePolite.romaji: sekkaku no chansu o bou ni futte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: せっかくのチャンスを棒に振ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I threw away a golden chance.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: muda ni suru (waste).

entries.literal: the second dance (a clown copying the first dancer)
entries.use: Almost always X no ni no mai ni naru, usually as a warning: senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni (so you don't end up like your senpai). X is the person or event whose mistake you'd repeat. Don't confuse it with ni no ashi o fumu (hesitate).

example.romaji: senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni ne
example.ja: 先輩の二の舞にならないようにね
example.english: Don't end up like your senpai, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: zenkai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: 前回の二の舞にならないようにしましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's not repeat what happened last time.

entries.notes: Formal: ni no mai o enjiru (repeat the same mistake).

entries.english: get on track, start running smoothly
entries.use: Said about a business, a project or a new life once it starts running smoothly, usually as yatto kidou ni notte kita (it's finally on track). Unlike choushi ni noru, there's nothing cocky about it.

example.romaji: mise mo yatto kidou ni notte kita yo
example.ja: 店もやっと軌道に乗ってきたよ
example.english: The shop's finally getting on its feet.

examplePolite.romaji: mise mo yatto kidou ni notte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 店もやっと軌道に乗ってきました
examplePolite.english: The shop is finally on track.

entries.notes: Literal twin: going into orbit.

entries.literal: go back to the starting square (of a board game)
entries.use: Said when a setback wipes out all progress on a plan, a search or a negotiation, mostly in the past: mata furidashi ni modotta. furidashi ni modoru is what happens to you; ichi kara yarinaosu is what you then choose to do.

example.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modotchatta
example.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻っちゃった
example.english: Now we're back to square one.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modorimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻りましたね
examplePolite.english: So we're back to square one again.

entries.notes: Scrapping a plan on purpose is hakushi ni modosu.

entries.use: Said after lost work or a failed plan, and about making a fresh start in life. The noun form is just as common: ichi kara yarinaoshi da (back to the beginning).

example.romaji: zenbu kiechatta, ichi kara yarinaoshi da yo
example.ja: 全部消えちゃった、一からやり直しだよ
example.english: It all got deleted. I have to start from scratch.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu kiete shimatte, ichi kara yarinaoshi desu
examplePolite.ja: 全部消えてしまって、一からやり直しです
examplePolite.english: Everything got deleted, so I have to start from scratch.

entries.notes: Variant: ichi kara denaosu (make a fresh start, of a person).

entries.kana: あぶないはしをわたる
entries.use: Mostly said when refusing a risky or shady plan: sonna abunai hashi wa wataranai (I won't take that kind of risk). It's usually about money or bending rules, not physical danger.

example.romaji: sonna abunai hashi, wataritakunai yo
example.ja: そんな危ない橋、渡りたくないよ
example.english: I don't want to take a risk like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna abunai hashi wa wataritakunai desu
examplePolite.ja: そんな危ない橋は渡りたくないです
examplePolite.english: I'd rather not take that kind of risk.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: risuku ga takai (it's too risky).

entries.english: dig your own grave, give yourself away
entries.use: Said when someone makes things worse for themselves, most often by talking too much and giving themselves away: jibun de boketsu hotta. Common as a self-mocking groan.

example.romaji: yokei na koto itte boketsu hotta
example.ja: 余計なこと言って墓穴掘った
example.english: I said too much and dug my own grave.

examplePolite.romaji: yokei na koto o itte, boketsu o hotte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 余計なことを言って、墓穴を掘ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I said too much and dug myself a hole.

entries.notes: Same idea: jibun no kubi o shimeru (tighten the noose on yourself).

entries.use: Said when two things are separated by almost nothing: a win and a loss, a near miss (kami hitoe de tasukatta), or the set line tensai to baka wa kami hitoe (genius and idiot are a hair apart).

example.romaji: tensai to baka wa kami hitoe tte iu yo ne
example.ja: 天才とバカは紙一重って言うよね
example.english: They say there's a fine line between genius and idiot.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni kami hitoe deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 本当に紙一重でしたね
examplePolite.english: That really came down to a hair.

entries.notes: Near-twin: kan ippatsu (by a hair).

entries.englishIdiom: get too big for one's boots
entries.use: The standard rebuke for someone smug after a little success or praise: ii ki ni naru na yo. It sounds sharper than choushi ni noru, which can be playful. Don't confuse it with ki ni naru (be on one's mind).

example.romaji: chotto homerareta kurai de ii ki ni naru na yo
example.ja: ちょっと褒められたくらいでいい気になるなよ
example.english: Don't get full of yourself over a little praise.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ii ki ni natte imashita
examplePolite.ja: ちょっといい気になっていました
examplePolite.english: I was getting a bit full of myself.

entries.notes: Sarcastic cousin: ii ki na mon da (must be nice).

entries.use: A warning about a mistake or scandal serious enough to cost someone their job: baretara kubi ga tobu yo. Mostly future or conditional; for someone already fired, say kubi ni natta.

example.romaji: konna misu baretara kubi ga tobu yo
example.ja: こんなミスバレたらクビが飛ぶよ
example.english: If this mistake gets out, heads will roll.

examplePolite.romaji: kore ga baretara kubi ga tobimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: これがバレたらクビが飛びますよ
examplePolite.english: If this gets out, someone's losing their job.

entries.notes: Literal twin: a real beheading in period dramas.

entries.use: Said about not forcing a plan, a relationship or a career and seeing where it goes: ato wa nagare ni makaseyou. It sounds relaxed, not lazy.

example.romaji: maa, ato wa nagare ni makaseyou
example.ja: まあ、あとは流れに任せよう
example.english: Well, let's just see where it goes from here.

examplePolite.romaji: ato wa nagare ni makasemashou
examplePolite.ja: あとは流れに任せましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's let things take their course from here.

entries.notes: Same meaning: nariyuki makase.

entries.literal: the back face (of the die) comes up
entries.use: Said when a plan or a kind gesture produces the opposite of what you wanted, almost always in the past: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni deta (I meant well, but it backfired).

example.romaji: yokare to omotte yatta noni, urame ni deta
example.ja: 良かれと思ってやったのに、裏目に出た
example.english: I meant well, but it backfired.

examplePolite.romaji: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni demashita
examplePolite.ja: 良かれと思ってしたことが裏目に出ました
examplePolite.english: What I did with good intentions backfired.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: gyaku kouka (counterproductive).

entries.english: get stuck with the worst job or role
entries.use: The grumble when you end up with the job, role or seat nobody wanted, through bad luck or being too nice: mata binbou kuji hiichatta. hame ni naru is about the chore itself; binbou kuji is about being the unlucky one.

example.romaji: mata binbou kuji hiichatta yo
example.ja: また貧乏くじ引いちゃったよ
example.english: I got stuck with the short straw again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata binbou kuji o hiite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: また貧乏くじを引いてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I drew the short straw again.

entries.english: something came over me (a sudden lapse)
entries.use: The set excuse for an out-of-character lapse, like cheating, pocketing something or a cruel remark, almost always as tsui ma ga sashita (something just came over me). Said about yourself, or to excuse someone else.

example.romaji: gomen, tsui ma ga sashita n da
example.ja: ごめん、つい魔が差したんだ
example.english: Sorry, something just came over me.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui ma ga sashite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: つい魔が差してしまいました
examplePolite.english: I gave in to temptation for a moment.

entries.notes: Unrelated to ma ga warui (bad timing) despite the shared sound ma.

entries.english: it worked out in the end, so fine
entries.use: Said when luck covered a mistake or a messy process: maa, kekka oorai jan. Casual and a bit cheeky, often used to brush off criticism of how you got there.

example.romaji: maa, kekka oorai jan
example.ja: まあ、結果オーライじゃん
example.english: Well, it worked out in the end.

examplePolite.romaji: kekka oorai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 結果オーライですね
examplePolite.english: Well, it all worked out.

entries.notes: oorai is 'all right', the fielder's call in baseball.

entries.politeJa: 踏んだり蹴ったりです
entries.use: The casual bad-day summary when several bad things pile up: kyou wa fundari kettari da. Said mostly about yourself, usually after listing the mishaps.

example.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari da yo
example.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりだよ
example.english: Today's been one thing after another.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりでした
examplePolite.english: Today was one thing after another.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: tsuitenai (I'm out of luck).

entries.kana: さんどめのしょうじき
entries.english: the third try will be the one
entries.literal: the third time is the honest one
entries.use: Said before a third attempt at an exam, a confession or a game, or after it finally works: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da. It is the hopeful answer to nido aru koto wa sando aru.

example.romaji: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da!
example.ja: 今度こそ三度目の正直だ！
example.english: Third time's the charm!

examplePolite.romaji: sandome no shoujiki de, yatto goukaku shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 三度目の正直で、やっと合格しました
examplePolite.english: Third time lucky, I finally passed.

entries.use: The stock complaint about pay, bonuses, pensions or interest: boonasu wa suzume no namida hodo. Said about money, not other small amounts.

example.romaji: boonasu, suzume no namida datta yo
example.ja: ボーナス、雀の涙だったよ
example.english: My bonus was a pittance.

examplePolite.romaji: boonasu wa suzume no namida deshita
examplePolite.ja: ボーナスは雀の涙でした
examplePolite.english: The bonus was next to nothing.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: hon no sukoshi (just a tiny bit).

entries.use: Almost always hotobori ga sameru made (until it blows over), about lying low after a scandal, a fight or a gaffe.

example.romaji: hotobori ga sameru made, shibaraku otonashiku shitoko
example.ja: ほとぼりが冷めるまで、しばらくおとなしくしとこ
example.english: Let's keep a low profile till it blows over.

examplePolite.romaji: hotobori ga sameru made matta hou ga ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: ほとぼりが冷めるまで待った方がいいですよ
examplePolite.english: Better wait until it blows over.

entries.english: your own fault, you brought it on yourself
entries.literal: rust that came out of the blade itself
entries.use: A saying for trouble someone caused themselves, often said about yourself with a rueful laugh: mi kara deta sabi da ne. Softer and more self-aware than jigou jitoku.

example.romaji: maa, mi kara deta sabi da ne
example.ja: まあ、身から出た錆だね
example.english: Well, it's my own fault.

examplePolite.romaji: mi kara deta sabi desu kara, shikata arimasen
examplePolite.ja: 身から出た錆ですから、仕方ありません
examplePolite.english: It's my own fault, so there's nothing to be done.

entries.notes: Four-character twin: jigou jitoku.

entries.use: Said about a clumsy mistake that spoils something, mostly in the past and often about yourself: doji funda. In polite talk it's a self-deprecating admission: tonda doji o funde shimaimashita.

example.romaji: yabai, doji funda
example.ja: やばい、ドジ踏んだ
example.english: Ugh, I blew it.

examplePolite.romaji: tonda doji o funde shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: とんだドジを踏んでしまいました
examplePolite.english: I made a silly blunder.

entries.notes: Casual verb: dojiru (dojitta); a clumsy person is a doji.

entries.english: a godsend, just what you'd hoped for
entries.literal: not even (something) you'd dare wish for
entries.use: Almost always before a noun: negatte mo nai chansu / hanashi (a chance you couldn't have hoped for). Said when an offer or a bit of luck is better than you'd dared to hope.

example.romaji: sore, negatte mo nai chansu jan
example.ja: それ、願ってもないチャンスじゃん
example.english: That's the chance of a lifetime!

examplePolite.romaji: negatte mo nai ohanashi desu
examplePolite.ja: 願ってもないお話です
examplePolite.english: That's a wonderful offer.

entries.english: can't afford it, out of reach
entries.use: Said mostly while shopping or window-shopping: takakute te ga denai. It can also mean a task is beyond you (muzukashikute te ga denai). The positive te ga deru usually means 'lash out, start hitting'.

example.romaji: ii kedo, takakute te ga denai yo
example.ja: いいけど、高くて手が出ないよ
example.english: It's nice, but way out of my price range.

examplePolite.romaji: ii n desu kedo, takakute te ga demasen
examplePolite.ja: いいんですけど、高くて手が出ません
examplePolite.english: It's nice, but it's too expensive for me.

entries.notes: Plain alternative: takakute kaenai (too expensive to buy).

entries.english: take proper responsibility; draw a clear line
entries.use: Two everyday uses: owning up to a mess properly, often by apologising or resigning (kejime o tsukenai to), and keeping things clearly apart, like work and private life (kouji no kejime). keri o tsukeru ends a matter; kejime is about doing it properly.

example.romaji: kono ken wa chanto kejime tsukenai to
example.ja: この件はちゃんとけじめつけないと
example.english: I need to take proper responsibility for this.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ken wa kichinto kejime o tsukemasu
examplePolite.ja: この件はきちんとけじめをつけます
examplePolite.english: I'll take proper responsibility for this matter.

entries.notes: kouji no kejime: keeping work and private life apart.

entries.english: an offer too good to be true
entries.use: Said about deals, jobs and investments that sound suspicious, nearly always with doubt: sonna umai hanashi aru wake nai (there's no way that's real), or umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (every sweet deal has a catch).

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, aru wake nai jan
example.ja: そんなうまい話、あるわけないじゃん
example.english: There's no way a deal that good is real.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa nai to omoimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話はないと思いますよ
examplePolite.english: I doubt a deal that good really exists.

entries.notes: Saying: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (a sweet deal always has a catch).

entries.english: end up the loser, get nothing for your trouble
entries.use: Said when doing the right or trusting thing leaves you worse off: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru (those who play it straight lose out). Don't confuse it with baka ni suru (make fun of) or baka ni naranai (costs add up).

example.romaji: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru n da yo ne
example.ja: 真面目にやった方がバカを見るんだよね
example.english: The ones who play it straight always lose out.

examplePolite.romaji: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru n desu yo ne
examplePolite.ja: 真面目にやった方がバカを見るんですよね
examplePolite.english: Those who do things properly end up losing out.

entries.notes: Saying: shoujikimono ga baka o miru (honesty doesn't pay).

entries.english: be on a roll; ride a trend
entries.use: Said of a team, a business or a person on a good run, usually nami ni notteru, or of catching a trend: jidai no nami ni noru. Unlike choushi ni noru, it's praise.

example.romaji: ano chiimu, ima nami ni notteru ne
example.ja: あのチーム、今波に乗ってるね
example.english: That team's on a roll right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ano chiimu wa ima nami ni notte imasu ne
examplePolite.ja: あのチームは今波に乗っていますね
examplePolite.english: That team is really on a roll at the moment.

entries.notes: Literal twin: riding an actual wave.

blocks.label: Enough already
blocks.rationale: Snapping at someone who has gone too far, the most common mood phrases of the topic.
blocks.interference: ii kagen ni shite (stop it) and katte ni shite (go ahead then) share the 'ni shite' ending but mean nearly opposite things.

blocks.label: Losing your temper
blocks.rationale: Getting angry, from the everyday hara ga tatsu to the sharper onomatopoeic flare-ups.
blocks.interference: atama ni kuru and kachin to kuru both end in kuru; katto naru and kachin to kuru are both sound-word anger.

blocks.label: Change of heart
blocks.rationale: Your mind shifting: changing it, getting ready, resetting, or a sudden lapse.
blocks.interference: kimochi o kirikaeru and shinki itten are near-synonyms for a fresh start; ki ga kawaru is changing a decision, not resetting your mood.

blocks.label: Shocked and spooked
blocks.rationale: Reactions to a fright or a shock: creeped out, scared, mind blank, dumbfounded.
blocks.interference: kimi ga warui and shinzou ni warui both end in warui (creepy vs. nerve-racking); kimi ga warui also echoes kimari ga warui in Caught out.

blocks.label: Feeling better
blocks.rationale: Tension or gloom leaving: satisfied, at ease, cheered up, distracted, unburdened.
blocks.interference: Four 'ki ga' frames that all mean feeling better; ki ga sumu sounds close to ki ga susumanai in Not in the mood.

blocks.label: Not in the mood
blocks.rationale: How keen you are to do something, with ki ga muku as the positive counterpart.
blocks.interference: Five 'ki ga' frames: susumanai (not keen), noranai (not in the mood), muku (feel like it), hikeru (feel bad doing it), omoi (dread).

blocks.label: Spite and jealousy
blocks.rationale: Petty feelings toward others: dislike, gloating, lashing out, jealousy.
blocks.interference: zamaa miro (rude) and ii kimi (milder) mean the same thing; the kimi in ii kimi is 'feeling', the same word as in kimi ga warui.

blocks.label: Cool it
blocks.rationale: What you say to someone who is heated or tense.
blocks.interference: atama o hiyasu (cool your head) against atama ni kuru (get mad); kata no chikara o nuku (relax) against kata no ni ga oriru (relieved) in Feeling better.

blocks.label: At wits' end
blocks.rationale: Fed up or out of options: going crazy, at a loss, reckless, stifled, sick of it.
blocks.interference: yake (reckless) and iyake (fed up) sound alike; ki ga kuruisou, iki ga tsumaru and iyake ga sasu all mean fed up.

blocks.label: Down and worried
blocks.rationale: Low, discouraged or anxious states.
blocks.interference: ki ga meiru and ki o otosu are both feeling down; ki ni yamu shares the 'ki ni' frame with ki ni kuwanai; ki ga ki ja nai and munasawagi ga suru are both worry.

blocks.label: Caught out
blocks.rationale: Being exposed: it shows on your face, sheepish, a truth that stings, wanting to vanish.
blocks.interference: kimari ga warui sounds close to kimi ga warui; mimi ga itai is easy to confuse with mune ga itamu in Heartfelt.

blocks.label: Heartfelt
blocks.rationale: Being deeply moved: heartache, pride in someone, being moved, overflowing emotion.
blocks.interference: mune ga itamu (it pains me) and mune ga ippai (overwhelmed) both use the chest; gutto kuru echoes kachin to kuru.

blocks.label: Smart or crazy
blocks.rationale: What someone's head is like: off its hinges, sharp, quick, quick to pick things up.
blocks.interference: atama ga kireru (sharp) vs plain kireru (snap, lose it); atama no kaiten ga hayai vs nomikomi ga hayai, both 'ga hayai' (fast thinker vs fast learner).

blocks.label: Immature
blocks.rationale: Faults you scold someone for: selfish, childish for their age, dithering, quitting after three days.
blocks.interference: ii toshi shite vs ii kagen ni shite: both scolding lines that start with ii.

blocks.label: Kind or nasty
blocks.rationale: Good or bad toward others: thoughtful, trusting, genuinely nasty, teasingly mean.
blocks.interference: hito ga ii / hito ga warui are not opposites: warui is a teasing 'that's mean', while tachi ga warui is truly nasty; ki ga kiku vs the literal ki ga tsuku (notice).

blocks.label: Skill and judgement
blocks.rationale: How capable someone is: skilled hands, shrewd, a poor judge, savvy.
blocks.interference: nukeme ga nai (shrewd, praise) vs miru me ga nai (poor judge, criticism): same 'ga nai' shape, opposite tone; youryou ga ii can hint at cutting corners, unlike ude ga ii.

blocks.label: Talk and secrets
blocks.rationale: The kuchi set: all talk, keeps secrets, sharp-tongued, blabs, smooth talker.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga katai (discreet) vs kuchi ga karui (blabs) sound alike; kuchi ga warui (blunt) vs kuchi ga umai (flattering); kuchi ni au (taste) sits in another block.

blocks.label: In a group
blocks.rationale: What someone is like with others: the generous one, the loner, the fun one, the carer.
blocks.interference: kimae ga ii, nori ga ii, mendoumi ga ii: three 'ga ii' praises (generous vs game vs caring).

blocks.label: Stubborn
blocks.rationale: Won't bend: rigid thinking, won't listen, proud, won't let go, won't admit defeat.
blocks.interference: atama ga katai (rigid) vs kuchi ga katai (discreet); akirame ga warui (can't let go) vs oujougiwa ga warui (won't concede); iji o haru vs mie o haru.

blocks.label: Tastes and likeness
blocks.rationale: What suits whom and who is alike: suits one's nature or palate, birds of a feather, identical, everyone differs.
blocks.interference: shou ni au (suits one's nature) vs kuchi ni au (suits one's palate): same 'ni au'.

blocks.label: Temper
blocks.rationale: The ki ga set for temperament: feisty, short-tempered, timid, hasty, plus caving under pressure.
blocks.interference: ki ga hayai (jumping the gun) vs ki ga mijikai (impatient); ki ga yowai (timid) vs oshi ni yowai (caves when pushed); ki ga tsuyoi vs ki ga yowai.

blocks.label: Hidden side
blocks.rationale: The person behind the surface: scheming, not as they look, transformed, faking sweetness, good at heart.
blocks.interference: hara ga kuroi (secretly scheming) vs neko o kaburu (faking innocence); ne wa ii vs hito ga ii.

blocks.label: Big or petty
blocks.rationale: Ego: condescending, big-hearted, humble, showing off, small-minded.
blocks.interference: ue kara mesen vs koshi ga hikui (high gaze vs low hips); kokoro ga hiroi vs utsuwa ga chiisai (opposites with different nouns); mie o haru vs iji o haru.

changelog.change: Added 18 idioms the user asked for ("could we get more"), which overrides the computed task's 'never add items'. All 4 reviewers flagged the topic as thin. Every addition uses an existing candidate id, has a corpus count I checked myself, and was recommended by at least one reviewer, most by several: kuchi-dake (31 + 39 for kuchi bakkari/kuchisaki dake), kuchi-ga-katai (26), kuchi-ga-karui (5; kept with katai as a natural pair), kuchi-ga-warui (23+), kuchi-ga-umai (16), kuchi-ni-au (19; the collocation list's cuts sent it here as 'very common'), ippiki-ookami (68), kiku-mimi-o-motanai (38), nukeme-ga-nai (46), atama-ga-kireru (35), kokoro-ga-hiroi (22), hito-ga-kawaru (23), yuuzuu-ga-kikanai (11), ki-ga-hayai (10), oujougiwa-ga-warui (9), mie-o-haru (6+), nomikomi-ga-hayai (5), utsuwa-ga-chiisai (7). Left out: sama-ni-naru, because almost all of its 131 hits are 様に = 'you ni' or 王様/神様; seken-shirazu and hanashi-ga-wakaru, which are not in the candidate pool. kuchi-ga-katai/karui, kuchi-ni-au and kiku-mimi-o-motanai may also sit in the talk or relations drafts; the cross-topic consistency pass removes any duplicate.

Rebuilt contrast groups around the additions: kuchi (kuchi dake / katai / karui / warui / umai), sharp (atama ga kireru, atama no kaiten ga hayai, nomikomi ga hayai), good-at (ude ga ii, youryou ga ii, nukeme ga nai), stubborn (atama ga katai, iji o haru, yuuzuu ga kikanai, kiku mimi o motanai), not-letting-go (akirame ga warui, oujougiwa ga warui), big-or-petty (kokoro ga hiroi, utsuwa ga chiisai), fit-au (shou ni au, kuchi ni au), temperament now includes ki ga hayai.

Headword is now haraguroi (腹黒い / はらぐろい, polite haraguroi desu), because 腹が黒 gets 0 hits and the fused form gets 24 (all 4 reviewers). noun, particle and verb fields set to null; literal 'black-bellied'. use rewritten to say the full form is hardly ever said; notes reduced to the noun haraguro. Slug kept.

use no longer says 'nearly always n ja nai with ga dropped' (corpus: 121 with ga, 71 without) and now covers talking about a third person. englishIdiom 'have a screw loose' set to null (tone mismatch). One-member contrastGroup 'crazy' set to null.

english changed to 'nasty, vicious, hard to deal with' (dropped 'worse than it looks'). use adds the mean-drunk case (nomu to tachi ga warui). alsoIn changed to seikaku ga warui. commonness raised to 4 (about 60 genuine hits once 私たちが悪い is excluded).
english changed to 'rigid, inflexible in one's thinking'. use adds the teasing case of someone stuck on a riddle.

blocks.label: Lending a hand
blocks.rationale: Offering and giving help, from a quick hand to joining forces and going to great trouble.
blocks.interference: te o kasu (lend a hand) vs chikara o kasu (lend your support) share kasu, and chikara ni naru (be a help) vs chikara o awaseru (join forces) share chikara, so drill the verb as well as the noun.

blocks.label: Dealing with people
blocks.rationale: How you treat someone: do what they say, take them on, speak to them, count on them.
blocks.interference: iu koto o kiku (obey) vs kuchi o kiku (be on speaking terms) both end in kiku; aite ni suru (take on / bother with) vs ate ni suru (count on) differ by one sound.

blocks.label: Butting in
blocks.rationale: Getting your hand, mouth or neck into someone else's business, plus the retort to it.
blocks.interference: te o dasu (lay a finger on) vs kuchi o dasu (butt in) swap only the body part; kuchi o dasu vs kubi o tsukkomu are near-synonyms; kao o dasu (show up) is in the get-together block.

blocks.label: Owing favours
blocks.rationale: What people say when favours are owed, asked for, accepted and repaid.
blocks.interference: kari ga aru (I owe you one) is a debt to settle, while on ni kiru (I'm deeply grateful) is thanks; okotoba ni amaete accepts an offer, and isshou no onegai is the begging ask.

blocks.label: Having someone's back
blocks.rationale: Caring about someone, taking their side and urging them on.
blocks.interference: ki ni kakeru (look out for) sounds like the versatility list's ki ni suru / ki ni naru; kata o motsu (take their side) vs senaka o osu (push them to go for it).

blocks.label: Being a burden
blocks.rationale: Being the one who holds others back, or the one who has to put up with it.
blocks.interference: ashi o hipparu (drag down) vs ashidematoi ni naru (be dead weight) both involve legs; sewa ga yakeru describes the handful, and shirinugui o suru is what the person cleaning up does.

blocks.label: Squaring up
blocks.rationale: Lines for picking fights, brushing people off and calling both sides out.
blocks.interference: teki ni mawasu (make an enemy of) vs kenka o uru (pick a fight); shitta kotcha nai and nanisama no tsumori are rough, so keep them casual-only.

blocks.label: Clicking and fancying
blocks.rationale: Whether two people get on, and whether someone is into you.
blocks.interference: ki ga au (get along) vs ki ga aru (fancy someone) differ by one sound; ki o hiku (try to catch their eye) is the action and myaku ga aru (there's a chance) is the sign.

blocks.label: At a get-together
blocks.rationale: Showing up to a gathering, dampening the mood and wrapping it up.
blocks.interference: kao o dasu (show up) vs te o dasu / kuchi o dasu in Butting in; mizu o sasu (spoil the mood) vs mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) share mizu.

blocks.label: Letting things go
blocks.rationale: Forgiving, overlooking or holding a grudge after a falling-out.
blocks.interference: mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) vs nakatta koto ni suru (pretend it never happened) vs oome ni miru (let it slide); ne ni motsu is the opposite.

blocks.label: Reading people
blocks.rationale: Sensing what others feel or want without being told.
blocks.interference: kuuki o yomu (read the room) vs kaoiro o ukagau (anxiously watch one person's mood); aite no mi ni naru is empathy, while ishin denshin is understanding each other without words.

blocks.label: Taking offense
blocks.rationale: Upsetting people or being upset by them.
blocks.interference: ki o waruku suru (you take offense) vs ki ni sawaru (something grates on you): they differ in who is affected; don't merge ki ni sawaru with the list's ki ni suru / ki ni naru.

blocks.label: Who you know
blocks.rationale: Ties, networks and the small-world sayings.
blocks.interference: en o kiru (cut ties) vs en ga aru (be meant to be) share en; kao ga hiroi (know lots of people) isn't one of the kao idioms in Face and flattery.

blocks.label: Close and distant
blocks.rationale: Who is inside your circle and how far you let them in.
blocks.interference: aka no tanin (a complete stranger) vs tanin gyougi (too formal with someone close) share tanin; kaya no soto (out of the loop) vs yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi (our family's way).

blocks.label: Couples
blocks.rationale: Romantic relationships, from crossing the line to bickering like an old married couple.
blocks.interference: yori o modosu (get back together) vs futamata o kakeru (two-time); kenka suru hodo naka ga ii vs kenka o uru (pick a fight) in Squaring up.

blocks.label: Face and flattery
blocks.rationale: Keeping people sweet, and saving or losing face.
blocks.interference: ii kao o suru (play nice / disapprove), kao o tateru (let them save face) and kao o tsubusu (embarrass them) all use kao; goma o suru (suck up) vs kigen o toru (humour someone).

All four reviewers found the topic thin: 38 after the cuts, from the largest pool (157), with face and trust nearly empty. The additions are chosen by commonness, and every slug is an existing candidate id. High corpus counts: ki ni kakeru 274, chikara o kasu 204, chikara o awaseru 129, shitta kotcha nai 124, kokoro o hiraku 110, ki o hiku 78, otagaisama 74, issen o koeru 70, hone o oru 58, en o kiru 56, on ni kiru 52, aite no mi ni naru 51, teki ni mawasu 50, ohiraki ni suru 41, shirinugui o suru 37, en ga aru 25. Everyday idioms the film corpus undercounts: sewa ga yakeru, uma ga au, kao o tateru, kao o tsubusu, myaku ga aru, isshou no onegai, kaya no soto, tanin gyougi, uramikko nashi, dotchi mo dotchi, atama ga agaranai, kaoiro o ukagau, kado ga tatsu, ii kao o suru, mizu o sasu. Spoken sayings: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii, yoso wa yoso uchi wa uchi, rui wa tomo o yobu. None is in the collocation list or another topic's final selection. Topic is now 72.

Reordered most common first (commonness, then count), as the form reviewer asked: nanisama no tsumori and ashidematoi ni naru come up from the bottom, ki ga aru and ne ni motsu go above lower-count items, and ishin denshin is last.

blocks.label: Saying it
blocks.rationale: The core 'say it' idioms: putting something into words, plus 'needless to say'.
blocks.interference: kuchi ni suru and kuchi ni dasu both mean say aloud; kuchi ni suru can also mean eat or drink in formal speech, and kuchi ni dasu stresses voicing what was held inside.

blocks.label: Hearing
blocks.rationale: The mimi idioms for hearing, listening and disbelief.
blocks.interference: mimi ni suru = you hear it, mimi ni hairu = word reaches you, komimi ni hasamu = catch it in passing; mimi o kasu is listening, and is mostly said in the negative.

blocks.label: About the talk
blocks.rationale: Five fixed hanashi remarks about where a discussion stands.
blocks.interference: hanashi ga chigau (not what we agreed) vs hanashi wa betsu (a separate matter); hanashi ga hayai (that's easy) vs hanashi ga mienai (I'm lost).

blocks.label: Secrets
blocks.rationale: Sharing and keeping things quiet, and gossip that gets out.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga katai and kuchi ga karui are opposites; kuchi ga suberu is a one-off slip, while kuchi ga karui is a trait.

blocks.label: Look who's talking
blocks.rationale: Calling out hypocrisy or nerve, and admitting your own.
blocks.interference: yoku iu yo and kotchi no serifu jab the other person, hito no koto ienai turns it on yourself, and tana ni ageru describes the hypocrisy.

blocks.label: Straight talk
blocks.rationale: Talking directly: face to face, frankly, to the point, settling it.
blocks.interference: hara o watte hanasu (open up honestly) vs hanashi o tsukeru (settle a matter); tantou chokunyuu = get to the point, men to mukatte = to someone's face.

blocks.label: Wrong words
blocks.rationale: Things that should not have been said, and the replies that shut them down.
blocks.interference: baka iwanaide (nonsense) vs engi demo nai (don't jinx it); jirai o fumu (hit a nerve by accident) vs kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu (say what you don't mean, usually in anger).

blocks.label: Conversation flow
blocks.rationale: Moving a conversation along or interrupting it.
blocks.interference: kuchi o hasamu (butt in) vs hanashi no koshi o oru (derail someone mid-story).

blocks.label: Big talk
blocks.rationale: Boasting and blowing things up.
blocks.interference: kuchi dake (all talk, no action) vs ooguchi o tataku (brag about what you'll do) vs hanashi o moru (pad out a story).

blocks.label: Spill or stay silent
blocks.rationale: Confessing versus stonewalling, then the never-tell vows.
blocks.interference: kuchi o waru (finally talk) vs shira o kiru (play dumb); hakaba made motte iku keeps a secret for life, while kuchi ga sakete mo ienai refuses ever to say it.

blocks.label: Warned you
blocks.rationale: Warning ahead, telling someone again and again, and 'I told you so' afterwards.
blocks.interference: nen o osu (remind to make sure) vs kugi o sasu (stern warning in advance); mimi ni tako ga dekiru is the listener's complaint, kuchi o suppaku shite iu is the speaker's.

blocks.label: Sharp tongue
blocks.rationale: Harsh speech and fault-finding.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga warui (a harsh tongue, as a trait) vs hitokoto ooi (one remark too many) vs kechi o tsukeru (pick holes in something); not the single word kechi (stingy).

blocks.label: Lies
blocks.rationale: Outright lies, fudging, white lies and groundless rumours.
blocks.interference: makka na uso (a flat lie) vs ne mo ha mo nai (a baseless rumour); saba o yomu fudges a number, usually someone's age.

blocks.label: How you put it
blocks.rationale: How things are phrased: softened, spun, blunt, or not meant literally.
blocks.interference: oburaato ni tsutsumu (soften it) vs mi mo futa mo nai (brutally blunt); kotoba no aya (just a figure of speech) vs mono wa iiyou (it's all in how you put it).

blocks.label: Comebacks
blocks.rationale: Winning and losing the verbal exchange.
blocks.interference: ippon torareta (you got me) vs guu no ne mo denai (left with nothing to say); aa ieba kou iu describes someone who always has a retort.

changelog.change: Added 25 items, going against the step's 'never add items' rule. The user's own request ('could we get more' sets; Japanese idioms whatever English has) overrides the script, and all four reviewers rated the topic thin as a major issue. Only talk candidates proposed by 2 or more reviewers were added, each under its candidate id, so merge.py picks up its measured count and drops its cut verdict. None of them is in another topic's final selection (checked against final_compact.json) or in the collocation list. Counts were re-run with count_cli.py: hara-o-watte-hanasu 36, hanashi-o-tsukeru 75, mimi-ni-hairu 49, kotoba-no-aya 23, engi-demo-nai 10, shira-o-kiru 15, ma-ga-motanai 0 (under-counted casual talk), ooguchi-o-tataku 22, ii-dokyou-shiteru 22, hakaba-made-motte-iku 7, komimi-ni-hasamu 19, kokoro-ni-mo-nai 12, jirai-o-fumu 12, hanashi-ga-mienai 8, kuchi-o-waru 103, hanashi-o-awaseru 10, ippon-torareta 7, mono-wa-iiyou 2, baka-iwanaide 154 (all baka iu forms), hanashi-no-koshi-o-oru 2, kechi-o-tsukeru 22, ne-mo-ha-mo-nai 2, kuchi-ga-sakete-mo-ienai 3, kuchi-ni-suru 196, mimi-o-utagau 6. New groups: big-talk (kuchi-dake, ooguchi-o-tataku), talking-it-out, said-the-wrong-thing, dont-say-that, spill-or-stonewall, never-tell, keeping-it-going. mimi-hear-listen gains mimi-ni-hairu and komimi-ni-hasamu.

dropped.reason: Two reviewers (meaning, register) cut it. It's a literal collocation: sorasu just means 'divert', and it's the transitive twin of hanashi ga soreru, which is already in 21-list-collocations.

blocks.label: Giving it everything
blocks.rationale: Four ways to say you are putting everything into something, from the everyday isshou kenmei to the dramatic shinu ki de.
blocks.interference: kiai o ireru (fire yourself up) and ki o nuku (ease off) are near-opposites that both use ki; shinu ki de means resolve, not real danger.

blocks.label: Getting there
blocks.rationale: Getting started and making progress: warm to the idea, find you can do it if you try, pick up the skill, get the knack, and small amounts add up.
blocks.interference: sono ki ni naru (warm to the idea) is not ki ni naru (be on your mind); mi ni tsukeru also means to wear something.

blocks.label: Hard work
blocks.rationale: A lot of work, or work that takes real effort and care.
blocks.interference: te ga kakaru (needs a lot of looking after) and te ga konde iru (made with real care) both use te ga; hone ga oreru can also mean a bone literally breaks.

blocks.label: Too much
blocks.rationale: Something is beyond you: out of control, you give up, it's too daunting or too heavy, or you're no match for it.
blocks.interference: ha ga tatanai and tachiuchi dekinai both mean 'no match' (teeth won't sink in, can't cross swords); te ni oenai (out of control) is easy to mix up with te ga mawaranai (no time to get to it).

blocks.label: Pacing the work
blocks.rationale: Timing a task: stall for time, make a start, take a breather, find there's no end to it, reach a good place to stop.
blocks.interference: kiri ga nai (no end to it) and kiri ga ii (a good place to stop) differ by one word; te o tsukeru (start on it) can be confused with te o nuku (cut corners).

blocks.label: Quick and easy
blocks.rationale: No trouble at all: over in a flash, happy to do it, easy.
blocks.interference: oyasui goyou answers a favour someone asks you, while asameshi mae describes how easy a task is.

blocks.label: Hands full
blocks.rationale: The te ga set for being busy: tied up, at capacity, can't get to it, and the opposite, free for a moment.
blocks.interference: te ga aku (free) and te ga hanasenai (tied up) are opposites in the same te ga frame; te ippai sounds a lot like te ni oenai.

blocks.label: Slacking off
blocks.rationale: Not giving it full effort: ease off, leave it half-done, cut corners.
blocks.interference: te o nuku (cut corners on the work) and ki o nuku (let your guard down) differ only in te vs ki.

blocks.label: Swamped
blocks.rationale: Being overloaded: no time for that, a deadline looming, so busy your head spins, can't keep it up, desperate for any help.
blocks.interference: me ga mawaru can also mean you are literally dizzy; neko no te mo karitai overlaps with te ippai (hands full).

blocks.label: Losing heart
blocks.rationale: Running out of will: you hit a wall, lose the will to go on, say you can't take it.
blocks.interference: kokoro ga oreru (lose the will) and hone ga oreru (be hard work) share oreru but mean different things.

blocks.label: Having an idea
blocks.rationale: Knowing or not knowing who, why or what, and denying it, all at the top of the counts (357, 251).
blocks.interference: kentou mo tsukanai (no guess at all) and kokoroatari ga nai (nothing comes to mind) both mean 'no idea'; mi ni oboe ga nai means 'I didn't do it', not 'I don't know'.

blocks.label: Eyes glued
blocks.rationale: Keeping your eyes on someone, or being unable to look away.
blocks.interference: me o hanasu (take your eyes off, usually 'me o hanasu na') and me ga hanasenai (can't take them off): the switch from o to ga flips who is in control.

blocks.label: Not yourself
blocks.rationale: Someone acting out of character, and the 'snap out of it' answer.
blocks.interference: dou ka shiteru (you're out of your mind) vs dou iu kaze no fukimawashi (what's got into you, said of unusual kindness); ki ga shirenai says you can't read them, not that they're mad.

blocks.label: Doesn't add up
blocks.rationale: Judging whether something makes sense, from 'baffling' to 'logical but it won't sit right'.
blocks.interference: suji ga tooru (it holds together) is the positive of tsujitsuma ga awanai; fu ni ochinai is a feeling that persists even when the logic works; wake ga wakaranai vs nani ga nan da ka wakaranai (lost about what is going on).

blocks.label: Paying close attention
blocks.rationale: Careful attention: looking things over, minding others, double-checking.
blocks.interference: ki o kubaru (be attentive to others, a compliment) vs ki o mawasu (overthink, read too much into things): same ki o + verb frame.

blocks.label: Looking away
blocks.rationale: Choosing not to see something, plus missing what's right under your nose.
blocks.interference: me o tsuburu (overlook it, let it slide) vs me o somukeru (refuse to face it) vs mite minu furi (pretend you didn't see it).

blocks.label: On your mind
blocks.rationale: Something you can't stop thinking about, from mild worry to total preoccupation.
blocks.interference: atama kara hanarenai and atama ga ippai are both 'preoccupied'; ki ni kakaru is a gentler nagging worry and is easy to blur with ki ni naru from the versatility list.

blocks.label: Catching the eye
blocks.rationale: Things that draw the eye, and setting your sights on someone.
blocks.interference: me ni tsuku (it catches your eye) vs me o tsukeru (you single someone out): the particle flips who is acting; me o hiku (deliberately eye-catching) vs me ga iku (your gaze drifts to it).

blocks.label: Distracted
blocks.rationale: A wandering mind, from being scattered to being miles away.
blocks.interference: ki ga chiru (scattered by your surroundings) vs ki o torareru (pulled away by one thing); uwa no sora and kokoro koko ni arazu both mean 'miles away'.

blocks.label: Taking it lightly
blocks.rationale: Underrating a person or a problem.
blocks.interference: amaku miru (underestimate someone) vs kangae ga amai (your own thinking is naive): both are built on amai.

blocks.label: Hunches and surprises
blocks.rationale: Feelings about what's coming: it's nothing, a premonition, never saw it coming, a revelation.
blocks.interference: ki no sei (it's just your imagination) vs mushi no shirase (a feeling that turned out right); omoi mo yoranai and yume ni mo omowanai both mean 'never imagined'.

blocks.label: Comes to mind
blocks.rationale: Ideas and pictures surfacing, or nearly surfacing.
blocks.interference: atama ni ukabu (an idea comes to mind) vs me ni ukabu (you can picture it); pin to kuru means it clicks or rings a bell.

blocks.label: Fair point
blocks.rationale: Conceding that someone's reaction or view makes sense.
blocks.interference: muri mo nai (no wonder, understandable) vs ichiri aru (you have a point); ii sen itteru means close to the right answer, not agreement.

blocks.label: Believing it
blocks.rationale: How much of what you hear you believe, from taking it as true to not falling for it.
blocks.interference: ma ni ukeru (take it seriously) vs unomi ni suru (swallow it gullibly); hanshin hangi (half believing) vs hanashi hanbun ni kiku (take it with a pinch of salt).

blocks.label: Obvious or hidden
blocks.rationale: Things in plain sight vs things below the surface.
blocks.interference: me ni mieteru (the outcome is predictable) vs ichimoku ryouzen (clear at a glance) vs kao ni kaite aru (your feelings show); ura ga aru (a hidden catch, negative) vs oku ga fukai (hidden depth, positive).

blocks.label: Can't resist
blocks.rationale: Desire and temptation pulling at your attention.
blocks.interference: me ga nai (be crazy about it, fondly) vs me ga kuramu (be blinded by greed): both start me ga; me no doku is a temptation better left unseen.

blocks.label: Taking it in
blocks.rationale: Whether information sinks in or the head won't work.
blocks.interference: atama ni ireru (make sure you take it in) vs atama ni hairanai (it won't go in); migi kara hidari means in one ear and out the other.

blocks.label: Gains and windfalls
blocks.rationale: Ways something good comes your way, from simply getting it to unexpected luck.
blocks.interference: te ni ireru (you get it) vs te ni hairu (it comes to you) is a transitive/intransitive pair; tanabota is unearned luck, negatte mo nai is a chance you'd hoped for.

blocks.label: A rough time
blocks.rationale: Going through something bad, from a bad experience to one blow after another.
blocks.interference: hidoi me ni au (an awful time) vs itai me ni au (paying for a mistake); ma ga warui (bad timing, 間) vs ma ga sashita (a lapse, 魔) in Getting carried away.

blocks.label: Losing the job
blocks.rationale: Being fired, firing someone, or leaving a line of work.
blocks.interference: kubi ni naru (you get fired) vs kubi ni suru (you fire someone); kubi ga tobu ties the firing to a specific failure; ashi o arau is quitting by choice, not being fired.

blocks.label: Making a move
blocks.rationale: Moves and timing from go and shogi: acting, having no other option, getting in first or being beaten to it.
blocks.interference: te o utsu (take action, settle for) vs sente o utsu (move first); saki o kosareru is being on the losing side of sente o utsu.

blocks.label: The short end
blocks.rationale: Ending up with something unfair: a chore you didn't want, the blame, the losing side, the worst lot.
blocks.interference: hame ni naru (being stuck doing something) vs hame o hazusu (letting loose), which share the word hame; baka o miru (end up the loser) vs baka ni naranai (costs add up).

blocks.label: Serves you right
blocks.rationale: Bad outcomes you caused yourself, and paying for them.
blocks.interference: jigou jitoku and mi kara deta sabi both mean it's your own fault; tsuke ga mawatte kuru is old habits catching up with you later; bachi ga ataru is punishment from heaven.

blocks.label: Closing the matter
blocks.rationale: Bringing a matter to an end: settling it, declaring it done, owning it, letting it die down.
blocks.interference: keri o tsukeru (finish it off) vs kejime o tsukeru (take responsibility or draw a line), which share o tsukeru; ikken rakuchaku is said once it's done.

blocks.label: Getting carried away
blocks.rationale: Losing your restraint: getting cocky, going overboard, getting full of yourself, a sudden lapse.
blocks.interference: choushi ni noru (getting cocky) vs nami ni noru and kidou ni noru (things going well), all built on noru; ma ga sashita (魔) vs ma ga warui (間).

blocks.label: Bound to happen
blocks.rationale: Remarks about what is sure to happen: only a matter of time, experts slip too, and what comes after two tries.
blocks.interference: nido aru koto wa sando aru (bad luck repeats) vs sandome no shoujiki (the third try works) make opposite predictions about the third time.

blocks.label: Whatever happens
blocks.rationale: Taking outcomes calmly, before or after they happen.
blocks.interference: sono toki wa sono toki (deal with it when it comes, before the fact) vs kekka oorai (it worked out, after the fact); naru you ni naru is a shrug, nagare ni makaseru is choosing to let go.

blocks.label: All for nothing
blocks.rationale: Effort or chances that are lost, and being too late to fix it.
blocks.interference: mizu no awa (effort comes to nothing) vs bou ni furu (you throw a chance away yourself); torikaeshi ga tsukanai (can't be undone) vs ato no matsuri (too late to act).

blocks.label: Taking a gamble
blocks.rationale: Taking a chance: trying with nothing to lose, betting everything, risky deals, offers that look too good.
blocks.interference: damemoto (low stakes, nothing to lose) vs ichi ka bachi ka (all or nothing); abunai hashi o wataru usually hints at something shady.

blocks.label: Backfires and blunders
blocks.rationale: Moves that go wrong: playing into their hands, giving yourself away, repeating a failure, slipping up.
blocks.interference: boketsu o horu (you give yourself away) vs urame ni deru (a plan has the opposite effect); omou tsubo is said from the winner's side; ni no mai is repeating someone else's mistake.

blocks.label: Close calls
blocks.rationale: Barely escaping harm, and the one lucky part of a bad situation.
blocks.interference: kiki ippatsu (a near disaster) vs kami hitoe (a razor-thin gap, often between winning and losing); inochibiroi suru is the verb for escaping.

blocks.label: Progress and setbacks
blocks.rationale: How a project is going: back to the start, past the worst, on track, on a roll.
blocks.interference: furidashi ni modoru (being forced back to the start) vs ichi kara yarinaosu (choosing to start again); kidou ni noru (running smoothly) vs nami ni noru (on a roll).

blocks.label: Worth the money
blocks.rationale: Money and value: not worth it, costs adding up, can't afford it, getting your money back, a tiny amount.
blocks.interference: wari ni awanai (doesn't pay) vs moto o toru (get your money's worth); baka ni naranai vs baka o miru in The short end.

changelog.change: I added 30 idioms, taking the topic from 40 to 70. The fix-stage rule says never add items, but the relayed user request asks for more sets and for Japanese idioms whether or not English has one, and that request wins. Criterion for adding: two or more of the four reviewers flagged the idiom as a common one that was missing, and it is a fortune-category id in candidates.tsv, so slugs, counts and cut rows still join in merge.py. Counts rechecked with count_cli.py. Not added: idioms outside the candidate pool (engi ga warui 24, un ga muite kuru 13, inga ouhou 14, kami nomi zo shiru 37; these have no candidate id) and pool idioms only one reviewer named (te ga todoku, hara o kukuru, mono wa tameshi, atatte kudakero, kan ippatsu, zettai zetsumei, te o yogosu, shippo o tsukamu, boro ga deru and others). If another topic also placed ii ki ni naru, the cross-topic consistency pass should drop one copy.
